jesus.bio: Jesus Christ, the Son of God made man, the heart of all Scripture. Born in Bethlehem, He announced the Kingdom, healed the sick, and gave His life on the cross for the forgiveness of our sins, before rising on the third day. All the Old Testament announces Him; all the New Testament reveals Him.
jesus.histoire:
Born in Bethlehem of the virgin Mary (Luke 2:7), Jesus grew up in Nazareth in the home of the carpenter Joseph (Matthew 2:23). At about thirty years old, He was baptized by John in the Jordan: the heavens opened and the Father declared Him His beloved Son (Matthew 3:17).

For three years, He traveled throughout Galilee and Judea: He taught about the Kingdom, healed the sick, cast out demons, and forgave sins (Matthew 4:23). He chose twelve apostles to be with Him (Mark 3:14), fed the multitudes (John 6:11), walked on the sea (Matthew 14:25), and raised His friend Lazarus (John 11:43).

Betrayed by Judas, denied by Peter, condemned under Pontius Pilate, He was crucified at Golgotha where He bore the sin of the world (Luke 23:33). On the third day, the tomb was empty: He rose again (Luke 24:6). After forty days, He ascended into heaven (Acts 1:9)—and He will return to gather His own (Revelation 22:20).

parcours.d: The manger: "A Savior is born to you"
Flight from Herod
30 hidden years: the carpenter
The baptism: "This is My beloved Son"
40 days, three temptations, zero defeats
First miracle: water turned to wine
"His city": teachings, miracles, the Twelve
The Samaritan woman at the well: living water
"You are the Christ"—Peter's confession
His face shone like the sun
Lazarus awakened: "I am the Resurrection"
Bartimaeus healed, Zacchaeus transformed
"Not My will, but Yours be done"
The cross—"It is finished"—and the empty tomb
The Ascension: "I am with you always"

adam.bio: The first man, formed from the dust and animated by the breath of God. Placed in Eden to cultivate and keep the garden, he disobeyed with Eve—and through him sin entered the world, which the "last Adam," Jesus, came to redeem.
adam.histoire:
Formed from the dust of the ground, Adam receives the breath of life from God Himself (Genesis 2:7). Placed in the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it, he names the animals and receives the woman taken from his side: "bone of my bones, flesh of my flesh" (Genesis 2:23).

Through his disobedience—the fruit of the forbidden tree—sin enters the world, and death through sin (Genesis 3:6). But from the fall itself, God announces the victory of the woman's offspring over the serpent (Genesis 3:15).

Paul makes Adam the inverse figure of Christ: "For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive" (1 Corinthians 15:22). The first man foreshadows, in reverse, the last Adam.

eve.bio: The first woman, "mother of all living," created by God as a helper corresponding to Adam. Seduced by the serpent, she ate the forbidden fruit—yet from her offspring God promised the Savior who would crush the serpent's head.
eve.histoire:
Built by God from Adam's side, Eve is "the mother of all living" (Genesis 3:20). Seduced by the serpent—"Did God really say?" (Genesis 3:1)—she takes the fruit, gives it to her husband, and their eyes are opened to their nakedness.

But the promise spans the judgment: her offspring will crush the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15). At Cain's birth, she cries out, "I have acquired a man with the help of the Lord" (Genesis 4:1); after Abel's death, God grants her Seth, the line of promise (Genesis 4:25).

abraham.bio: The father of all believers. Called to leave his country on a simple promise, he trusted in the Lord, "and it was counted to him as righteousness." God made him a great nation and, through his descendants, the blessing of all the families of the earth.
abraham.histoire:
God calls Abram to leave Ur for a land He will show him, with an impossible promise: to make him a great nation (Genesis 12:1). Abram goes, not knowing where he is going — this is the foundational act of faith of the entire Bible (Hebrews 11:8).

God makes a covenant with him: his descendants will be like the stars of heaven. "Abram believed the Lord, and it was counted to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). Becoming Abraham, "father of a multitude," he receives at a hundred years old the son of promise, Isaac (Genesis 21:2).

On Mount Moriah, God tests his faith by asking him to offer Isaac; at the last moment, the Lord provides a ram Himself (Genesis 22:12) — a foreshadowing of Christ's sacrifice. Paul will make Abraham the father of all believers, justified by faith just as he was (Romans 4:16).

parcours.d: The call: "Go from your country"
Long stop; death of Terah, departure at 75 years old
First altar in Canaan: "I will give this land"
The famine, the lie about Sarah
Return to the altar; separation from Lot
The covenant, the stars, the three visitors
Birth of Isaac: the promised joy
The supreme test: "The Lord will provide"
Burial place of Sarah, then his own: died at 175 years old

sara.bio: Wife of Abraham, barren until age 90. She laughed when she heard the promise—then gave birth to Isaac, "the son of laughter," proof that nothing is too wonderful for the Lord.
sara.histoire:
Sarah followed Abraham through all his migrations, carrying with him the promise…and the long trial of barrenness. When three visitors announce that she will bear a child within a year, she laughs in secret—she is nearly ninety years old (Genesis 18:12).

But "is anything too hard for the Lord?" (Genesis 18:14). Sarah conceives and gives birth to Isaac, whose name means "he laughs": the laughter of disbelief becomes laughter of joy (Genesis 21:6). The New Testament cites her as an example of faith (Hebrews 11:11) and holds her up as mother to all women who hope in God (1 Peter 3:6).

isaac.bio: The son of promise, born to Abraham and Sarah in their old age. Offered on Mount Moriah and spared by God, he foreshadows the sacrifice of the only Son. Father of Esau and Jacob.
isaac.histoire:
Son of the miracle, born when Abraham was one hundred years old (Genesis 21:2), Isaac carries the promise from generation to generation. As a young man, he climbs Mount Moriah with his father, the wood of sacrifice on his shoulders — a striking foreshadowing of Christ bearing His cross (Genesis 22:6).

A man of peace, he digs again the wells of his father and yields before quarrels until God makes room for him (Genesis 26:22). He marries Rebekah, whom he loves (Genesis 24:67), and becomes father of twins: Esau and Jacob. It is through Jacob that the blessing will pass (Genesis 28:4) — God will now call Himself

jacob.bio: Son of Isaac, he obtained the birthright by deception and then encountered God at Bethel and wrestled with him at Peniel, where he received his new name: Israel. His twelve sons became the twelve tribes.
jacob.histoire:
Jacob was born holding his twin brother Esau's heel—quite the preview of things to come. He traded the birthright for a bowl of lentils (Genesis 25:33), then stole his father's blessing through deception (Genesis 27:19), and had to flee to his uncle Laban.

On the way, God revealed himself to him at Bethel: a ladder set between heaven and earth (Genesis 28:12). Twenty years later, at the ford of the Jabbok, a stranger wrestled with him until dawn; Jacob held on:

parcours.d: The birthright, the stolen blessing — the flight
The ladder: "I am with you, I will keep you"
20 years with Laban: Leah, Rachel, eleven sons
The night struggle: Jacob becomes Israel
Return to the altar of the beginning
The years of mourning: Joseph "devoured"
The reunion: "Joseph is still alive!"

joseph-at.bio: Sold by his brothers, slave then prisoner in Egypt, he was raised by God to the rank of governor to save his family from famine. "You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good."
joseph-at.histoire:
Jacob's favored son, Joseph receives the coat of many colors… and his brothers' jealousy. His dreams of greatness hasten his downfall: sold into slavery, brought down to Egypt (Genesis 37:28). There, everything he touches prospers, for the Lord is with him (Genesis 39:2) — until the false accusation of Potiphar's wife and imprisonment.

From prison to palace: Joseph interprets Pharaoh's dreams — seven fat cattle, seven lean cattle — and becomes governor of Egypt to prepare for the famine (Genesis 41:40). When his brothers come down seeking grain, they bow before him without recognizing him: the dreams are fulfilled.

His word of forgiveness is one of the heights of Scripture: "You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, to save the lives of many people" (Genesis 50:20). Joseph, betrayed then raised up to save his own, foreshadows Christ.

parcours.d: The dreams of the favored son — the coat
Sold by his brothers for twenty shekels
"The Lord was with him"; the accusation
The dreams of the cupbearer and the baker
The 7 cattle: governor at age 30
"You meant evil; God meant it for good"

moise.bio: Saved from the waters, called at the burning bush, he led Israel out of Egypt, opened the Red Sea, and received the Law at Sinai. The Lord spoke to him "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend."
moise.histoire:
Saved from the waters in a basket (Exodus 2:3), raised in Pharaoh's court, Moses flees to the desert after killing an Egyptian. There, at the burning bush, God calls him and reveals His name: "I AM WHO I AM" (Exodus 3:14).

Before Pharaoh, he brings the ten plagues, leads the Passover, and brings Israel out of Egypt; the Red Sea opens before his raised staff (Exodus 14:21). At Sinai, he receives the Law and the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:1) and speaks with God "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend" (Exodus 33:11).

For forty years, he carries a complaining people through the desert. He dies on Mount Nebo, in view of the promised land (Deuteronomy 34:5). On the mount of transfiguration, he appears at Jesus' side (Matthew 17:3)—the Law bearing witness to grace.

parcours.d: The basket on the Nile, Pharaoh's palace
Fugitive, shepherd, husband of Zipporah
"I AM WHO I AM": the calling
"Let my people go"; the Passover
The sea opens, the army swallowed up, the song
The law, the covenant, the tabernacle
38 years: the manna, water from the rock, intercession
The land seen from afar; death at 120 years old

ecrits.d: The five books of the law, foundation of all Scripture (Luke 24:27)
"Teach us to number our days aright"

aaron.bio: Moses' brother and his spokesman before Pharaoh, he became Israel's first high priest. His rod budded to confirm his calling—yet he also yielded to the people by crafting the golden calf.
aaron.histoire:
Moses' older brother and his spokesman before Pharaoh—"he shall be your mouth" (Exodus 4:16)—Aaron became Israel's first high priest, set apart with his sons to serve in the tabernacle (Exodus 28:1).

His ministry knew both shadow and light: it was he who fashioned the golden calf under the people's pressure (Exodus 32:4), yet it was also he who stood between the dead and the living, censer in hand, to stop the plague (Numbers 16:48). His rod budded in a single night, a sign of divine election (Numbers 17:8). The blessing he was commanded to pronounce still covers God's people: "The Lord bless you and keep you!" (Numbers 6:24).

josue.bio: Servant of Moses who became the conqueror of Canaan. Before Jericho as before every challenge, his strength rested on a single promise:
josue.histoire: A servant of Moses from his youth, Joshua was one of only two spies who believed God could give them the land (Numbers 14:8). After Moses' death, the Lord commissioned him:

parcours.d: Crossing on dry ground, twelve stones as a memorial
Seven times around, the trumpets, the walls fall
The defeat (Achan's sin), then the victory
"Sun, stand still!" — the long day of battle
"As for me and my household, we will serve the Lord"

caleb.bio: One of the twelve spies sent to Canaan — and one of only two who believed God would give the land. At 85 years old, still mighty, he claimed his mountain: "Perhaps the Lord will be with me."
caleb.histoire:
Of the twelve spies sent to Canaan, only Caleb and Joshua return full of faith: "Let us go up at once and take possession, for we are well able to overcome it!" (Numbers 13:30). Because of this trust, "because he has followed the Lord fully" (Numbers 14:24), he will enter the land when his entire generation falls in the wilderness.

Forty-five years later, at eighty-five years old, he claims his mountain — Hebron, held by giants: "I am still as strong today as I was the day Moses sent me" (Joshua 14:11). Caleb is the patron of all those who grow old without their faith aging a day.

debora.bio: A prophetess and judge of Israel, she administered justice under a palm tree and led Barak to victory against Sisera. Her famous song celebrates the Lord who fights for His people.
debora.histoire:
A prophetess, Deborah judged Israel under her palm tree, between Ramah and Bethel (Judges 4:5). When she conveys to Barak the Lord's command to face Sisera's army and his nine hundred iron chariots, he refuses to go without her: "If you will go with me, I will go" (Judges 4:8).

She goes up, and God puts the enemy army to flight at the Kishon Stream; the honor of victory belongs to women — Deborah, and Jael who strikes down Sisera (Judges 4:21). Her song is one of the oldest songs in the Bible: "So let all your enemies perish, O Lord!" (Judges 5:31).

gedeon.histoire: When the angel finds him, Gideon is threshing wheat in secret in a winepress, afraid of Midian—and hears himself greeted:

samson.bio: Dedicated to God from his mother's womb, equipped with supernatural strength, he judged Israel for twenty years. Betrayed by Delilah and deprived of his sight, he prayed one last time—and his death struck the Philistines more powerfully than his life.
samson.histoire:
Consecrated as a Nazirite from his mother's womb, announced by an angel (Judges 13:5), Samson received supernatural strength: he tore a lion apart with his bare hands (Judges 14:6), struck down a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone (Judges 15:15), and carried the gates of Gaza on his shoulders (Judges 16:3).

But the strong man was weak before Delilah: harassed, he revealed the secret of his hair; the Lord withdrew from him, and he did not know it (Judges 16:20). Blinded, chained, mocked in the temple of Dagon, he prayed one last time—"Remember me, I pray"—and his death struck the Philistines more powerfully than his life (Judges 16:30). Yet the epistle to the Hebrews counts him among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:32): grace writes straight with our crooked lines.

ruth.bio: A Moabite of faithful heart: "Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God." A gleaner in the fields of Boaz, she became his wife—and the great-grandmother of King David.
ruth.histoire:
A widow from Moab, a foreigner, Ruth chose to cling to Naomi her mother-in-law with words that have become immortal: "Your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:16).

In Bethlehem, she gleans in the field of Boaz, a relative of Naomi, who notices her and protects her (Ruth 2:12). Naomi guides her approach to him, and Boaz, as a "redeemer," marries her (Ruth 4:10): the foreigner fully enters the people of God.

Their son Obed will be the grandfather of David (Ruth 4:17)—and Ruth, one of four women named in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5). Grace knows no borders.

parcours.d: A widow, she chose Naomi: "Your people will be my people"
She gleans in the field of Boaz
The night of the redemption request
Wife of Boaz, mother of Obed, grandmother of David

booz.bio: A mighty and generous man of Bethlehem. By redeeming Ruth according to the law of redemption, he became an image of the Redeemer—the one who covers, protects, and restores.
booz.histoire:
A mighty and good man of Bethlehem, Boaz greets his harvesters with "The Lord be with you!" (Ruth 2:4)—the tone is set. He notices Ruth the gleaner, orders that grain be left for her, and blesses her courage (Ruth 2:16).

As a close relative, he accepts the right of redemption: he acquires Naomi's field and takes Ruth as his wife, to raise up the name of the deceased (Ruth 4:10). A figure of the "redeemer," Boaz foreshadows Christ who redeems His Bride. From his union with Ruth comes the royal line: Obed, Jesse, David (Ruth 4:22).

samuel.bio: Asked of God through Anne's tears, he heard the Lord call him from childhood: "Speak, for your servant is listening." The last judge and prophet, he anointed Israel's first two kings, Saul and then David.
samuel.histoire:
Son of Anne's prayer, consecrated to God from childhood, Samuel grew up at the sanctuary of Shiloh. One night, the Lord calls him by name; Eli whispers the answer to him: "Speak, for your servant is listening" (1 Samuel 3:10). None of his words will fall to the ground (1 Samuel 3:19).

Last of the judges and first of the great prophets, he leads Israel, and when the people demand a king "like all the nations," he anoints Saul reluctantly (1 Samuel 10:1). After Saul's rejection, God sends him to Bethlehem to Jesse: "The Lord does not look at what man looks at… the Lord looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). He anoints David, the youngest, among his brothers (1 Samuel 16:13).

saul-roi.bio: Israel's first king, taller than all the people—yet his heart did not follow. His disobedience cost him the throne: "Obedience is better than sacrifice."
saul-roi.histoire:
Israel's first king, handsome and a head taller than all the people (1 Samuel 9:2), Saul begins in humility—he is found hiding among the baggage on the day of his coronation (1 Samuel 10:22).

But power reveals his heart: he offers a sacrifice without the right to do so (1 Samuel 13:9), spares what God had condemned, and hears the verdict: "Obedience is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22). The Spirit withdraws; jealousy of David consumes him unto murderous madness (1 Samuel 18:9).

Abandoned by God, he ends up consulting a medium at En-dor (1 Samuel 28:7) and dies on Mount Gilboa with his sons (1 Samuel 31:4). His life is a solemn warning of a magnificent calling ruined by disobedience.

david.histoire:
A shepherd of Bethlehem, overlooked by all the day Samuel visits the house of Jesse, David is nonetheless the one God saw: "The Lord looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). Anointed among his brothers, he struck down Goliath with a sling and immense faith: "You come against me with sword and spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the Lord Almighty" (1 Samuel 17:45).

Pursued for years by Saul's jealousy, he twice refuses to kill "the Lord's anointed" (1 Samuel 24:7). Becoming king, he captures Jerusalem, brings up the ark dancing with all his might (2 Samuel 6:14), and receives the promise of an eternal throne—the Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7:16).

His fall with Bathsheba and the murder of Uriah (2 Samuel 11:15) are reported without flinching; his repentance too: "Create in me a pure heart, O God" (Psalm 51:10). Poet of the Psalms, "a man after [God's] own heart" (Acts 13:22), he is the ancestor and the figure of the Messiah, the "Son of David" (Matthew 1:1).

parcours.d: The forgotten shepherd, anointed by Samuel
Goliath: "I come to you in the name of the Lord"
The harp, the victories—and the king's jealousy
The years on the run; he spares Saul twice
King of Judah, then of all Israel
The ark, the promise of an eternal house—and the fall

ecrits.d: From the cry of the caves (Psalm 57) to royal praise—"The Lord is my shepherd" (Psalm 23), "Create in me a pure heart, O God" (Psalm 51)

goliath.bio: The giant of Gath, champion of the Philistines, who defied the army of the living God for forty days. A stone from a sling, cast in faith, was enough to bring him down.
goliath.histoire:
Champion of Gath, six cubits and a span tall — nearly ten feet — Goliath defied the battalions of Israel for forty days, morning and evening (1 Samuel 17:16). His armor weighed five thousand shekels of bronze; his words crushed: "I defy the armies of Israel this day" (1 Samuel 17:10).

Facing him, a shepherd with no armor and one certainty: "The battle is the Lord's" (1 Samuel 17:47). A stone from a sling to the forehead, and the giant fell face-first to the ground (1 Samuel 17:49). Goliath remains the name of all that seems invincible — until a heart believes.

salomon.bio: Son of David, he asked God not for wealth but for wisdom—and received both. Builder of the Temple, author of proverbs and songs, he nonetheless ended by turning his heart away.
salomon.histoire:
Son of David and Bathsheba, Solomon received from God in a dream at Gibeon the most staggering proposal in Scripture: "Ask what you wish that I may give it to you" (1 Kings 3:5). He asks for a discerning heart to judge the people—and receives in addition wealth and glory (1 Kings 3:12).

His judgment between the two mothers reveals his wisdom to all Israel (1 Kings 3:27). He builds the temple of Jerusalem, where the glory of the Lord descends as a cloud (1 Kings 8:11), composes proverbs and songs (1 Kings 4:32), receives the amazed Queen of Sheba (1 Kings 10:7).

But his seven hundred foreign wives turn his heart toward other gods (1 Kings 11:4): the kingdom will be torn apart after him. Ecclesiastes carries his conclusion both disillusioned and luminous: "Fear God and keep His commandments, for this is man's all" (Ecclesiastes 12:13).

ecrits.d: "Vanity of vanities": the sum of all under the sun
The most beautiful of songs: love, the flame of the Lord

elie.bio: The prophet of fire. He shut up the heavens by prayer, challenged the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel, heard God in a still, small voice, and was taken up to heaven in a chariot of fire.
elie.histoire:
Elijah appears without genealogy to confront King Ahab: it will not rain except at his word (1 Kings 17:1). Fed by ravens at the Brook Cherith, then by the widow of Zarephath whose flour never runs out (1 Kings 17:16), he embodies total dependence.

On Mount Carmel, alone against four hundred fifty prophets of Baal, he issues the challenge of fire; the Lord answers with fire, and the people fall on their faces (1 Kings 18:38). Then, exhausted and threatened by Jezebel, he flees to the desert and asks for death—and God meets him at Horeb, not in the storm but in a still, small voice (1 Kings 19:12).

He is taken up to heaven in a whirlwind, in a chariot of fire (2 Kings 2:11). Malachi announces his return before the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:5); he appears beside Moses at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:3). James cites him as a model: his prayer was "of a man like us" (James 5:17).

parcours.d: "As the Lord God of Israel lives... there shall be neither dew nor rain"
Fed by the ravens
The flour that never fails; the child raised to life
The fire falls: "The Lord, He is God!"
Depression, the still, small voice
The chariot of fire: taken up to heaven

elisee.bio: Elijah's successor, he asked for a double portion of his spirit—and his miracles doubled: oil multiplied, lepers healed, the dead raised. The prophet of the God who provides.
elisee.histoire:
Called from the plow in his field, Elisha burns his equipment and follows Elijah (1 Kings 19:21). As his master is taken up, he dares to ask for "a double portion of your spirit" (2 Kings 2:9)—and picks up the mantle fallen from heaven.

His ministry overflows with miracles of compassion: the waters of Jericho cleansed (2 Kings 2:21), the widow's oil multiplied (2 Kings 4:6), the Shunnamite woman's son raised to life (2 Kings 4:35), Naaman the Syrian healed of leprosy in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:14), the iron axhead that floats (2 Kings 6:6).

When the Syrian army surrounds Dothan, he reassures his servant: "Those who are with us are greater in number than those who are with them"—and God opens the young man's eyes to the mountain full of chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:17).

parcours.d: Elijah's mantle: he receives a double portion of the Spirit
The bitter waters cleansed by salt
The upper room, then the Shunnamite woman's son restored to life
In service to kings; the siege and abundance announced
He announces Hazael's reign and weeps over Israel

ezechias.bio: King of Judah who did what was right: he purified the Temple, broke down the idols, and when faced with the Assyrian invasion, he spread the threatening letter before the Lord. God answered—and added fifteen years to his life.
ezechias.histoire:
King of Judah, Hezekiah did what was right "as David had done": he broke down the idols, reopened the temple, and celebrated a memorable Passover (2 Chronicles 30:26). When Sennacherib and Assyria threatened Jerusalem, he spread the letter of blasphemy before the Lord and prayed (2 Kings 19:14); the angel of the Lord struck the Assyrian camp in the night (2 Kings 19:35).

Dying of sickness, he wept and prayed again: God added fifteen years to his life and made the shadow go back on the dial of Ahaz (2 Kings 20:6). With the prophet Isaiah at his side, he embodies trust: "He trusted in the Lord… and did not depart from following Him" (2 Kings 18:5).

josias.bio: King at eight years old, he made the Book of the Law—discovered in the Temple—echo throughout the land and led Judah's greatest reform.
josias.periode: Before him, there was no king who turned to the Lord with all his heart.

m.v:
Crowned at eight years old, Josiah sought God from his youth (2 Chronicles 34:3). During temple repairs, the forgotten Book of the Law was discovered; when the young king heard it read, he tore his clothes (2 Kings 22:11).

His reform was the most radical in Judah's history: idols crushed, high places demolished, and a Passover "such as had not been kept since the days of the judges" (2 Kings 23:22). Scripture gives him a unique tribute: "Before Josiah, there was no king who turned to the Lord with all his heart" (2 Kings 23:25). One discovery alone—the Word recovered—had been enough to transform a nation.

esdras.bio: A scribe skilled in the Law, who returned from Babylon to teach Israel. He had "devoted himself to study and to observe the Law of the Lord, and to teach it."
esdras.histoire:
A scribe skilled in the law of Moses, Ezra went up from Babylon to Jerusalem with the favor of the king, "because the good hand of his God was upon him" (Ezra 7:9). His secret is captured in one verse: "Ezra had devoted himself to the study and observance of the Law of the Lord, and to teaching it" (Ezra 7:10) — study, practice, teach, in that order.

Before the public square, he reads the Book of the Law from morning until noon; the people weep and then hold a great celebration, "for the joy of the Lord is your strength" (Nehemiah 8:10). With Nehemiah, he rebuilds the people while the other restores the walls.

nehemie.bio: Cupbearer to the Persian king, deeply moved by the ruins of Jerusalem. He prayed, fasted, then built: the walls were rebuilt in 52 days, trowel in one hand and sword in the other.
nehemie.histoire:
As cupbearer to the Persian king, Nehemiah learns that the walls of Jerusalem lie in ruins: he weeps, fasts, and prays (Nehemiah 1:4). Then he dares to ask the king for permission to go rebuild—after a quick prayer between the question and the answer (Nehemiah 2:4).

On site, he inspects by night, mobilizes each family to work on a section of wall, and stands firm against the mockery of Sanballat: "The God of heaven will give us success" (Nehemiah 2:20). Weapon in one hand, trowel in the other (Nehemiah 4:17), the people complete the wall in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15). Nehemiah remains the model of a leader who prays as if everything depends on God and works as if everything depends on him.

esther.bio: Jewish orphan who became queen of Persia "for such a time as this." At the risk of her life, she appeared before the king and saved her people from Haman's decree of extermination.
esther.histoire:
A Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, Hadassah becomes Esther, queen of Persia, without revealing her people (Esther 2:17). When Haman obtains a decree of extermination against the Jews, Mordecai sends her a message that echoes through the centuries: "Who knows whether you have not attained the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14).

After three days of fasting, she risks her life by appearing before the king without being called: "If I perish, I perish" (Esther 4:16). Through two banquets and quiet courage, she reverses the decree; Haman is hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai (Esther 7:10). The feast of Purim still celebrates this deliverance — in a book where God's name never appears, yet His hand is everywhere.

mardochee.bio: Cousin and adoptive father of Esther. He refused to bow before Haman, discovered a plot against the king, and was elevated to the very position of the man who wanted to hang him.
mardochee.histoire:
A Jew of Susa, Mordecai raised his young orphaned cousin as his own daughter (Esther 2:7). Sitting at the king's gate, he uncovered an assassination plot—a service recorded and then forgotten in the royal records (Esther 2:23).

He refused to bow before Haman, triggering the rage of the king's favorite and a decree against his entire people (Esther 3:5). It was he who urged Esther to act "for such a time as this" (Esther 4:14). The night the king could not sleep, the records were read aloud—and Mordecai was paraded in triumph by the man who wanted to hang him (Esther 6:11). He ended as second in the kingdom, "seeking the good of his people" (Esther 10:3).

job.bio: A man of integrity and uprightness, stripped of everything in a single day. In the furnace he stood firm: "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord!" God restored him twofold.
job.histoire:
"Blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil" (Job 1:1): so God Himself introduces Job. In a single day, he loses his possessions and his ten children; his response astounds heaven: "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord!" (Job 1:21).

Covered with sores, misunderstood by his wife and weighed down by the speeches of his three friends, Job cries out, protests, questions—yet never lets go of God. In the heart of the night springs forth his confession: "I know that my Redeemer lives" (Job 19:25).

God answers from the midst of the storm, not with explanations but with His greatness (Job 38:4). Job puts his hand over his mouth: "My eyes have seen You" (Job 42:5). The Lord restored him twofold, and James cites him as an example: "You have heard of the patience of Job" (James 5:11).

esaie.bio: The prophet of Emmanuel. Purified by the coal from the altar—"Here am I, send me!"—he announced seven centuries in advance the suffering Servant, wounded for our sins, by whom we are healed.
esaie.histoire:
In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord seated on a high and exalted throne; the seraphim cried out, "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord Almighty!" (Isaiah 6:3). A burning coal purifies his lips, and he answers the call: "Here am I, send me!" (Isaiah 6:8).

Prophet to kings, he announces to Ahaz the sign of the virgin bearing a son, Emmanuel (Isaiah 7:14), consoles Hezekiah in the face of Assyria, and brings forth the greatest messianic prophecies: the child with four names (Isaiah 9:6), the suffering Servant "pierced for our transgressions... and by his wounds we are healed" (Isaiah 53:5).

His book, most quoted by the New Testament, ends with new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17). He is called "the evangelist of the Old Testament."

ezechiel.bio: A prophet of exile by the Kebar River. His visions span the centuries: the moving glory of God, a heart of stone transformed into a heart of flesh, a valley of dry bones coming back to life.
ezechiel.histoire:
A priest deported to Babylon, Ezekiel sees the heavens opened by the Kebar River: four living creatures, shining wheels, and the glory of the Lord upon a throne of sapphire (Ezekiel 1:28). God establishes him as a watchman over the house of Israel (Ezekiel 3:17).

A prophet of actions as much as words, he acts out the siege of Jerusalem, loses his wife without being able to mourn her—a sign for the people. He announces each person's accountability (Ezekiel 18:20) and the most intimate promise of the Old Testament: "I will give you a new heart… I will remove the heart of stone from your body" (Ezekiel 36:26).

His vision of dry bones coming back to life at the breath of the Spirit (Ezekiel 37:10) remains the image of all resurrection—of a people, of a church, of a life.

daniel.bio: Deported to Babylon, he resolved not to defile himself—and God elevated him to the court of four kings. An interpreter of dreams, a man of prayer even in the lions' den, he saw the end times.
daniel.histoire:
Deported to Babylon as a young man, Daniel "resolved not to defile himself" at the king's table (Daniel 1:8)—the first victory is won on the plate. God gives him wisdom and understanding of visions; he reveals to Nebuchadnezzar his dream of the statue with feet of clay (Daniel 2:44).

Under four kings and two empires, he serves without wavering. His three companions walk through the furnace with a fourth man "like a son of the gods" (Daniel 3:25); he himself, an octogenarian, is thrown to the lions for continuing to pray three times a day, windows open toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10)—and God shuts the lions' mouths (Daniel 6:22).

His visions reach to the "Son of Man coming on the clouds" (Daniel 7:13), a title Jesus would claim for himself. Three times, heaven calls him "greatly beloved" (Daniel 10:11).

jonas.bio: The prophet who ran away. Cast into the sea, kept three days in the belly of a great fish, he finally obeys — and the entire city of Nineveh repents. A sign of Christ's death and resurrection.
jonas.histoire:
Sent to Nineveh, capital of the enemy Assyrians, Jonah boards a ship to Tarshish — due west, the opposite direction (Jonah 1:3). The storm, the casting of lots, and the prophet thrown into the sea: "a great fish" swallows him, prepared by the Lord (Jonah 1:17). From the belly of the fish rises his prayer: "Salvation belongs to the Lord" (Jonah 2:9).

Vomited up, sent again, he preaches a single sentence — and all of Nineveh repents, from the king to the cattle (Jonah 3:5). Jonah is angry enough to die: he knew God was "compassionate and merciful, slow to anger" (Jonah 4:2). The lesson of the plant that grows and withers concludes the book: God loves our enemies too.

Jesus will make him his own sign: "As Jonah was three days in the belly of the fish, so the Son of Man will be..." (Matthew 12:40).

parcours.d: Called to Nineveh, he flees and boards a ship for Tarshish
The storm; thrown overboard at his own request

marie.bio: A young woman from Nazareth who answered the impossible with faith:
marie.periode: I am the Lord's servant; let it be to me according to your word.
passages: She bore, raised, and followed the Savior all the way to the cross.

m.v: A young woman from Nazareth, betrothed to Joseph, Mary received a visit from the angel Gabriel:
Greetings, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you
(Luke 1:28). Her response set history's salvation in motion:
I am the Lord's servant; let it be to me according to your word

(Luke 1:38).

She sings the Magnificat at Elizabeth's home (Luke 1:46), gives birth to the Savior in a stable (Luke 2:7), and treasures all these things in her heart (Luke 2:19). At Cana, it is she who triggers the first miracle:

joseph-nt.bio: A carpenter from Nazareth, a righteous man. Warned in a dream, he took Mary as his wife, gave the child the name Jesus, and protected the holy family even to Egypt.
joseph-nt.histoire:
A carpenter from Nazareth, a "righteous man" (Matthew 1:19), Joseph discovers that his betrothed is expecting a child. He decides to break the engagement quietly to avoid shaming her—until an angel speaks to him in a dream: "Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife, for that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit" (Matthew 1:20).

Joseph obeys each dream: he takes Mary as his wife, names the child Jesus (Matthew 1:25), flees to Egypt to protect him from Herod (Matthew 2:14), and later settles in Nazareth (Matthew 2:23). A silent adoptive father—the Gospel records not a single word from him—he protects, works, and passes on the faith. It is as "the carpenter's son" that Jesus will be known (Matthew 13:55).

jean-baptiste.bio: The voice crying in the wilderness. Clothed in camel hair, he called for repentance, baptized Jesus in the Jordan, and pointed him out: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world."
jean-baptiste.histoire:
Announced by the angel Gabriel to his father Zechariah (Luke 1:13), filled with the Spirit even in his mother's womb, John grew up in the wilderness. Clothed in camel hair and fed on locusts and wild honey (Matthew 3:4), he is "the voice of one crying in the wilderness: 'Make ready the way of the Lord'" (Matthew 3:3).

He baptizes in the Jordan a people in repentance, and points to Jesus with a sentence that sums up the Gospel: "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29). He baptizes Jesus himself, at Jesus' request (Matthew 3:15), then steps back: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30).

Imprisoned for rebuking Herod, he dies beheaded (Matthew 14:10). Jesus will say of him: among those born of women, there has not appeared anyone greater (Matthew 11:11).

parcours.d: "Voice of one crying: Prepare the way of the Lord"
He baptizes the crowds—then Jesus: "Behold, the Lamb of God"
Imprisoned by Herod; "Are you the one who is to come?"

pierre.bio: A Galilean fisherman who became a fisher of men. Impulsive, he walked on water, confessed Christ, denied him three times—then, restored, opened the doors of the Church at Pentecost.
pierre.histoire: A fisherman of Galilee, Simon is brought to Jesus by his brother Andrew; Jesus renames him Cephas—Peter (John 1:42). After a miraculous catch, he leaves everything:

judas.bio: One of the Twelve, the group's treasurer, who betrayed his Master for thirty pieces of silver—with a kiss. His name remains the Gospel's gravest warning about a heart never truly given.
judas.histoire:
Chosen among the Twelve, treasurer of the group, Judas Iscariot followed Jesus for three years—and used to help himself from the money bag (John 12:6). For thirty pieces of silver, the price of a slave, he handed his Master over to the chief priests (Matthew 26:15).

At the last meal, Jesus offered him the dipped bread—a final gesture of friendship; "Satan entered into him" (John 13:27). In the night of Gethsemane, he betrayed him with a kiss: "Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?" (Luke 22:48).

Seized with remorse, he returned the money, but remorse is not repentance: he went and hanged himself (Matthew 27:5). His place among the Twelve was given to another (Acts 1:26). His story warns us: you can walk very close to Jesus and never belong to Him.

marthe.bio: Sister of Mary and Lazarus, in Bethany. Busy with service, gently rebuked — "only one thing is necessary" — yet she spoke one of the most beautiful confessions: "You are the Christ, the Son of God."
marthe.histoire:
In her home in Bethany, Martha welcomes Jesus and busies herself with great preparations while her sister Mary sits at the Master's feet. Her complaint sounds like us: "Lord, do You not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?" The answer is gentle and cutting: "Martha, Martha, you are worried and troubled about many things. But one thing is needed" (Luke 10:41).

When Lazarus dies, it is she, the active one, who runs to meet Jesus and speaks one of the greatest confessions in the Gospels: "Yes, Lord, I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world" (John 11:27) — just after receiving the revelation: "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25).

lazare.bio: Jesus' friend, dead for four days when the Master arrived in Bethany. Before his tomb, Jesus wept—then cried out:
lazare.histoire:
Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, is the friend whom Jesus loved (John 11:3). When he falls ill, his sisters send for the Master—who arrives four days after he has been buried.

Before the tomb, Jesus weeps (John 11:35), then reveals to Martha the heart of the Gospel:

nicodeme.bio: A Pharisee and ruler of the Jews who came to Jesus at night to question Him—and left with the most famous verse in the Bible:
nicodeme.histoire: A Pharisee and ruler of the Jews, Nicodemus came to Jesus by night—the caution of a notable, the thirst for truth (John 3:2). He received the word that has echoed through the centuries:

zachee.bio: Chief tax collector of Jericho, small in stature but great in curiosity. Perched on a sycamore tree, he was called by name — and salvation entered his house that very day.
zachee.histoire:
Chief tax collector of Jericho, rich and despised, Zacchaeus wanted to see Jesus; small in stature, he ran ahead and climbed into a sycamore tree (Luke 19:4). Under the tree, Jesus looked up and called him by name: "Zacchaeus, hurry and come down; for I must stay at your house today" (Luke 19:5).

The crowd grumbled—He was staying with a sinner! But grace had already done its work: Zacchaeus gave half his possessions to the poor and repaid fourfold what he had extorted (Luke 19:8). Jesus' conclusion sums up the entire Gospel: "The Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10).

pilate.bio: Roman governor of Judea. Convinced of Jesus' innocence, he washed his hands and yet delivered Him to the cross — history remembers that you cannot remain neutral before Christ.
pilate.histoire:
Roman governor of Judea, Pontius Pilate receives at his tribunal a prisoner whom his accusers want to see dead. His interrogation brushes against truth — "What is truth?" (John 18:38) — and he declares three times: "I find no fault in Him" (John 19:6).

Warned by his wife, pressed by the crowd demanding Barabbas, threatened — "You are not Caesar's friend" (John 19:12) — he gives in. He washes his hands before the crowd (Matthew 27:24), has Jesus scourged, and delivers Him to be crucified. On the cross, he nonetheless has written, unknowingly prophetic: "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews" (John 19:19). History remembers his name as that of all compromise: to know, and yet not to act.

herode.bio: King of Judea under Roman authority, a great builder and suspicious tyrant. Troubled by the birth of the "King of the Jews," he ordered the massacre of the children of Bethlehem. His sons and grandsons ruled after him.
herode.histoire:
King of Judea from 37 to 4 BC with Roman support, Herod magnificently enlarged the temple of Jerusalem. It was "in the days of Herod, king of Judea" that the angel announced the birth of John the Baptist (Luke 1:5).

When the wise men seek the newborn King of the Jews, "King Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him" (Matthew 2:3). Outwitted by the wise men, he "sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem" (Matthew 2:16). Joseph fled to Egypt with the child and his mother, and did not return until "Herod died" (Matthew 2:19).

His dynasty runs through the New Testament: his son Archelaus ruled over Judea (Matthew 2:22), his son Herod Antipas had John the Baptist beheaded, and his grandson Herod Agrippa I had the apostle James put to death (Acts 12:2).

etienne.bio: A man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, first of the seven deacons—and the first martyr. Stoned, his face like that of an angel, he died praying for his executioners, before the eyes of a certain Saul.
etienne.histoire:
Chosen among the seven to serve at the tables, Stephen, "full of faith and of the Holy Spirit" (Acts 6:5), performs wonders and confounds his opponents—his face appears "like that of an angel" (Acts 6:15).

Before the Sanhedrin, he traces all of Israel's history and concludes without trembling; the heavens open: "I see the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God" (Acts 7:56). Stoned outside the city, he dies like his Master, praying: "Lord, do not hold this sin against them!" (Acts 7:60).

The witnesses lay down their garments at the feet of a young man named Saul (Acts 7:58). The blood of the first martyr was already watering the conversion of the greatest apostle.

paul.bio: Persecutor of the Church struck down on the Damascus road, who became the Apostle to the Nations. Three missionary journeys, thirteen letters, prisons and shipwrecks — "It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me."
paul.histoire:
A Pharisee trained at the feet of Gamaliel, Saul of Tarsus persecutes the Church with zeal; he keeps watch over the cloaks of those who stone Stephen (Acts 7:58). On the road to Damascus, a light strikes him down: "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" (Acts 9:4). The enemy becomes an apostle.

With Barnabas and later Silas, he travels the empire on three great journeys: Cyprus, Galatia, Macedonia, Athens, Corinth, Ephesus. Beaten with rods, stoned, shipwrecked (2 Corinthians 11:25), he sings at midnight in the Philippian jail (Acts 16:25) and proclaims the unknown God before the Areopagus (Acts 17:23).

His letters—thirteen in all—form the doctrinal heart of the New Testament: justification by faith (Romans 5:1), a hymn to love (1 Corinthians 13:4), Christ in whom all fullness dwells (Colossians 2:9). A prisoner in Rome, he still writes: "Rejoice in the Lord always" (Philippians 4:4), before his final word: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith" (2 Timothy 4:7).

The silent years of preparation
Sought out by Barnabas; sent by the Spirit

Arrested; two years before Felix, Festus, Agrippa
"Not one of you will perish": 276 saved
A prisoner who evangelizes "with all boldness"

From Corinth: the hope of the Lord's return
The gifted and divided church; love greater than all
From Corinth: the Gospel expounded — the righteous will live by faith
The letters of Rome's captivity: Christ above all, joy in chains
The final letter, from prison: "I have kept the faith"

barnabas.bio: "Son of Encouragement": he sold his field for the Church, opened his trust to the converted Saul when everyone else was wary of him, and went with him to bring the Gospel to the nations.
barnabas.histoire:
Joseph of Cyprus, surnamed by the apostles Barnabas—"Son of Encouragement" (Acts 4:36)—sells his field and lays the proceeds at the apostles' feet. His entire ministry would mirror this gesture.

It is he who dares to present to the apostles the converted man from Damascus whom everyone still fears: without Barnabas, there would be no ministry of Paul (Acts 9:27). Sent to Antioch, he rejoices in the grace and goes to find Saul in Tarsus to bring him into the work (Acts 11:25); "a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith" (Acts 11:24).

Companion of Paul on the first missionary journey (Acts 13:2), he later defends his nephew Mark, to the point of parting ways with Paul to give him a second chance (Acts 15:39)—Mark whom Paul would one day call "useful for the ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11). The encourager had seen it rightly.

silas.bio: Paul's companion on the second missionary journey. At Philippi, beaten and thrown into prison, he sang God's praises at midnight—until the doors burst open.
silas.histoire:
An esteemed prophet of the Jerusalem church, Silas is chosen to carry the council's letter to Antioch (Acts 15:22). When Paul and Barnabas part ways, Paul takes Silas for the second missionary journey (Acts 15:40).

At Philippi, beaten and thrown into prison, he sings with Paul at midnight; the earthquake opens the doors and the jailer asks, "What must I do to be saved?" (Acts 16:30). He reappears in Thessalonica, Berea, and Corinth (Acts 18:5). Under his Latin name Silvanus, he also carries the pen of Peter's first letter (1 Peter 5:12)—a faithful companion to two of the greatest apostles.

timothee.bio: A young disciple from Lystra, trained in Scripture by his mother and grandmother, who became Paul's spiritual son. Two New Testament letters exhort him:
timothee.histoire:
A young disciple from Lystra, son of a believing Jewish woman and a Greek father, Timothy received his faith from his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5). Paul took him along on his second missionary journey (Acts 16:3), and Timothy became his "legitimate child in the faith" (1 Timothy 1:2).

Sent on difficult missions to Thessalonica, to Corinth, and then established in Ephesus, he received from Paul two letters full of tenderness and firmness: "Let no one despise your youth" (1 Timothy 4:12), "Stir up the gift of God which is in you" (2 Timothy 1:6), "Guard what has been entrusted to you" (2 Timothy 1:14).

Timid perhaps, but faithful surely: "I have no one else like him, who takes a genuine interest in your welfare," Paul writes to the Philippians (Philippians 2:20). It is to Timothy that the apostle will address his very last letter, from the depths of his Roman prison.

jacques-frere.bio: Brother of Jesus, unbeliever before the Resurrection, who became a pillar of the Jerusalem church. He decided at the council of nations and wrote the most practical letter of the New Testament: faith that acts.
jacques-frere.histoire:
As Jesus' brother in the flesh, James did not believe in him during his ministry (John 7:5). Everything changed at Easter: the Risen One appeared to him personally (1 Corinthians 15:7). We find him in the upper room with Mary and the disciples (Acts 1:14).

Becoming a pillar of the Jerusalem church (Galatians 2:9), it was he who decided at the council: the Law would not be imposed on converted gentiles (Acts 15:19). Paul visited him every time he passed through Jerusalem (Acts 21:18).

His letter is the most concrete in the New Testament: faith without works is dead (James 2:17), the tongue is a fire (James 3:6), the fervent prayer of the righteous has great power (James 5:16). The unbeliever turned servant signs simply: "James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ" (James 1:1).

apollos.bio: A Jew from Alexandria, eloquent and well-versed in the Scriptures. More accurately instructed by Priscilla and Aquila, he became a mighty defender of the faith: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth."
apollos.histoire:
A Jew from Alexandria, "an eloquent man and mighty in the Scriptures" (Acts 18:24), Apollos preaches with fervor in Ephesus—yet knows only John's baptism. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain to him "the way of God more accurately" (Acts 18:26): great eloquence accepts humble correction.

In Achaia, he becomes a mighty help, "vigorously refuting the Jews publicly" and demonstrating through the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ (Acts 18:28). In Corinth, some claim him against Paul; the apostle sweeps away the rivalry: "I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth" (1 Corinthians 3:6).

cain.bio: Adam and Eve's firstborn, a tiller of the ground, and murderer of his brother Abel. His name speaks of the anger that smolders and God's question: "If you do well, will you not be accepted?"
cain.histoire:
A farmer, Cain brings an offering of the fruit of the ground; God regards Abel's offering, not his. Instead of examining himself, he grows angry—and God warns him: "Sin crouches at the door... but you must master it" (Genesis 4:7).

In the fields, he rises up against his brother and kills him. "What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries out to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). Marked with a protective sign, he goes away from the presence of the Lord. John draws the warning from this: do not be "like Cain, who was of the evil one" (1 John 3:12).

abel.bio: Shepherd, second son of Adam, first righteous man and first victim in history. His accepted offering cost him his life—and his blood still speaks.
abel.histoire:
A shepherd of flocks, Abel offers the firstborn of his flock, and the Lord looks with favor on him and on his offering (Genesis 4:4). This favor earns him the hatred of his brother, who kills him in the fields.

Hebrews illuminates the difference: "By faith Abel offered God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain… and by faith he still speaks, though he is dead" (Hebrews 11:4). Jesus names him the first of the righteous who were persecuted (Matthew 23:35)—and the blood of Christ "speaks better things than that of Abel" (Hebrews 12:24).

henoc.histoire:
In the litany of generations—"and he died...and he died"—Enoch stands out: "Enoch walked with God; and he was not, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24).

Hebrews clarifies: before his translation, he had received the testimony that he was pleasing to God—"but without faith it is impossible to please Him" (Hebrews 11:5). Jude cites his prophecy of judgment (Jude 1:14). Only two men left the earth without dying: Enoch and Elijah—two walkers with God.

lot.bio: Abraham's nephew, who chose the fertile plain of Sodom "like a garden of the Lord"—and nearly lost everything there. Saved by grace, but trailing behind.
lot.histoire:
Having come up from Ur with Abraham, Lot had to separate from him when their flocks grew too large. He lifted his eyes, saw the well-watered plain of the Jordan, and chose—until he pitched his tents toward Sodom (Genesis 13:12).

When judgment fell, two angels literally pulled him by the hand, "for the Lord wanted to spare him" (Genesis 19:16). His wife looked back and became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:26); Jesus would make her a warning: "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32). Yet Peter called him righteous, his soul tormented by what he saw (2 Peter 2:8): you can be saved by the skin of your teeth.

agar.bio: Egyptian servant of Sarah, mother of Ishmael. Twice in the wilderness, twice met by the God who sees: "You are the God who sees me."
agar.histoire:
Given to Abraham by impatient Sarah, Hagar conceives—and contempt settles between the two women. Pregnant and mistreated, she flees to the wilderness, where the angel of the Lord finds her by a spring. She then gives God one of His most beautiful names: "You are the God who sees me"—El-Roi (Genesis 16:13).

Years later, cast out with her son and an empty water skin, she sits down so she won't have to watch the child die. "God heard the voice of the child"—Ishmael, "God hears"—and opened her eyes to a well (Genesis 21:19). The rejected slave is the first person in the Bible to whom an angel appears.

ismael.bio: Son of Abraham and Hagar, the child of human impatience, yet blessed: twelve princes would come from him. His name means
ismael.histoire:
Born from Sarah's plan to "help" the promise, Ishmael grew up as Abraham's firstborn—until Isaac's birth. His mocking laughter at the child's weaning led to his banishment (Genesis 21:9).

But God heard the boy dying in the desert, saved him, and renewed His promise: "I will make him a great nation" (Genesis 21:18); he became an archer in the Desert of Paran, father of twelve princes (Genesis 25:16). Paul would make the two sons an allegory of two covenants—the flesh and the promise (Galatians 4:23).

rebecca.bio: Wife of Isaac, found at the well through the prayer of Abraham's servant. Mother of twins Esau and Jacob—and strategist of the diverted blessing.
rebecca.histoire:
At the well in the city of Nahor, Rebekah answered exactly the sign requested by the servant in prayer: she gave water to the man... and his ten camels (Genesis 24:19). To the question "Will you go with this man?" she simply answered, "I will go" (Genesis 24:58).

Barren for twenty years, she conceives through Isaac's prayer twin sons who already struggle within her; the Lord reveals to her: "The older will serve the younger" (Genesis 25:23). It is this oracle she believes she is serving by orchestrating Jacob's deception for the blessing (Genesis 27:13)—she will never see her favored son again.

esau.bio: Jacob's twin brother, a red-haired impulsive hunter who sold his birthright for a bowl of lentils—then wept over a lost blessing.
esau.histoire:
A hunter and man of the field, favored by his father, Esau one day returns exhausted and trades away his birthright for bread and a bowl of lentil stew: "He ate and drank, then got up and left. This is how Esau despised his birthright" (Genesis 25:34).

When Jacob also steals his blessing, he lets out "a loud and bitter cry" (Genesis 27:34) and plots to kill him. Twenty years later, though, he runs to meet him, embraces him, and weeps (Genesis 33:4)—one of the Bible's most beautiful forgivenesses. Hebrews holds up the warning: that no one "profane like Esau" should sell his inheritance for a moment (Hebrews 12:16).

rachel.bio: Jacob's beloved, "beautiful in form and beautiful in appearance," for whom he served fourteen years "which seemed to him but a few days." Mother of Joseph and Benjamin.
rachel.histoire:
Jacob meets her at the well and alone rolls away the stone to water her flock. He serves seven years for her, "and they seemed to him but a few days because of the love he had for her" (Genesis 29:20)—before being deceived on his wedding morning and serving seven more years.

Long barren while fruitful Leah bears children, she cries out, wrestles, hopes—until Joseph: "God has taken away my reproach" (Genesis 30:23). She dies giving birth to Benjamin on the road to Bethlehem, where Jacob sets up a pillar (Genesis 35:19). Jeremiah and then Matthew will hear "Rachel weeping for her children" (Matthew 2:18).

lea.histoire:
Substituted for her sister on the wedding night through Laban's deception, Leah carries throughout her life the wound of not being chosen. The names of her sons are her intimate journal: "The Lord has seen my humiliation… this time my husband will cling to me… "

At the fourth, something shifts: "This time I will praise the Lord. So she named him Judah" (Genesis 29:35) — praise. From the unloved wife descend Judah, thus David, thus Christ (Matthew 1:2). God writes His greatest stories with broken hearts.

laban.bio: Brother of Rebekah, Jacob's father-in-law and rival: twenty years of mutual deception, ten wage changes — and a deceiver deceived.
laban.histoire:
Welcoming at first — "You are my bone and my flesh" (Genesis 29:14) — Laban reveals himself as a master of manipulation: he substitutes Leah for Rachel on the wedding night, demands seven more years, changes Jacob's wages ten times (Genesis 31:7).

But God watches over the fugitive: "I have seen all that Laban is doing to you" (Genesis 31:12). The final pursuit ends not in battle but in a covenant at the stone heap of Galeed: "May the Lord watch between you and me" — the Mizpah (Genesis 31:49). Jacob had found someone more cunning than himself, and God had used it to shape him.

juda-fils.bio: The fourth son of Jacob, who proposed selling Joseph—then offered his own life for Benjamin. From his tribe would come David and the "Lion of Judah."
juda-fils.histoire:
It was Judah who proposed selling Joseph—"What profit is there if we kill our brother?" (Genesis 37:26)—and Judah again who goes through the troubling episode with Tamar, emerging from it by confessing: "She is more righteous than I" (Genesis 38:26).

The man had changed when famine brings the brothers back to Egypt: before the unknown governor, he offers himself as a slave in place of Benjamin, so as not to break his father's heart (Genesis 44:33). This plea causes Joseph to burst into tears.

Dying Jacob leaves him the royal oracle: "The scepter shall not depart from Judah… until Shiloh comes" (Genesis 49:10). Revelation responds: "The Lion of the tribe of Judah has prevailed" (Revelation 5:5).

miriam.bio: Eldest sister of Moses and Aaron, a prophetess. She watched over the baby's basket, led the dances at the Red Sea—and learned the hard way to respect authority.
miriam.histoire:
She was the older sister stationed by the Nile's edge who dared suggest to Pharaoh's daughter a nurse—the child's own mother (Exodus 2:7). After the Red Sea, "Miriam the prophetess" took up the tambourine and led all the women: "Sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously" (Exodus 15:21).

At Hazeroth, she and Aaron challenged Moses' authority; struck with leprosy, she was healed by the prayer of the very one she had criticized—"O God, I pray, heal her!" (Numbers 12:13). Micah counts her among the three leaders sent in the Exodus (Micah 6:4).

jethro.bio: Priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law — and history's first organizational consultant: "What you are doing is not good; you will surely wear yourself out."
jethro.histoire:
Fugitive Moses finds in him a roof, a wife — Zipporah — and forty years of training in the desert as a shepherd (Exodus 3:1).

After the Exodus, Jethro joins the camp, rejoices, offers sacrifices... and observes Moses judging the people alone from morning to evening. His counsel has echoed through the centuries: "You will surely wear out... choose capable men who fear God, and delegate to them" (Exodus 18:21-22). Moses listened — the first delegation in sacred history came from a pagan father-in-law who became a believer: "Now I know that the Lord is greater than all gods" (Exodus 18:11).

balaam.bio: A diviner from Mesopotamia hired to curse Israel — whose mouth could only speak blessings. His donkey saw the angel before he did.
balaam.histoire:
Paid by Balak, king of Moab, to curse Israel, Balaam set out with a divided heart — and his donkey stopped three times before the angel he could not see, until she spoke (Numbers 22:28).

Four times, the curse he was commanded to pronounce turned into a blessing from his mouth: "How can I curse those whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8), culminating in the messianic prophecy: "A Star shall come out of Jacob; A Scepter shall rise out of Israel" (Numbers 24:17).

But the man loved "the wages of unrighteousness" (2 Peter 2:15): his counsel caused Israel to fall through seduction (Numbers 31:16). You can prophesy correctly and still end badly — "the way of Balaam" remains a warning (Jude 1:11).

rahab.bio: A prostitute of Jericho who hid the spies and believed in the God of Israel before Israel did. The scarlet cord at her window saved her — and she entered the lineage of the Messiah.
rahab.histoire:
On the wall of Jericho, Rahab hides the two spies and makes a stunning confession of faith: "The Lord your God is God in heaven above and on the earth below" (Joshua 2:11). She negotiates the lives of her household in exchange for a sign: the scarlet cord tied to her window (Joshua 2:18).

When the walls fall, her house stands (Joshua 6:25). She marries Salmon and becomes the mother of Boaz — the genealogy of Jesus names her explicitly (Matthew 1:5). Hebrews counts her among the heroes of faith (Hebrews 11:31), and James uses her as proof that faith acts (James 2:25).

jephthe.bio: Rejected son turned deliverer of Gilead, victor over Ammon—and author of the Bible's most tragic vow.
jephthe.histoire:
Son of a prostitute, cast out by his half-brothers, Jephthah becomes a bandit chief in the land of Tob—then the man everyone pleads with to return when Ammon attacks (Judges 11:6). The Spirit of the Lord comes upon him.

Before the battle, he makes a rash vow: to offer whatever comes out first from his house upon his return (Judges 11:31). The victory is complete; but it is his only daughter who comes out dancing to meet him. His story cries out the gravity of words spoken before God (Ecclesiastes 5:2)—and yet Hebrews counts him, by grace, among the men of faith (Hebrews 11:32).

eli-pretre.bio: High priest at Shiloh, failing father of unworthy sons, yet mentor to young Samuel: he taught him how to respond to God.
eli-pretre.histoire:
At Shiloh, Eli first mistakes the silently praying woman—Hannah—for a drunkard before blessing her request (1 Samuel 1:17). He will raise the child of that prayer, Samuel.

His tragedy: his own sons despise the Lord, and he "did not rebuke them" (1 Samuel 3:13). Yet his greatness: when young Samuel hears the voice in the night, it is Eli who discerns it and teaches him the answer—"Speak, Lord, for Your servant is listening" (1 Samuel 3:9). He dies upon learning of the capture of the ark, struck down by the news more than by his fall (1 Samuel 4:18).

anne-samuel.bio: The barren woman who prayed silently at Shiloh, received Samuel, and gave him back to God. Her song foreshadows Mary's.
anne-samuel.histoire:
Provoked by her rival, misunderstood by her husband, Hannah pours out her soul before the Lord — her lips move, her voice is not heard, so much so that Eli thinks she is drunk (1 Samuel 1:13). She makes a vow: if God gives her a son, he will belong to him all the days of his life.

The Lord remembers her. She names the child Samuel — "I have asked him of the Lord" — and, when weaned, brings him back to Shiloh: "So I lend him to the Lord" (1 Samuel 1:28). Her song turns the world upside down: "The Lord raises the poor from the dust" (1 Samuel 2:8) — Mary will sing it in turn (Luke 1:52).

jonathan.bio: Son of Saul, heir to the throne — and the true friend of the man who would take it. The purest friendship in the Bible.
jonathan.histoire:
A man of faith above all: with only his armor-bearer, he scales the rock of the Philistines — "nothing can hinder the Lord from saving by many or by few" (1 Samuel 14:6).

After Goliath, "the soul of Jonathan was knit to the soul of David" (1 Samuel 18:1): he gives David his robe, his sword, his bow — the insignia of the prince. Against his own father's fury, he protects David, warns him by the sign of the arrows, renews the covenant: "May the Lord be between you and me forever" (1 Samuel 20:42). He will know how to "strengthen his hand in God" in the wilderness (1 Samuel 23:16).

He falls at Gilboa at Saul's side; David's lament weeps over "a love more wonderful than the love of women" (2 Samuel 1:26).

abigail.histoire:
When Nabal insults David's messengers, four hundred swords are already moving toward Carmel. Abigail comes down to meet them with provisions, throws herself at David's feet, and delivers one of Scripture's most skillful pleas: that he not burden himself with "blood shed without cause"—David's soul will remain "bound in the bundle of life with the Lord" (1 Samuel 25:29).

David blesses God for her: "Blessed be your good sense, and blessed be you" (1 Samuel 25:33). When Nabal dies of a stroke ten days later, David sends for her and marries her. Her gentleness had disarmed six hundred men.

absalom.bio: Son of David, the most handsome man in Israel — and the usurper of his father's heart. His hair was his glory and his downfall.
absalom.histoire:
Avenger of his sister Tamar, exiled, then recalled but not received, Absalom nursed a patient ambition for four years: posted at the gate, he "stole the hearts of the people of Israel" (2 Samuel 15:6).

His conspiracy drove David from Jerusalem, barefoot and head covered on the Mount of Olives (2 Samuel 15:30). But in the forest of Ephraim, his hair caught on the branches of a terebinth tree; suspended "between heaven and earth," he was pierced by Joab (2 Samuel 18:14).

Victory tasted like mourning: "O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you!" (2 Samuel 18:33) — David's cry foreshadows another Father giving His Son.

bath-scheba.bio: Wife of Uriah, taken by David; mother of the dead child, then of Solomon. From the king's greatest sin, God brought forth the lineage of the Messiah.
bath-scheba.histoire:
One evening, from his rooftop, David sees her; he sends, he takes her—she is the wife of Uriah the Hittite, away on campaign for the king (2 Samuel 11:4). The adultery deepens into murder: Uriah falls on the front lines, by the king's order.

"What David had done displeased the Lord" (2 Samuel 11:27). The child dies despite the king's broken fast. But grace writes the rest: Bathsheba bears Solomon, "and the Lord loved him" (2 Samuel 12:24). It is she who, years later, will make her son's claim to the throne known (1 Kings 1:17)—and Matthew inscribes her in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:6).

nathan.bio: Prophet at David's court: bearer of the promise of an eternal throne, and of the parable that brought the king to his knees — "You are the man!"
nathan.histoire:
Through Nathan passes the Davidic covenant: "Your house and your kingdom will be established forever" (2 Samuel 7:16).

And it is he whom God sends after the crime: he tells the king the story of the poor man's lamb stolen by the rich man. David burns with anger — and the prophet strikes: "You are the man!" (2 Samuel 12:7). The king confesses: "I have sinned against the Lord"; forgiveness answers at once (2 Samuel 12:13) — Psalm 51 will keep the tears of it. Faithful to the end, Nathan ensures the enthronement of Solomon (1 Kings 1:45).

joab.bio: Commander of David's army, indispensable strategist and ruthless operative: loyal to the throne, formidable to all—even to the king.
joab.histoire:
David's nephew, Joab takes Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 11:6) and wins every battle of the reign. But his sword answers only to his own law: he murders Abner out of revenge (2 Samuel 3:27), executes Absalom suspended despite the king's order (2 Samuel 18:14), stabs Amasa his rival (2 Samuel 20:10).

Yet he carries the letter condemning Uriah (2 Samuel 11:14)—the man of dark deeds knows everything. Rallying to the wrong pretender at the end, he dies clinging to the altar's horns (1 Kings 2:34). A mighty servant with an insubordinate heart: effectiveness without obedience ends badly.

achab.bio: King of Israel, husband of Jezebel, builder of the temple of Baal: "he did more to provoke the Lord to anger than all the kings of Israel who were before him." The adversary of Elijah.
achab.histoire:
Under Jezebel's influence, Ahab sets up Baal worship in Israel (1 Kings 16:32). Elijah rises against him: drought, then Mount Carmel. "Is that you, you troubler of Israel?" — "No, it's you" (1 Kings 18:17).

Naboth's vineyard affair reveals his heart: he sulks over a vineyard, lets Jezebel kill, goes down to take possession — and finds Elijah in the vineyard: "You have killed, and also taken possession!" (1 Kings 21:19). Against all odds, he humbles himself, and God delays judgment (1 Kings 21:29).

He dies in battle, disguised in vain: an arrow "by chance" finds the gap in his armor (1 Kings 22:34).

jezabel.bio: Princess of Sidon who became queen of Israel, priestess of persecution: she made even Elijah tremble. Her name became synonymous with idolatrous seduction.
jezabel.histoire:
Daughter of the king of Sidon, Jezebel brought Baal with her: four hundred and fifty of his prophets ate at her table (1 Kings 18:19) while she destroyed those of the Lord (1 Kings 18:4). After Mount Carmel, her threat drives Elijah to the wilderness (1 Kings 19:2).

For a vineyard she refused, she orchestrated a false trial and had Naboth stoned: "Rise up, take possession" (1 Kings 21:15). The prophetic sentence was fulfilled to the letter under Jehu: painted at her window, she was thrown down (2 Kings 9:33). Revelation would make her name the symbol of all seduction that leads the servants of God astray (Revelation 2:20).

naaman.bio: Syrian general, "a mighty man of valor, but a leper." Seven dippings in the Jordan, on the word of a little servant girl — and the flesh of a child.
naaman.histoire:
Everything succeeds for Naaman, commander of the Syrian army — "but he was a leper" (2 Kings 5:1). Hope comes from below: a small Israelite captive speaks of the prophet of Samaria.

At Elisha's house, no grand welcome: a messenger, and a humbling command — dip seven times in the Jordan. Naaman is angered: he expected a great gesture, the rivers of Damascus are better! His servants reason with him; he goes down, dips himself, "and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a young child" (2 Kings 5:14).

The healed pagan confesses the God of Israel and refuses payment for grace (2 Kings 5:15). Jesus will mention him in Nazareth (Luke 4:27): grace overflows all boundaries.

parcours.d: Army commander with leprosy; an Israelite servant girl speaks of a prophet
At the king of Israel's house, then before Elisha's house
Seven dippings: "his flesh was restored like that of a child"
"There is no other God in all the earth"

nebucadnetsar.bio: King of Babylon, destroyer of Jerusalem, empire builder — humbled to eat grass like cattle, then restored to confess the Most High God.
nebucadnetsar.histoire:
As God's instrument of judgment, Nebuchadnezzar burned the temple and deported Judah (2 Kings 25:9). But in Babylon, God pursued the king himself: the dream of the statue (Daniel 2:28), the furnace from which three men emerged without the smell of fire — "Blessed be the God of Shadrach…" (Daniel 3:28).

Pride resists: "Is not this the great Babylon that I have built?" (Daniel 4:30). The sentence strikes mid-sentence: driven out, he eats grass like cattle for seven years.

With reason restored, the greatest king in the world writes one of the Bible's most beautiful doxologies: "I praise and exalt and glorify the King of heaven… he is able to bring down those who walk in pride" (Daniel 4:37).

schadrac.bio: The three companions of Daniel, cast into the furnace for refusing to bow down—and joined in the fire by a fourth "like a son of the gods."
schadrac.histoire:
Before the golden statue and the furnace heated seven times hotter, their answer becomes the charter of all faith's resistance: "Our God is able to deliver us… But even if he does not, know this, O king, that we will not serve your gods" (Daniel 3:18). That "but even if" is worth all of Babylon's gold.

Bound, thrown in, they walk free in the midst of the fire—four men instead of three, "and the appearance of the fourth is like a son of the gods" (Daniel 3:25). They come out without a burn, without the smell of fire. Nebuchadnezzar blesses their God "who has sent his angel" (Daniel 3:28): his presence in the furnace is worth more than the absence of the furnace.

cyrus.bio: Persian emperor who overthrew Babylon and sent the exiles back to rebuild the temple — named by Isaiah one hundred fifty years before his birth.
cyrus.histoire:
Isaiah had named him in advance: "I say of Cyrus: He is My shepherd, and he will accomplish all My will" (Isaiah 44:28) — the Lord even calls him "His anointed" (Isaiah 45:1).

In the first year of his reign over Babylon, "the Lord awakened the spirit of Cyrus": his edict sent the Jews back to Jerusalem, with the temple vessels and an order to rebuild (Ezra 1:2). The history of empires is a glove in God's hand: "The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord" (Proverbs 21:1).

zorobabel.bio: Prince of Judah, leader of the first return from exile and rebuilder of the temple: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit."
zorobabel.histoire:
A descendant of David, Zerubbabel led the first caravan of return and raised the altar in the midst of ruins, "for fear was upon them" (Ezra 3:3). With foundations laid, the elders wept while the young shouted with joy.

Faced with opposition that halted the work for fifteen years, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah revived his courage: "Be strong, Zerubbabel!… for I am with you" (Haggai 2:4). And the word bearing his name echoes through the centuries: "Not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6). He appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:12).

haman.bio: A favorite of the Persian king who plotted to destroy all the Jews because of one man's offense—and was hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai.
haman.histoire:
Elevated above all the princes, Haman could not tolerate a single knee that would not bow: that of Mordecai. His revenge aimed at an entire people—the lot (the "pur") fixed the day of the massacre (Esther 3:7).

Divine irony seized the narrative: the night the king could not sleep, Haman had to lead in triumph the man he had just prepared to hang (Esther 6:11). At Esther's banquet, the queen exposed him: "The oppressor and enemy is Haman, this vile man!" (Esther 7:6). He was hanged on the gallows of fifty cubits that had been prepared for Mordecai (Esther 7:10): "Whoever digs a pit will fall into it" (Proverbs 26:27).

osee-prophete.bio: The prophet of broken marriage: God made him marry Gomer the unfaithful to show Israel the wounded heart—and the unstoppable love—of their God.
osee-prophete.histoire:
"Go, take yourself a wife of harlotry" (Hosea 1:2): Hosea's life becomes the living parable of betrayed covenant. Gomer leaves him; God commands him to redeem her and love her again, "as the Lord loves the children of Israel" (Hosea 3:1).

His book alternates between heartrending complaints and burning declarations: "What shall I do with you, Ephraim?… My heart churns within Me" (Hosea 11:8). He calls: "Come, and let us return to the Lord… He will heal us" (Hosea 6:1), and promises: "I will love them freely" (Hosea 14:4). Paul and Peter will quote his oracle: "I will call them My people, who were not My people" (Romans 9:25).

jean-apotre.histoire: John was mending his nets with his brother James when Jesus called them; they left the boat and their father (Matthew 4:21-22). With Peter and James, he formed the inner circle: the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1), the room of Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:37), Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). Jesus nicknamed them

parcours.d: Called in Zebedee's boat, with James
From the inner circle: the Transfiguration, Gethsemane
"Behold your mother": Mary entrusted to the beloved disciple
Pillar of the Church with Peter and James
A long ministry as elder: "Little children, love one another"
Exiled "for the word of God": the Revelation

ecrits.d: "That you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, and that believing you may have life"
God is Light, God is Love: the letters of the elder
The Revelation of Jesus Christ, received on Patmos

andre.bio: Brother of Simon Peter, first a disciple of John the Baptist. The man of introductions: he brings Peter, the boy with five loaves, and Greeks to Jesus.
andre.histoire:
Andrew follows John the Baptist when he points to Jesus: "Behold, the Lamb of God." He spends the day with Jesus, then runs to find his brother: "We have found the Messiah"—and he brings Simon to Jesus (John 1:35-42). The first evangelism in history: a brother bringing another brother.

It is Andrew again who spots the boy with five barley loaves and two fish before the multiplication (John 6:8-9), and he who, with Philip, introduces Greeks who came to see Jesus (John 12:20-22). Called by the shore with Peter—"I will make you fishers of men" (Matthew 4:18-19)—he is among the Twelve (Acts 1:13). A quiet apostle whose ministry is summed up in one gesture: bringing someone to Jesus.

jacques-zebedee.bio: Elder brother of John, one of Jesus' three closest companions. First of the Twelve to shed his blood: Herod Agrippa had him beheaded.
jacques-zebedee.histoire:
Called along with his brother John while they were mending nets in their father Zebedee's boat (Matthew 4:21-22), James belongs to the inner circle: he witnesses the Transfiguration (Mark 9:2), the raising of Jairus' daughter (Mark 5:37), and Jesus' agony in Gethsemane (Mark 14:33). Jesus gives the two brothers the nickname Boanerges, "sons of thunder" (Mark 3:17).

Their mother asks Jesus for the two highest places in His kingdom; Jesus replies: "Are you able to drink the cup that I am about to drink?" (Matthew 20:20-23). James would drink it first: around 44 AD, King Herod "killed James the brother of John with the sword" (Acts 12:1-2)—the first apostle to be martyred, faithful to his Master's word.

philippe-apotre.bio: An apostle from Bethsaida, like Andrew and Peter. He is the one who brings Nathanael—
philippe-apotre.histoire:
