Zephaniah preaches under the young Josiah, before or during the reform: the "Day of the Lord" is near, a "day of distress and anguish" (Zephaniah 1:15) for Jerusalem's complacent idolatry, for those people "who say in their heart, The Lord will not do good, nor will He do evil" (Zephaniah 1:7-12). The outcome: "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the earth… Seek righteousness, seek humility! Perhaps you will be hidden in the day of the Lord's anger" (Zephaniah 2:3).

After the storm, the song: "The Lord your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing" (Zephaniah 3:17). The God of judgment is the same God who sings over His people.

aggee.bio: Prophet of the return from exile who awakened the temple construction project stalled for sixteen years: "Is it a time for you to dwell in your paneled houses, when this house is in ruins?"
aggee.histoire:
The people kept saying, "The time has not come for the Lord's house to be rebuilt." Haggai turned it around: "Is it a time for you to dwell in your paneled houses?… You plant much, but harvest little… Consider your ways carefully!" (Haggai 1:2-7). In twenty-three days, Zerubbabel, Joshua, and all the people were at work — "I am with you, says the Lord" (Haggai 1:12-14; Ezra 5:1-2).

To the elders weeping over the lost glory of the first temple: "The glory of this latter house will be greater than the former… And in this place I will give peace" (Haggai 2:3-9). Four dated messages, one project relaunched: sometimes God's will is simply to get back to work.

zacharie-prophete.bio: Companion of Haggai at the return from exile, prophet of eight night visions—and of the most precise announcements of the Messiah: the humble king on a donkey, the thirty pieces of silver, the Shepherd struck down.
zacharie-prophete.histoire:
With Haggai, Zechariah supports the rebuilding of the temple (Ezra 5:1-2; 6:14). His night visions address the discouragement of the remnant: the golden lampstand fed without human hand—"Not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the Lord of hosts" (Zechariah 4:6)—and this promise: "those who despised the day of small beginnings will rejoice" (Zechariah 4:10).

No prophet has drawn the Messiah more clearly: the king "righteous and victorious…humble and mounted on a donkey, On a donkey, the foal of a donkey" (Zechariah 9:9—Matthew 21:4-5), the wage of thirty pieces of silver cast to the potter (Zechariah 11:12-13), "they will look on me, the one they have pierced" (Zechariah 12:10—John 19:37), the Shepherd struck and the sheep scattered (Zechariah 13:7—Matthew 26:31). And "toward evening there will be light" (Zechariah 14:7).

malachie.bio: The last prophet of the Old Testament. A tense dialogue —
malachie.histoire:
The temple is rebuilt, but the fervor is gone: cut-rate offerings, weary priests — "Which one of you would shut the doors so that you don't light my altar's fire in vain?" (Malachi 1:6-10) — broken marriages: "I hate divorce, says the Lord" (Malachi 2:16), withheld tithes: "Bring the whole tithe into the storehouse… Put me to the test in this way… and see if I will not throw open the floodgates of heaven for you" (Malachi 3:10).

The book — and the Old Testament — closes with two promises: "For you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its rays" (Malachi 4:2), and the sending of Elijah before the great day (Malachi 4:5-6) — fulfilled in John the Baptist (Matthew 11:13-14). Then four hundred years of silence, until a voice crying in the wilderness.

josue-sacrificateur.bio: High priest of the return from exile, builder of the altar and temple with Zerubbabel. In Zechariah's vision, the accused one in filthy garments whom God clothes with festive robes.
josue-sacrificateur.histoire:
Son of Jehozadak, returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel, Joshua first rebuilt the altar "though they had reason to fear the peoples of the land" (Ezra 3:2-10), then laid the foundation of the temple and resumed the work at the voice of Haggai (Haggai 1:12-14).

Zechariah saw him in vision standing before the angel of the Lord, Satan at his right hand to accuse him, dressed in filthy garments. "The Lord rebuke you, Satan!… Remove his filthy garments!… See, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with festive robes" (Zechariah 3:1-5). Then the promise: "I will bring my servant, the Branch" (Zechariah 3:8). The high priest justified by grace alone, a figure of every believer—and crowned as a sign of the King-Priest to come (Zechariah 6:11-13).

theophile.bio: "Most Excellent Theophilus": the recipient of Luke's two books — a quarter of the New Testament written so that one man could "know the certainty of the things you have been taught."
theophile.histoire:
Luke dedicates his Gospel to him: "it seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write to you an orderly account, most excellent Theophilus, that you may know the certainty of those things in which you were instructed" (Luke 1:3-4). The title "most excellent" suggests a high-ranking official — the same title borne by Felix (Acts 23:26).

Acts opens again for him: "Theophilus, I made the first account of all that Jesus began both to do and teach" (Acts 1:1). His name means "friend of God": every reader of Luke inherits his place.

herodias.bio: Wife of Herod Philip who left him for his brother Herod Antipas. John the Baptist condemned their union—she obtained his head on a platter through her daughter's dance.
herodias.histoire:
"It is not lawful for you to have your brother's wife": John's word lands the prophet in prison—"Herodias nursed a grudge against him and wanted to kill him," but Herod feared John, "knowing that he was a righteous and holy man... and he liked to listen to him" (Mark 6:17-20).

Her moment comes at the birthday banquet: Herodias's daughter dances, the king swears up to half his kingdom, and the mother whispers her request: "The head of John the Baptist"—delivered on a platter (Mark 6:21-28). The bitterness that refuses truth ends by demanding the head of the one who speaks it.

anne-sacrificateur.bio: Former high priest, father-in-law of Caiaphas, true patriarch of priestly power. Jesus was first brought before him on the night of his arrest.
anne-sacrificateur.histoire:
Luke dates John the Baptist's ministry to "the time of the high priests Annas and Caiaphas" (Luke 3:2): deposed by Rome, Annas retained the title in custom and power within his family — five of his sons and his son-in-law became high priests.

On the night of Gethsemane, Jesus was led "first to Annas" (John 18:12-13): his first interrogation, his first blow — "If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike Me?" (John 18:19-24). He appears again before the Sanhedrin, which forbade the apostles to speak in Jesus's name (Acts 4:5-6). The institution judged its God — without recognizing Him.

jairus.bio: A synagogue leader who fell at Jesus' feet for his twelve-year-old daughter who was dying. Between his plea and his house: a crowd, a healing that
jairus.histoire:
A notable of the synagogue at the feet of a rabbi in dispute: "My little daughter is at the point of death. Come and lay Your hands on her, that she may be healed, and she will live" (Mark 5:22-23). On the way, the woman with the issue of blood stops the procession—and while this happens, the worst news arrives: "Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?" (Mark 5:35).

Jesus turns to the father: "Do not be afraid; only believe" (Mark 5:36). In the room, before the mockers, He takes the child's hand: "Talitha, koum!" which means, "Little girl, I say to you, arise" (Mark 5:41-42). God's delay is never an abandonment: it prepares a greater glory.

bartimee.bio: The blind beggar of Jericho who cried out louder than the crowd: "Son of David, have mercy on me!" He threw his cloak, regained his sight — and followed Jesus on the way.
bartimee.histoire:
Sitting by the roadside, Bartimaeus hears that Jesus of Nazareth is passing by — his last chance before Jerusalem. He cries out; people rebuke him; "but he cried out all the more: 'Son of David, have mercy on me!'" (Mark 10:46-48). Jesus stops: "Call him."

Then this detail Mark preserved: "The blind man threw off his cloak, jumped to his feet, and came to Jesus" — the beggar's cloak, his livelihood spread out, abandoned behind him (Mark 10:49-50). "What do you want me to do for you?… Rabboni… that I may receive my sight… Go, your faith has healed you." "Immediately he received his sight and followed Jesus along the road" (Mark 10:51-52): the road that led up to the cross.

simon-cyrene.bio: A passerby returning from the fields, conscripted to carry Jesus's cross. Mark names his sons, Alexander and Rufus—a sign that carrying the cross one morning had won over his entire family.
simon-cyrene.histoire:
Jesus, exhausted from the flogging, was helped by soldiers who "compelled a certain man, Simon a Cyrenian, the father of Alexander and Rufus, as he was coming out of the country" to carry His cross (Mark 15:21). Luke sharpens the image: "they laid the cross on him, that he might bear it after Jesus" (Luke 23:26)—the very definition of a disciple (Luke 9:23).

That Mark names his sons suggests the church at Rome knew them; Paul greets "Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother and mine" (Romans 16:13). A task imposed on one Easter morning, becoming the honor of a lineage: no one carries the cross by chance.

malchus.bio: Servant of the high priest who came to arrest Jesus in Gethsemane. Peter's sword cut off his right ear—Jesus's last miracle while free was to heal it.
malchus.histoire: In the garden, Peter draws his sword and strikes:

cleopas.bio: One of the two disciples on the road to Emmaus, the one whose name Luke preserved. "We were hoping…": his discouragement on Easter evening became the path for all burning hearts.
cleopas.histoire:
On the road to Emmaus, the stranger asks what they are talking about. "One of them, named Cleopas, answered Him: 'Are You the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have You not known the things which happened there in these days?'" (Luke 24:18). What follows is the most honest of confessions: "We were hoping that it was He who was going to redeem Israel" (Luke 24:21)—hope in the past tense.

The traveler opens to them "in all the Scriptures the things concerning Himself"; at the breaking of bread, their eyes are opened (Luke 24:27-31). "Was not our heart burning within us?"—and Cleopas retraces the road by night back to Jerusalem to announce the Living One (Luke 24:32-35).

salome-disciple.bio: A Galilean disciple, likely the mother of James and John. She served Jesus with her possessions, stood near the cross, and brought spices to the tomb on the morning of the resurrection.
salome-disciple.histoire:
Mark names her among the women who "followed him and served him when he was in Galilee" and who watched the crucifixion from a distance: "Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James the Less and of Joses, and Salome" (Mark 15:40-41). Matthew, in the same passage, speaks of "the mother of the sons of Zebedee" (Matthew 27:56)—the one who had asked for her sons to sit on two thrones (Matthew 20:20-22).

"When the Sabbath was past, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome bought spices, so that they might go and anoint Jesus" (Mark 16:1)—and received from the young man in white the first announcement: "He is risen; He is not here" (Mark 16:6). A mother's clumsy ambition, purified into the faithfulness of a disciple.

jeanne-susanne.bio: Healed women who financed the mission: Joanna, wife of Herod's steward, Susanna and several others "assisted him with their own means." Joanna was among those on Easter morning.
jeanne-susanne.histoire:
Luke pulls back the curtain on the economics of ministry: with the Twelve walked "some women who had been healed of evil spirits and infirmities: Mary, called Magdalene… Joanna the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, Susanna, and several others, who provided for him from their means" (Luke 8:1-3). Money from Herod's house was feeding the Gospel.

Joanna appears again on that decisive morning: among those who found the stone rolled away and "told all these things to the eleven" — who did not believe them (Luke 24:1-11). Serving with your resources, without title or platform: the Gospel also walked on those faithfuls.

marie-bethanie.bio: Sister of Martha and Lazarus. Three scenes, three times at Jesus' feet: to listen, to weep, to pour out costly perfume.
marie-bethanie.histoire:
In her home, while Martha busied herself with serving, Mary "sat at the Lord's feet and listened to what he said." The verdict: "Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her" (Luke 10:39-42). At Lazarus's death, she falls again at his feet—"Lord, if you had been here"—and her tears move Jesus to tears (John 11:32-35).

Six days before Passover, she breaks open the jar: a pound of pure nard, the perfume on his feet, wiped with her hair—three hundred denarii "wasted," Judas protests. Jesus defends her: "Leave her alone. She has kept this perfume for the day of my burial" (John 12:1-8), and Mark adds: "Wherever the gospel is preached throughout the world, what she has done will also be told, in memory of her" (Mark 14:9).

samaritaine.bio: The woman at the well in Sychar, coming to draw water at an hour when she would meet no one. A conversation about living water—and an entire city brought to Jesus through her testimony.
samaritaine.histoire:
Jesus "had to go through Samaria" (John 4:4). Tired, sitting by the well at the sixth hour, he asks her for a drink—a Jew asking a Samaritan woman, a quiet scandal. Then he offers: "If you knew the gift of God... you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water" (John 4:7-14). Five husbands, a sixth who is not: she knows herself known—and it is to her that he reveals himself: "I who speak to you am he" (John 4:16-26).

She leaves her jar, runs to the city: "Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did" (John 4:28-29). Many believed "because of the woman's testimony," then because of him: "he really is the Savior of the world" (John 4:39-42). The shame avoided at noon became the first awakening outside Israel.

rhode.bio: The servant girl in the home of Mary, the mother of John Mark. She recognized Peter's voice when he was delivered — and in her joy, she forgot to open the door for him while the church was praying... without really believing it.
rhode.histoire:
Peter, released from prison by an angel the night before his execution, knocks on the door of the house where "many people had gathered and were praying" for him (Acts 12:5-12). Rhoda comes to listen: "When she recognized Peter's voice, she was so overjoyed she ran back without opening it and exclaimed, 'Peter is at the door!'" (Acts 12:13-14).

The response from the intercessors: "You're out of your mind!… It must be his angel." And Peter "kept on knocking" (Acts 12:15-16). The most delightful scene in Acts: God answers faster than the faith of those who pray — and it's a servant girl who believed first.

agabus.bio: Prophet from Jerusalem: he announced the great famine—triggering the first collection—then, with Paul's belt, the chains that awaited him in Jerusalem.
agabus.histoire:
Coming down to Antioch, Agabus "declared through the Spirit that a great famine would come over the whole earth"; the disciples immediately decide to send relief to the brothers in Judea through Barnabas and Saul (Acts 11:27-30)—the prophecy that invented solidarity among churches.

Years later, in Caesarea, he takes Paul's belt, binds his own hands and feet: "The Jewish leaders in Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt this same way" (Acts 21:10-11). Everyone begs Paul not to go; he answers: "I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 21:12-13). The prophecy did not turn the apostle away: it prepared him.

simon-magicien.bio: The sorcerer of Samaria who "amazed the people" — baptized, then exposed when he tried to buy the power to give the Holy Spirit. His name became a word: simony.
simon-magicien.histoire:
All Samaria regarded him as "the power of God, called the Great Power" (Acts 8:9-11). When Philip proclaims Christ, Simon believes, is baptized, and becomes fascinated by the miracles he witnesses (Acts 8:12-13).

But when the Spirit is given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, the old impulse returns: "Give me also this power" — with money. Peter cuts through it: "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money!… Your heart is not right before God" (Acts 8:18-23). Simon's last word is ambiguous: "Pray to the Lord for me yourselves" (Acts 8:24). You can frequent miracles and still haggle — grace cannot be purchased; it must be received.

enee.bio: A paralyzed man in Lydda, bedridden for eight years. One sentence from Peter—
enee.histoire:
While visiting the believers in Lydda, Peter finds "a man named Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years" (Acts 9:32-33). No fanfare: "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; get up and roll up your mat." And immediately he got up (Acts 9:34)—the healer is named, and it's not Peter.

"All those who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord" (Acts 9:35). Eight years of paralysis, transformed into regional revival: no bed is too old for the word of Christ.

elymas.bio: The sorcerer Bar-Jesus, attached to the proconsul of Cyprus Sergius Paulus. He opposed the Gospel—and was struck with temporary blindness that opened the proconsul's eyes.
elymas.histoire:
At Paphos, the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a "man of understanding," calls for Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God; Elymas "withstood them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith" (Acts 13:6-8).

Then Saul—"also called Paul," and here the name shifts—fixes his gaze on him, filled with the Holy Spirit: "O full of all deceit and all fraud, you son of the devil… you shall be blind, and not see the sun for a season." Mist falls on the sorcerer, and the proconsul believes, "being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord" (Acts 13:9-12). The former blind man of Damascus knew better than anyone that blindness can be a mercy.

denys-damaris.bio: The fruits of Athens: when most mocked the Areopagus speech, "some" believed—including Dionysius the Areopagite, judge of the highest court, and a woman named Damaris.
denys-damaris.histoire:
At the Areopagus speech—the unknown God, the Creator who does not dwell in temples, the call to repentance—the resurrection shattered the audience: "Some mocked, while others said, 'We will hear you again on this matter'" (Acts 17:22-32).

But the next verse saved Athens from failure: "However, some men joined him and believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others with them" (Acts 17:34). A judge from the elite and a woman about whom we know nothing else: the Gospel does not count its fruit in crowds, but in names.

eutychus.bio: The young man from Troas, sitting by the window during Paul's lengthy discourse: fallen asleep, dropped from the third story, picked up dead—and brought back to life. His name means "fortunate."
eutychus.histoire:
Last evening in Troas: the breaking of bread, many lamps in the upper room, and Paul who "continued his discourse until midnight" (Acts 20:7-8). Eutychus, perched on the windowsill, "sank into a deep sleep as Paul spoke on and on. When he was overcome by sleep, he fell from the third story and was picked up dead" (Acts 20:9).

Paul comes down, throws himself on him, wraps his arms around him: "Do not be troubled, for his life is in him"—then goes back up, breaks bread, and speaks on until daybreak. "The young man was brought back alive, and they were not a little comforted" (Acts 20:10-12). Even our sleep is no match for the life of God.

epaphras.bio: Founder of the church at Colossae, a "faithful minister of Christ." His secret ministry: "he is always wrestling for you in his prayers."
epaphras.histoire:
It was from him that the Colossians "learned" the Gospel: "Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant… who is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf" (Colossians 1:7). The church that Paul never visited is the fruit of this disciple from the region.

His portrait is captured in the final greeting: "Epaphras, who is one of you, sends greetings: a servant of Jesus Christ, he is always wrestling for you in his prayers, that you may stand firm, mature and fully assured in all the will of God. For I can testify that he has great concern for you" (Colossians 4:12-13). A fellow prisoner with Paul (Philemon 1:23), he founded through the Word—and sustained through prayer.

epaphrodite.bio: The messenger of the Philippians to Paul in prison: "my brother, my fellow worker and fellow soldier." Sick "unto death" for the work of Christ—honor such people, Paul writes.
epaphrodite.histoire:
The Philippians sent him with their gift for imprisoned Paul (Philippians 4:18). There, Epaphroditus "was indeed sick, and came close to death; but God had mercy on him, and not on him only but on me also, that I might not have sorrow upon sorrow" (Philippians 2:25-27). A touching detail: what troubled him was that his people had learned of his illness (Philippians 2:26).

Paul sends him back as the bearer of the letter, with this instruction: "Receive him therefore in the Lord with all gladness, and hold such people in esteem. For indeed he came close to death for the work of Christ, risking his life" (Philippians 2:28-30). The heroes of the Gospel are sometimes faithful carriers of provision all the way to the end.

tychique.bio: "The beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord": Paul's trusted courier, bearer of letters to the Ephesians and Colossians.
tychique.histoire:
From Asia, Paul's companion from the great collection onward (Acts 20:4), Tychicus is the man of liaison missions: "That you also may know my affairs and how I am doing, Tychicus, a beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, will make known to you all things. I am sending him to you for this very purpose, that he may know your circumstances and comfort your hearts" (Ephesians 6:21-22; Colossians 4:7-8).

To the very end, Paul sends him out again—to Ephesus (2 Timothy 4:12), to Crete to assist Titus (Titus 3:12). Two epistles of the Bible arrived in his satchel: without faithful carriers, we would have no inspired letters on our tables.

demas.bio: Three mentions, one trajectory: "Demas, my fellow worker"… "Demas"… "Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world". The briefest warning in the New Testament.
demas.histoire:
During Paul's first imprisonment, Demas appears among the close companions: "Epaphras… Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my fellow workers" (Philemon 1:23-24). In Colossians, already, his name passes without praise: "Luke the beloved physician greets you, as does Demas" (Colossians 4:14).

Then in Paul's last letter, at the hour of the stake: "Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world, and has departed for Thessalonica" (2 Timothy 4:10). Scripture tells us nothing more—no spectacular fall, no scandal: a love that changed its object. You do not leave the work in a day; you leave it first in the order of your loves.

publius.bio: "The chief man of the island" of Malta. He received the shipwrecked survivors for three days; Paul healed his father of fever—and the whole island brought their sick.
publius.histoire:
After the shipwreck, "there was, in the vicinity, a property belonging to the chief man of the island named Publius, who received us and entertained us courteously for three days" (Acts 28:7)—two hundred and seventy-six soaked shipwrecked survivors, welcomed unconditionally.

His father "was lying down, sick with fever and dysentery; and Paul went in to him and prayed, and laid his hands on him and healed him. So when this was done, the rest of those on the island who had diseases also came and were cured" (Acts 28:8-9). Hospitality shown to a shipwrecked prisoner brought healing to the entire island.

jude-frere.bio: Brother of James—and therefore of Jesus, whom he called by nothing but
jude-frere.histoire: The people of Nazareth mention him among the carpenter's brothers:

gaius-diotrephe.bio: Two faces of one church, in the Bible's shortest letter: Gaius, who "walks in the truth" and welcomes the brothers — and Diotrephes, "who loves to be first."
gaius-diotrephe.histoire:
John writes "to Gaius, the beloved": "I pray that you may prosper in all things and be in health, just as your soul prospers" (3 John 1:1-2). His joy: "to hear that my children walk in truth" — and Gaius proves it by welcoming traveling missionaries, "that we may be fellow workers for the truth" (3 John 1:3-8).

In contrast, Diotrephes, "who loves to have the preeminence among them": he rejects the apostle's authority, spreads malicious words, refuses the brothers and casts out those who receive them (3 John 1:9-10). Between the two, Demetrius with a good testimony (3 John 1:12), and John's rule: "Do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. He who does good is of God" (3 John 1:11). In every church, the question remains: who wants to be first, and who wants to serve?

simon-zelote.bio: One of the Twelve, nicknamed "the Zealot"—probably a former militant of the resistance against Rome, sitting at the same table as Matthew the tax collector.
simon-zelote.histoire: Of him, the Gospels keep only a nickname—"the Zealot" (Luke 6:15), "the Canaanite" (Matthew 10:4)—which speaks volumes about his past: the Zealots wanted to drive Rome out by force. Yet Jesus calls him into the same team as Matthew, a tax collector who gathered taxes for Rome. The sworn enemy and the collaborator, reconciled around the same Master: the Twelve are already a sermon. You find him faithful in the Upper Room, in prayer, after the Ascension (Acts 1:13).

jacques-alphee.bio: A quiet apostle among the Twelve, sometimes called "James the Less." No words from him are recorded—only his faithfulness.
jacques-alphee.histoire: He appears in all four lists of the apostles (Matthew 10:3, Mark 3:18, Luke 6:15, Acts 1:13)—and that's it. Not a word, not a miracle told, not a single question. Tradition calls him "James the Less" to distinguish him from the son of Zebedee. Yet his silence holds an enormous lesson: you can be chosen by Jesus, sent by Jesus, faithful to the end, without ever making headlines. The Kingdom is full of servants whom only the Father has seen (Matthew 6:4).

thaddee.bio: One of the Twelve Apostles, called Thaddaeus or "Jude, son of James." He is the one who asks Jesus at the Last Supper: "Lord, why do you intend to show yourself to us and not to the world?"
thaddee.histoire: Matthew and Mark call him Thaddaeus (Mark 3:18), Luke calls him "Jude, son of James" (Luke 6:16). John carefully specifies "Jude (not Iscariot)" — bearing almost the same name as a traitor requires clarification. His only recorded words reveal a true theologian's question: "Lord, why do you intend to show yourself to us and not to the world?" (John 14:22). Jesus' answer is one of the most beautiful promises in the Gospel: "If anyone loves me, he will obey my teaching. My Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him" (John 14:23).

zebedee.bio: A fisherman of Galilee, father of James and John, husband (presumably) of Salome. He let his two sons go when Jesus called them.
zebedee.histoire: An established fishing business owner, with a boat and hired hands (Mark 1:20): the family enterprise was thriving. Jesus passes by, calls James and John — "leaving their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired hands, they followed him" (Mark 1:20). Scripture records neither protest nor complaint from this father who suddenly saw both his sons and his legacy walk away. Releasing your children to God's calling without holding them back: perhaps that's the greatest quiet offering in the New Testament.

eunuque-ethiopien.bio: High minister of finance for Candace, queen of Ethiopia. He was reading Isaiah in his chariot when Philip joined him—the first named African convert in Acts.
eunuque-ethiopien.histoire: A finance minister returns from Jerusalem, where his status as a eunuch barred him from the assembly (Deuteronomy 23:1). In his chariot, he reads Isaiah 53—the sheep led to slaughter—but doesn't understand. God pulls Philip away from a revival in Samaria for one man on a desert road: "Do you understand what you're reading?" (Acts 8:30). Starting from that passage, Philip "proclaimed to him the good news of Jesus." First water in sight: "Look, here is water; what prevents me from being baptized?" (Acts 8:36). He continued on his way "with joy"—and with him, the gospel went forth to Africa. Isaiah had promised it: the faithful eunuch will receive "an everlasting name" (Isaiah 56:4-5).

sergius-paulus.bio: Roman proconsul of Cyprus, "a man of intelligence," the first high-ranking magistrate converted during Paul's first missionary journey.
sergius-paulus.histoire: In Paphos, the governor of the island "called for Barnabas and Saul, and desired to hear the word of God" (Acts 13:7)—a rare curiosity among a high Roman official. His occult advisor, the sorcerer Elymas, opposed this; Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, struck him with temporary blindness. "Then the proconsul, seeing what had been done, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord" (Acts 13:12). Note: it was the teaching that struck him, even more than the miracle. The gospel had just reached the elite of the Empire.

aristarque.bio: A Macedonian from Thessalonica, Paul's travel companion: dragged into the riot at Ephesus, aboard during a shipwreck, and imprisoned with the apostle.
aristarque.histoire: He always shows up at the worst times—that's his glory. In the riot at Ephesus, the crowd drags him into the theater (Acts 19:29). When Paul sails as a prisoner to Rome, Aristarchus is on board, volunteering for the storm and shipwreck (Acts 27:2). And from Rome, Paul writes: "Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, sends you greetings" (Colossians 4:10). Some friends are there for your successes; Aristarchus is the friend for riots, shipwrecks, and prisons. Christian friendship is measured in those places (Proverbs 17:17).

onesiphore.bio: A Christian from Ephesus who, in Rome, searched prison after prison for Paul "unashamed of his chains" — and found him.
onesiphore.histoire: In his final letter, abandoned by nearly everyone ("all those in Asia have turned away from me," 2 Timothy 1:15), Paul remembers just one: "May the Lord show mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains. On the contrary, when he came to Rome, he eagerly searched for me and found me" (2 Timothy 1:16-17). Searching for a prisoner in Nero's Rome meant compromising yourself: Onesiphorus — "bringer of help," that's what his name means — did it anyway.

crispus.bio: Ruler of the synagogue in Corinth, converted along with his entire household — one of the few people Paul baptized with his own hands.
crispus.histoire: In Corinth, opposition from the synagogue pushes Paul to teach... in the house next door. And then comes the news: "Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord with all his household" (Acts 18:8) — the very leader of the place that had just closed its door to the gospel. Many Corinthians follow. Paul baptizes him personally, something rare for him (1 Corinthians 1:14). The conversion of a single leader can open an entire city to the gospel.

jason.bio: Paul's host in Thessalonica: when the riot couldn't find the apostle, it was Jason who was dragged before the magistrates — he paid the bail.
jason.histoire: Housing Paul came at a cost. In Thessalonica, opponents stir up the city, besiege Jason's house, and failing to find the missionaries, "dragged Jason and some brothers before the city magistrates" under the most explosive charge of the Empire: "They are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying there is another king, Jesus" (Acts 17:6-7). Jason posts bail and sends Paul away by night. Paul later greets him among "his relatives" (Romans 16:21). Hospitality is sometimes an act of courage.

trophime.bio: Christian from Ephesus, companion of Paul. His mere presence in Jerusalem served as a pretext for the riot that led to the apostle's arrest.
trophime.histoire: Jews from Asia, seeing Trophimus in the city with Paul, jump to the worst conclusion: "He has even brought Greeks into the temple" (Acts 21:28-29). It was false—but the riot erupts, and Paul is arrested: the beginning of the long road that will take him to Rome. Last mention, touching in its simplicity: "I left Trophimus sick at Miletus" (2 Timothy 4:20). Even surrounded by apostles, you can remain sick for a time: the health of God's servants is in God's hands, not a machine.

evodie-syntyche.bio: Two gospel workers in Philippi who "struggled together with Paul"—and whom the apostle publicly urges to reconcile.
evodie-syntyche.histoire: "I plead with Euodia and I plead with Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord" (Philippians 4:2). Two precious women—Paul testifies that they "contended at my side in the cause of the gospel" and that their "names are in the book of life" (Philippians 4:3)—yet at odds, so much so that their conflict reaches across the sea to Paul's prison cell. He takes neither side: he asks for help on their behalf and brings them back "in the Lord," the only ground where conflicts dissolve. Being useful to God does not shield you from quarrels; the gospel, however, demands reconciliation (Matthew 5:23-24).

nabot.bio: Owner of a vineyard in Jezreel, neighbor to King Ahab's palace. He refused to sell his ancestral inheritance—and was murdered on false charges.
nabot.histoire: "May the Lord forbid that I should give you the inheritance of my fathers!" (1 Kings 21:3): Naboth defends not a possession, but a covenant—the law forbade the sale of family inheritance (Leviticus 25:23). Ahab sulks; Jezebel orchestrates: a false trial, false witnesses, stoning. But when the king descends to claim the vineyard, Elijah is waiting for him: "Have you murdered and also taken possession?" (1 Kings 21:19). Naboth's blood cries out, and God hears it—as He hears every innocent crushed by the powerful (Psalms 9:12).

asaph.bio: Chief of David's singers, prophet with the cymbal, author of twelve psalms—including Psalm 73, the most honest faith crisis in the psalter.
asaph.histoire: David appoints the Levites, with Asaph at their head, "to invoke, to praise and to celebrate the Lord, the God of Israel" before the ark (1 Chronicles 16:4-5); his sons "prophesied accompanied by the harp, the lute, and cymbals" (1 Chronicles 25:1-2)—for Asaph, music is a ministry. But his masterpiece is a confession: "My feet had almost slipped... for I envied the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (Psalm 73:2-3). The answer comes neither from reasoning nor from a miracle: "Till I went into the sanctuary of God" (Psalm 73:17). And the crisis ends at its peak: "Whom have I in heaven but you? And earth has nothing I desire besides you" (Psalm 73:25).

obed-edom.bio: The man who sheltered the ark of God for three months after Uzzah's tragedy —
obed-edom.histoire: After Uzzah's death, no one wants the ark anymore: David, seized with fear, has it placed in the home of Obed-Edom of Gath. Three months later, word reaches the palace:

barzillai.bio: A wealthy elderly man from Gilead who supplied David with provisions while fleeing from Absalom — and refused any reward: "Why should the king grant me this kindness?"
barzillai.histoire: When David crosses the Jordan, broken and hungry, Barzillai, eighty years old, comes down from his mountains with beds, grain, honey, and cheese because, they said, "The people have suffered from hunger, weariness, and thirst in the wilderness" (2 Samuel 17:27-29). With victory restored, David wants to take him to finish his days at court: the old man declines with magnificent freedom — "How many more years will I live?… Let your servant return, that I may die in my own city, near the grave of my father and mother" (2 Samuel 19:34-37). He sends Kimham in his place. On his deathbed, David will commend him again to Solomon (1 Kings 2:7): kindness remembers for a long time.

elkana.bio: Husband of Hannah and father of Samuel. Each year he went up to Shiloh to worship—and he loved Hannah, the barren one, with a double portion.
elkana.histoire: In a household torn by the rivalry of two wives, Elkanah held fast to faithfulness: "This man went up year by year from his city to Shiloh, to worship before the Lord of hosts" (1 Samuel 1:3). To Hannah, humiliated by her barrenness, he gave a double portion, for he loved Hannah (1 Samuel 1:5), along with this tender and clumsy word: "Am I not better to you than ten sons?" (1 Samuel 1:8). When Hannah devoted her future son to God, he did not oppose her: "Do what seems good to you" (1 Samuel 1:23). Israel's greatest prophet-judge grew upon this quiet foundation.

achija.bio: Prophet of Shiloh who tore his new cloak into twelve pieces to announce to Jeroboam the division of the kingdom—then, blind and aged, unmasked the disguised queen.
achija.histoire: On a country road, Ahijah seizes his new cloak and tears it into twelve pieces: "Take for yourself ten pieces! For thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Behold, I will tear the kingdom from the hand of Solomon" (1 Kings 11:30-31). Years later, Jeroboam—now king, now idolatrous—sends his wife disguised to consult the old prophet who has become blind. But God sees for him: "Come in, wife of Jeroboam; why do you pretend to be another? " (1 Kings 14:6). You can deceive men, but never the One who speaks through them.

hanania-prophete.bio: Prophet from Gibeon who contradicted Jeremiah during a crisis: "Within two years, the yoke of Babylon will be broken." He died that very year, just as Jeremiah had announced.
hanania-prophete.histoire: Facing the wooden yoke that Jeremiah wore, Hananiah prophesies what everyone wants to hear: in two years, everything will return to normal (Jeremiah 28:2-4). He tears off the yoke and breaks it — a spectacular gesture, shallow theology. Jeremiah first responds: "Amen! May the Lord do so!" (Jeremiah 28:6) — he would have loved it to be true — then returns with the word he received: an iron yoke will replace the wood, "Behold, I will remove you from the face of the earth; you will die this year, because you have uttered rebellion against the Lord" (Jeremiah 28:13-16). He died in the seventh month. The criterion remains: the word fulfilled (Deuteronomy 18:22), not the popularity of the message.

sanballat.bio: Governor of Samaria, fierce opponent of Nehemiah: mockery, armed threats, traps, and open letters—nothing stopped the wall.
sanballat.histoire: His arsenal is a complete manual of opposition: mockery—"What are these feeble Jews doing?" (Nehemiah 4:2), echoed by his ally Tobiah: "If a fox jumped on it, he would break down their stone wall!" (Nehemiah 4:3)—then armed threat, then the trap invitation—"let us meet together in one of the villages in the Plain of Ono"—repeated four times (Nehemiah 6:2-4), an open letter of slander, and even a hired prophet to push Nehemiah into hiding in the temple. Nehemiah's tireless response: "I am doing a great work and I cannot come down" (Nehemiah 6:3), and prayer. The wall was completed in fifty-two days—"all the nations...recognized that this work had been accomplished by our God" (Nehemiah 6:15-16).

schaphan.bio: Secretary to King Josiah: he read the Book of the Law to the king when it was discovered in the temple—triggering Judah's greatest reform. His sons would protect Jeremiah.
schaphan.histoire: Sent to settle construction accounts, Shaphan returned from the temple with far more: "The priest Hilkiah has given me a book. And Shaphan read it aloud before the king" (2 Kings 22:10). This reading pierced Josiah's heart and triggered the deepest reform in Judah's history. Shaphan also founded a rare lineage: his son Ahikam would save Jeremiah from death (Jeremiah 26:24), his son Gemariah would plead with the king not to burn the scroll (Jeremiah 36:25), his grandson Gedaliah would govern the survivors. An entire family standing with God's Word, across three generations.

jotham-roi.bio: King of Judah, son of Uzziah. Sixteen years of faithful reign and building — "he became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God."
jotham-roi.histoire: He grew up in the shadow of a terrible lesson: his father Uzziah, a great king but overcome by pride, struck with leprosy for forcing his way into the temple (2 Chronicles 26:16-21). Jotham learns it all: "he did what was right in the sight of the Lord… only, he did not enter the temple of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 27:2) — faithfulness without presumption. He builds the upper gate of the temple, cities, towers, and wins his wars. And the text reveals his secret in one sentence to remember: "Jotham became mighty, because he prepared his ways before the Lord his God" (2 Chronicles 27:6).

ruben.bio: Firstborn son of Jacob and Leah, ancestor of the tribe of Reuben. He wanted to save Joseph from his brothers, but lost his birthright through a grave sin.
ruben.histoire: Leah calls him Reuben, for "the Lord has seen my humiliation" (Genesis 29:32). It is he who restrains his brothers from killing Joseph and proposes the pit, for "he had the intention to deliver him from their hands"; returning too late, he tears his clothes (Genesis 37:21-22, 29-30). But his liaison with Bilhah (Genesis 35:22) costs him his firstborn status: "Unstable as water, you shall not excel" (Genesis 49:3-4)—the birthright passes to the sons of Joseph (1 Chronicles 5:1). His tribe will settle east of the Jordan (Numbers 32).

simeon-fils.bio: Second son of Jacob and Leah. With Levi, he avenged his sister Dinah through a massacre; held hostage in Egypt by Joseph. His tribe was absorbed into that of Judah.
simeon-fils.histoire: His name echoes Leah's prayer: "the Lord has heard" (Genesis 29:33). After the outrage done to Dinah, Simeon and Levi put Shechem to the sword (Genesis 34:25), and Jacob is angered. In Egypt, it is Simeon whom Joseph keeps bound until Benjamin's return (Genesis 42:24). Jacob's blessing becomes a warning: "I will divide them in Jacob" (Genesis 49:5-7)—the tribe of Simeon received its cities in the midst of Judah's territory (Joshua 19:1, 9).

levi-fils.bio: Third son of Jacob and Leah, ancestor of the Levites and the priesthood: Moses, Aaron, and the entire priestly family descended from him.
levi-fils.histoire: "This time my husband will become attached to me": Levi means attached (Genesis 29:34). His violence at Shechem brought him the same curse as Simeon—to be scattered (Genesis 49:7). But God reversed the sentence: at the golden calf, the sons of Levi took the Lord's side (Exodus 32:26-29), and the scattering became a calling. The tribe would have no territory, for "the Lord is his inheritance" (Deuteronomy 10:9): they lived in forty-eight cities throughout Israel to serve there (Numbers 35:7).

dan-fils.bio: First son of Bilhah, Rachel's servant. From his tribe came Oholiab, the craftsman of the tabernacle, and Samson.
dan-fils.histoire: Rachel, barren, cried out at his birth: "God has judged me" — Dan means he judged (Genesis 30:6). Jacob declared: "Dan will judge his people… Dan will be a serpent on the path" (Genesis 49:16-17). His tribe, cramped for space, migrated northward, captured the city of Laish, and renamed it Dan — but established an idolatrous cult there (Judges 18:27-31). Yet it gave Israel both Oholiab (Exodus 31:6) and Samson (Judges 13:2).

nephthali.bio: Second son of Bilhah. His territory in Galilee around the lake would become the heart of Jesus' ministry.
nephthali.histoire: "I have wrestled with my sister in a divine struggle and have prevailed": Naphtali carries the rivalry of Rachel and Leah in his name (Genesis 30:8). Jacob blesses him: "Naphtali is a deer set free" (Genesis 49:21). Barak, the commander of the army alongside Deborah, came from Kedesh in Naphtali (Judges 4:6). Isaiah announces that over "the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali," "the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light" (Isaiah 8:23; 9:1)—and Matthew sees Jesus establishing Himself in Capernaum there (Matthew 4:13-16).

gad-fils.bio: First son of Zilpah, Leah's servant. His tribe, known for warfare, settled east of the Jordan River.
gad-fils.histoire: "What good fortune!" Leah exclaims at his birth (Genesis 30:11). Jacob foretells a warlike tribe: "Gad will be attacked by bands of raiders, but he will attack them and pursue them" (Genesis 49:19). The Gadites received the pastures of Gilead (Numbers 32:33) and provided David with elite men, "like lions, and as swift as gazelles on the mountains" (1 Chronicles 12:8).

aser.bio: Second son of Zilpah. Tribe of the fertile lands of the northwest—and tribe of Anna the prophetess, who recognized the child Jesus in the temple.
aser.histoire: "How happy I am!" said Leah: Asher means happy (Genesis 30:13). His portion is abundance: "Asher's food will be rich; he will provide delicacies fit for a king" (Genesis 49:20), "Let him dip his foot in oil!" (Deuteronomy 33:24). Centuries later, an eighty-four-year-old widow from the tribe of Asher, Anna, praised God in the temple and spoke of the child Jesus "to all who were looking forward to the redemption of Jerusalem" (Luke 2:36-38).

issacar.bio: Fifth son of Leah. His descendants became famous for their discernment: they had
issacar.histoire: His birth follows the episode of the mandrakes; Leah sees in it a reward from God (Genesis 30:18). Jacob compares him to "a strong donkey" who prefers the rest of good land to risk (Genesis 49:14-15). But in David's time, the Bible makes the sons of Issachar a model: "men who understood the times and knew what Israel should do" (1 Chronicles 12:32).

zabulon.bio: Sixth and last son of Leah. A tribe in Galilee, named by Isaiah among the lands where the great light would rise.
zabulon.histoire: "This time my husband will live with me" (Genesis 30:20). Jacob declares that he "will dwell by the seashore" (Genesis 49:13). In Deborah's song, Zebulun is "a people who offered themselves willingly" for Israel's deliverance (Judges 5:18). Along with Naphtali, he is named in Isaiah's promise fulfilled when Jesus begins to preach in Galilee (Matthew 4:15-16).

benjamin.bio: The youngest son of Jacob and the only brother of Joseph through Rachel, who died giving birth to him. From his tribe would come Ehud, King Saul, Mordecai, and the apostle Paul.
benjamin.histoire: As Rachel lay dying, she called him Ben-Oni (son of my sorrow); Jacob renamed him Benjamin (son of the right hand) (Genesis 35:18). All the trials Joseph puts his brothers through revolve around him: the silver cup in his sack, then Judah offering to become a slave in his place (Genesis 44). Jacob compares him to "a wolf that tears prey" (Genesis 49:27). Paul would later proudly present himself as "of the tribe of Benjamin" (Philippians 3:5).

ephraim-fils.bio: Joseph's second son, born in Egypt. Jacob blessed him before his older brother: his tribe became the most powerful in the north, to the point that "Ephraim" often designates the entire kingdom of Israel.
ephraim-fils.histoire: Joseph names him Ephraim, because "God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction" (Genesis 41:52). Before old Jacob, nearly blind, he is placed on the left—but Jacob crosses his hands and places his right hand on him: "his younger brother shall be greater than he" (Genesis 48:14-19). Joshua was from this tribe (Numbers 13:8). The prophets will call all Israel by his name: "What shall I do with you, Ephraim?" (Hosea 11:8).

manasse-fils.bio: Eldest son of Joseph, adopted by Jacob along with his brother Ephraim. His tribe extended on both sides of the Jordan; Gideon came from it.
manasse-fils.histoire: "God has made me forget all my suffering": Joseph expresses through this name the healing of his family wound (Genesis 41:51). Jacob adopts him as his own son (Genesis 48:5), but blesses the younger son before him. The half-tribe of Manasseh received the north of Gilead and Bashan to the east (Numbers 32:33), the other half a territory to the west (Joshua 17). Gideon, "the least in my father's house," came from Manasseh (Judges 6:15).

dina.bio: Daughter of Jacob and Leah. Her dishonoring by the prince of Shechem triggered the terrible revenge of her brothers Simeon and Levi.
dina.histoire: Dinah goes out to see the daughters of the land; Shechem, son of Hamor, seizes and dishonors her, then wants to marry her (Genesis 34:1-4). Her brothers pretend to accept an alliance, demand the circumcision of the men of the city—and Simeon and Levi massacre them while they suffer (Genesis 34:25). The account hides nothing: neither the crime against Dinah, nor the excessive revenge that Jacob condemns (Genesis 34:30; 49:5-7).

bilha.bio: Servant of Rachel, given by her to Jacob to bear children; mother of Dan and Naphtali.
bilha.histoire: Laban had given her to Rachel on the day of her wedding (Genesis 29:29). Rachel, desperate for not having children, gives her to Jacob according to the custom of the time: "that she may bear children for me" (Genesis 30:3). Two sons are born, Dan and Naphtali, whom Rachel names herself. Later, Reuben lies with her, a sin that costs him his birthright (Genesis 35:22).

zilpa.bio: Servant of Leah, given to Jacob; mother of Gad and Asher.
zilpa.histoire: Laban gave her to Leah as a servant (Genesis 29:24). When Leah stopped bearing children, she in turn gave Zilpah to Jacob, who gave her two sons: Gad, "What good fortune!" and Asher, "How happy I am!" (Genesis 30:9-13). Two tribes of Israel were born from this voiceless servant in the account.

sem.bio: Son of Noah, ancestor of the Semitic peoples, of Abraham, and—through him—of Jesus.
sem.histoire: (Genesis 9:26)—the first time God is linked to the name of a lineage. The genealogy in Genesis 11 leads from Shem to Abraham, and Luke traces it all the way to Christ (Luke 3:36).

cham.bio: Son of Noah, ancestor of the peoples of Egypt, Cush, and Canaan. His lack of respect toward his father brought a curse upon his son Canaan.
cham.histoire: Ham saw his father naked and drunk in his tent, and went to tell his brothers instead of covering him (Genesis 9:22). Noah then cursed Canaan, Ham's son (Genesis 9:25). His descendants — Cush, Egypt (Mizraim), Put, and Canaan — populated Africa and the Near East (Genesis 10:6). The Psalms would call Egypt "the land of Ham" (Psalms 105:23). The curse was directed at Canaan alone: it never justified contempt toward any people, for all nations are called to Abraham's blessing (Genesis 12:3).

japhet.bio: Son of Noah, ancestor of the peoples of the coasts and islands: Greeks, Medes, and northern nations.
japhet.histoire: With Shem, he covers his father's nakedness (Genesis 9:23). Noah blesses him: "May God enlarge Japheth's possessions, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem" (Genesis 9:27)—a word often read as a promise of nations welcomed into Israel's blessing. His sons, including Javan (Greece) and Madai (the Medes), populate "the isles of the nations" (Genesis 10:2-5).

metuschelah.bio: Son of Enoch and grandfather of Noah: the oldest man in the Bible, who died at 969 years old.
metuschelah.histoire: "All the days of Methuselah were nine hundred and sixty-nine years; and he died" (Genesis 5:27). Son of Enoch, the man who "walked with God" and was taken up (Genesis 5:24), he is the father of Lamech and the grandfather of Noah. By adding up the ages in Genesis 5, his death falls in the very year of the flood: God's patience lasted through the end of a very long life.

lemec-cain.bio: A descendant of Cain, the first polygamist in the Bible, and author of a song of excessive vengeance.
lemec-cain.histoire: Lamech takes two wives, Adah and Zillah; his sons invent nomadic herding, music, and metalworking (Genesis 4:19-22). Then he sings: "I have killed a man for wounding me… If Cain is avenged sevenfold, then Lamech seventy-sevenfold" (Genesis 4:23-24). This is the progress of civilization without God, and of violence with it. Jesus will reverse this number exactly: forgive "up to seventy times seven" (Matthew 18:22).

lemec-noe.bio: Son of Methuselah and father of Noah, who looked to his son for relief from the toil of work.
lemec-noe.histoire: At the birth of his son, Lamech spoke a word of hope: "This one will bring us relief from our work and from the painful toil of our hands, which come from the ground the Lord has cursed" (Genesis 5:29). He names the child Noah, and it is indeed through him that God will give humanity a fresh start.

terach.bio: Father of Abraham, Nahor, and Haran. He left Ur of the Chaldeans for Canaan, but stopped at Haran, where he died.
terach.histoire: "Terah took his son Abram, and Lot… They went out together from Ur of the Chaldeans to go to the land of Canaan. And they came to Haran and dwelt there" (Genesis 11:31). He died in Haran at 205 years old, halfway through a promise he had never received. Joshua would recall that Terah and his household "served other gods" (Joshua 24:2): Abraham's faith was born in an idolatrous family, by pure grace.

nachor.bio: Abraham's brother who remained in Mesopotamia. Grandfather of Rebekah and Laban: it was in his family that Isaac and Jacob would find their wives.
nachor.histoire: Married to Milcah, he had eight sons, including Bethuel, father of Rebekah (Genesis 22:20-23). Abraham's servant departs to find a wife for Isaac "to the city of Nahor" (Genesis 24:10). Later, Laban swears by "the God of Abraham and of Nahor" (Genesis 31:53). His family shows how singular Abraham's choice was: to leave while his own people stayed.

bethuel.bio: Son of Nahor, nephew of Abraham, father of Rebekah and Laban.
bethuel.histoire: When Abraham's servant tells how God led him to the well and to Rebekah, Laban and Bethuel respond: "This thing comes from the Lord; we cannot speak to you bad or good" (Genesis 24:50). Jacob, fleeing Esau, will be sent "to Padan Aram, to the house of Bethuel, the father of your mother" (Genesis 28:2).

ketura.bio: Wife of Abraham after Sarah's death, mother of six sons, including Midian, ancestor of the Midianites.
ketura.histoire: "Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah" (Genesis 25:1). Among her sons was Midian, father of the people among whom Moses would find refuge and take a wife. Abraham gave gifts to these sons and then sent them to the east, away from Isaac, the child of the promise (Genesis 25:5-6).

eliezer-damas.bio: Steward of Abraham's household, his presumed heir before Isaac's birth.
eliezer-damas.histoire: "Lord God, what will You give me? I go childless; and the heir of my house is Eliezer of Damascus" (Genesis 15:2). God's answer is one of the most beautiful promises in the Bible: "Look toward heaven, and count the stars" — and Abram "believed in the Lord, and He accounted it to him for righteousness" (Genesis 15:5-6). He is often identified as the servant sent to find Rebekah (Genesis 24), but the text does not name him.

hamor.bio: Hivite prince of Shechem, from whom Jacob bought a field; father of Shechem who violated Dinah.
hamor.histoire: Jacob buys from his sons a field for one hundred pieces of silver and sets up an altar there (Genesis 33:19-20). After his son's violation of Dinah, Hamor negotiates an alliance—which ends in the massacre of his city (Genesis 34). This same field will later receive the bones of Joseph, brought back from Egypt (Joshua 24:32).

perets.bio: Son of Judah and Tamar, ancestor of Boaz, of David—and of Jesus.
perets.histoire: Twin of Zerah, he is born first even though his brother had already put out his hand: "What a breach you have made!" cries the midwife—hence his name, Perez, the breach (Genesis 38:29). Born of a troubled story, he becomes the royal line: the genealogy of Ruth goes "from Perez… to David" (Ruth 4:18-22), and Matthew inscribes him in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3). God writes straight with broken lines.

asnath.bio: Egyptian wife of Joseph, daughter of a priest of On, mother of Manasseh and Ephraim.
asnath.histoire: Pharaoh gives Asenath to Joseph the day he elevates him to rule over Egypt (Genesis 41:45). Before the famine, she bears him two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim (Genesis 41:50-52) — two tribes of Israel therefore have an Egyptian mother: from the beginning, the family of promise is open to the nations.

oholiab.bio: Son of Ahisamak, from the tribe of Dan: a skilled craftsman, engraver, designer, and embroiderer who served as assistant to Bezalel in the construction of the tabernacle.
oholiab.histoire: the ability to teach" (Exodus 35:34): true skill is passed down. Oholiab was "skilled to engrave, to devise, and to embroider in blue, purple, and crimson fabrics" (Exodus 38:23).

hur.bio: Companion of Moses: with Aaron, he held up his hands during the battle against Amalek. Likely the grandfather of Bezalel.
hur.histoire: At Rephidim, "when Moses lifted his hand, Israel prevailed." When his arms grow tired, Aaron and Hur make him sit on a stone: "Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on one side and one on the other" until sunset (Exodus 17:11-12). An eternal picture of the ministry of support. When Moses goes up the mountain, he entrusts the people to Aaron and Hur (Exodus 24:14). A Hur of Judah, most likely him, is the grandfather of Bezalel, who will build the tabernacle (Exodus 31:2).

ithamar.bio: Fourth son of Aaron, a priest. He directed the Levites in the service of the tabernacle; from him descended the line of the priest Eli.
ithamar.histoire: After the death of Nadab and Abihu, struck down for offering strange fire, Ithamar and Eleazar remained the only priests alongside Aaron (Leviticus 10:6, 12). He kept the inventory of the tabernacle (Exodus 38:21) and directed the families of Gershon and Merari, who were responsible for the curtains and the frames (Numbers 4:28, 33). In David's time, the priestly families would be divided between his descendants and those of Eleazar (1 Chronicles 24:3-4).

amram.bio: A Levite, grandson of Levi, father of Aaron, Moses, and Miriam.
amram.histoire: "Amram took for himself Jochebed, his father's sister, as his wife; and she bore him Aaron and Moses" (Exodus 6:20). He lived one hundred thirty-seven years. Though no words from him are recorded, he belongs to that generation of parents honored by the epistle to the Hebrews: "By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden three months by his parents, because they saw he was a beautiful child; and they were not afraid of the king's command" (Hebrews 11:23).

jokebed.bio: Mother of Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. She hid Moses for three months, then entrusted him to the Nile in a basket—and was paid to nurse him.
jokebed.histoire: Exodus 2 does not name her, but it is she: seeing that her child is beautiful, she hides him for three months despite Pharaoh's command, then places him in a basket of papyrus coated with tar, among the reeds (Exodus 2:2-3). Pharaoh's daughter finds him—and, through Miriam's intervention, it is Jochebed herself who is hired, and paid, to nurse her son (Exodus 2:7-9). A mother's faith preserved Israel's deliverer (Hebrews 11:23).

dathan-abiram.bio: Two brothers from the tribe of Reuben, leaders of Korah's revolt against Moses; the earth opened and swallowed them.
dathan-abiram.histoire: Summoned by Moses, they refused: "We will not go up" — and they dared call Egypt "a land flowing with milk and honey" (Numbers 16:12-14). Their revolt rewrites history: slavery becomes regretted, deliverance a deception. "The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them, them and their households" (Numbers 16:31-33). The Psalm remembers it: "The earth opened and swallowed up Dathan" (Psalms 106:17).

filles-tselophchad.bio: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah: five sisters without a brother who asked Moses for their father's inheritance—and obtained from God a new law for daughters.
filles-tselophchad.histoire: Their father died in the wilderness without sons; by custom, his name would be erased and his share lost. The five sisters come forward before Moses, Eleazar, and the whole assembly:

eldad-medad.bio: Two of the seventy elders of Israel who prophesied in the camp, to Joshua's dismay—and to Moses' delight.
eldad-medad.histoire: The Spirit rests on the seventy elders gathered around the tent; Eldad and Medad, who remained in the camp, also prophesy (Numbers 11:25-26). Joshua, jealous for his master, cries out: "Moses, my lord, stop them!" Moses' answer is a prophecy of Pentecost: "Oh, that all the Lord's people were prophets and that the Lord would put his Spirit on them!" (Numbers 11:28-29; Acts 2:17).

zimri-cozbi.bio: A leader of the tribe of Simeon and a Midianite princess whose provocation, in the midst of a plague, was stopped by the zeal of Phinehas.
zimri-cozbi.histoire: At Baal-Peor, Israel turns to idolatry and sexual immorality, and a plague strikes the people. Before the eyes of Moses and the weeping assembly, Zimri brings the Midianite woman Cozbi into his tent (Numbers 25:6, 14–15). Phinehas pierces them through, and the plague stops; God gives him "a covenant of peace" (Numbers 25:12). The account reminds us that the public sin of a leader brings judgment upon an entire people.

balak.bio: King of Moab who paid the diviner Balaam to curse Israel — and received only blessings instead.
balak.histoire: Terrified by a people who "cover the face of the earth," Balak sends for Balaam: "Come now, I pray you, curse me this people" (Numbers 22:5-6). Three times he takes him to a high place, three times Balaam blesses — "How shall I curse whom God has not cursed?" (Numbers 23:8). Complete failure: no one can curse those whom God blesses. Micah makes it a memorial (Micah 6:5), and Revelation recalls how Balaam later taught Balak to make Israel fall through seduction (Revelation 2:14).

nachschon.bio: Son of Amminadab, prince of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness, first to present his offering at the dedication of the altar. Ancestor of David and Jesus.
nachschon.histoire: Chief of Judah, he camps to the east of the tabernacle, at the head of all Israel's journey (Numbers 2:3; 10:14). On the first day of the dedication of the altar, he presents the offering (Numbers 7:12). His sister Elisheba marries Aaron (Exodus 6:23): Judah and Levi, kingship and priesthood, are linked from the wilderness onward. The genealogy places him among the ancestors of David (Ruth 4:20) and of Christ (Matthew 1:4).

hobab.bio: A Midianite from the family of Moses' father-in-law, invited by him to guide Israel in the wilderness: "you will serve as our guide."
hobab.histoire: As Israel was about to leave Sinai, Moses insisted: "Please don't leave us, for you know the places where we camp in the wilderness, and you will serve as our guide. And if you come with us, we will share with you all the good that the Lord does for us" (Numbers 10:31-32). Moses, who had God's cloud, did not despise the experience of a desert man. His descendants, the Kenites, would settle among Israel (Judges 1:16; 4:11).

schiphra-pua.bio: The two Hebrew midwives who disobeyed Pharaoh to save the newborns — the first resisters of the Exodus.
schiphra-pua.histoire: Pharaoh commands them to kill the baby boys at birth. "But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them" (Exodus 1:17). When summoned, they get out of it with wit. "God dealt well with the midwives... And so, because the midwives feared God, He provided families for them" (Exodus 1:20-21). The Pharaoh of that era is unnamed; they are.

acsa.bio: Daughter of Caleb, given in marriage to Othniel, the conqueror of Kirjath-sepher. She dared to ask her father for springs of water—and received them.
acsa.histoire: Caleb promises his daughter to the one who takes Kirjath-sepher; Othniel conquers it (Joshua 15:16-17). Acsah, receiving land in the dry south, gets down from her donkey and says to her father: "Give me a blessing... also give me springs of water. And he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs" (Joshua 15:18-19). An audacity of faith that asks for more than the minimum—and a father who gives more than he is asked (Luke 11:13).

schamgar.bio: Judge of Israel who killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad.
schamgar.histoire: Only one verse is dedicated to him: "After him was Shamgar the son of Anath, who killed six hundred men of the Philistines with an ox goad; and he also delivered Israel" (Judges 3:31). A farmer's simple tool becomes mighty in God's hands. The Song of Deborah recalls the distress of his time: "In the days of Shamgar… the highways were abandoned" (Judges 5:6).

barak.bio: Commander of Israel's army called by the prophetess Deborah; he defeated Sisera at the Kishon River. Listed among the heroes of faith.
barak.histoire: Deborah summons him from Kedesh in Naphtali with God's command: to gather ten thousand men on Mount Tabor (Judges 4:6). Barak hesitates: "If you will go with me, I will go"—and Deborah warns that the glory of victory will belong to a woman (Judges 4:8-9). Yet he descends from Tabor, and the Lord routes Sisera's nine hundred chariots (Judges 4:14-15). The epistle to the Hebrews lists him among those who, "by faith, conquered kingdoms" (Hebrews 11:32-33).

sisera.bio: Commander of the army of Jabin, a Canaanite king, with nine hundred iron chariots. Defeated by Barak, he was killed by Jael in her tent.
sisera.histoire: For twenty years, his nine hundred iron chariots oppressed Israel (Judges 4:3). Routed at the Kishon, he fled on foot to Jael's tent, where she gives him milk, covers him—then drives a tent peg through his temple while he sleeps (Judges 4:17-21). Deborah's song ends with a poignant image: his mother at the window, wondering "why is his chariot so long in coming?" (Judges 5:28).

thola.bio: Judge of Israel for twenty-three years, from the tribe of Issachar.
thola.histoire: "After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, a man of Issachar, arose to deliver Israel; he lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim. He judged Israel twenty-three years" (Judges 10:1-2). After the bloody chaos of Abimelech, God gives twenty-three years of peace with no exploits recorded: ordinary faithfulness is also a deliverance.

jair-juge.bio: A judge of Gilead for twenty-two years, father of thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys.
jair-juge.histoire: "After him arose Jair, a Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years. And he had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty cities, which are called Havoth Jair to this day" (Judges 10:3-4). A time of quiet prosperity — just before the people fell back into idolatry (Judges 10:6).

ibtsan.bio: A judge of Israel from Bethlehem, for seven years.
ibtsan.histoire: "After him, Ibzan of Bethlehem was judge in Israel. He had thirty sons and thirty daughters whom he married off outside his family, and he brought in thirty young women from outside for his sons. He was judge in Israel for seven years" (Judges 12:8-9). His alliances reveal a man who built bonds between the clans of Israel.

elon-juge.bio: Judge of Israel for ten years, from the tribe of Zebulun.
elon-juge.histoire: "After him, Elon of Zebulun was judge in Israel; and he judged Israel ten years. Then Elon of Zebulun died and was buried at Aijalon in the country of Zebulun" (Judges 12:11-12). Ten years of service, two verses: many faithful servants have no other memory than God's.

abdon-juge.bio: Judge of Israel for eight years, from Pirathon in Ephraim, with forty sons and thirty grandsons.
abdon-juge.histoire: "After him, Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite was judge in Israel. He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. He was judge in Israel for eight years" (Judges 12:13-14). He is the last of the "minor judges" before the forty years of Philistine oppression that precede Samson.

manoach.bio: A man of Dan from Zorah, father of Samson. Together with his wife, he received a visit from the angel of the Lord who announced the birth of the deliverer.
manoach.histoire: The angel appears first to his barren wife; Manoah prays for him to return: "Please let him teach us what we should do for the child who will be born" (Judges 13:8). He asks for his name: "Why do you ask my name? It is wonderful" (Judges 13:18). During the burnt offering, the angel ascends in the flame of the altar. Manoah is afraid: "We will surely die, because we have seen God"; his wife, wiser, replies that God would not have shown them all these things only to cause them to die (Judges 13:22-23).

mica-ephraim.bio: A man from Ephraim who made an idol and hired a Levite as his private priest—a portrait of religion made to order.
relations: Sanctuary taken by the tribe of
mica-ephraim.histoire: Micah steals eleven hundred shekels from his mother, returns them, and she dedicates the money "to the Lord"… to make an idol (Judges 17:2-4). He sets up a sanctuary, then hires a young Levite: "Now I know that the Lord will be good to me, because I have this Levite as my priest" (Judges 17:13). The Danites steal everything from him—idol and priest alike (Judges 18:18-24). The refrain of the book says it all: "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 17:6).

isai.bio: A man from Bethlehem, grandson of Boaz and Ruth, father of David and his seven brothers. The prophet announces that from the
isai.histoire: Samuel comes to anoint a king; Jesse presents his sons one by one, the most impressive first. God sets them all aside: "Man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). They must go fetch the youngest, who is tending the sheep. Centuries later, when royalty is nothing but a stump, Isaiah promises: "A Branch will come up from the stump of Jesse" (Isaiah 11:1)—Paul will see in this Jesus, the hope of the nations (Romans 15:12).

eliab.bio: Firstborn son of Jesse, David's brother. Samuel thought him chosen for his impressive appearance—God did not.
eliab.histoire: When Eliab steps forward, Samuel thinks:

merab.bio: Saul's eldest daughter, promised to David but given to another.
merab.histoire: When the time comes, Saul gives her to Adriel of Meholah (1 Samuel 18:19)—a royal promise broken among many others.

abischai.bio: Nephew of David, brother of Joab and Asahel: a formidable and loyal warrior, quick to strike—too quick, often.
abischai.histoire: He enters by night with David into Saul's sleeping camp:

asael.bio: Brother of Joab and Abishai, "as light-footed as a gazelle in the field." Killed by Abner while pursuing him; his death triggered a cycle of revenge.
asael.histoire: He relentlessly pursued Abner, never turning right or left. Abner pleaded with him twice to give up: "Why should I strike you down and kill you?" — then struck him with the butt of his spear (2 Samuel 2:18-23). Joab avenged his brother by assassinating Abner at the gate of Hebron (2 Samuel 3:27) — a cycle of bloodshed that David would grieve until his death (1 Kings 2:5).

ittai.bio: A Philistine from Gath, a foreigner in exile, who chose to follow David in flight: "Wherever my lord the king goes, there your servant will go as well."
ittai.histoire: When David flees Absalom, he says to Ittai, a recent arrival: "Why should you come with us? Go back." The response of this foreigner echoes that of Ruth: "As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives, surely in whatever place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will your servant be" (2 Samuel 15:19-21). David entrusts him with a third of his army (2 Samuel 18:2).

huschai.bio: "David's friend": he pretended to join Absalom to thwart Ahithophel's counsel—and saved the king.
huschai.histoire: David had just prayed: "Thwart the counsel of Ahithophel!" At the summit of the Mount of Olives, Hushai arrives, his tunic torn—the answer to prayer (2 Samuel 15:31-34). Infiltrated among Absalom's followers, he counters Ahithophel's formidable plan with a flattering and slow one that prevails: "The Lord had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel" (2 Samuel 17:14). He warns David in time to cross the Jordan.

tsiba.bio: A servant of Saul's household who revealed to David the existence of Mephibosheth—then slandered him to enrich himself.
tsiba.histoire: It was through him that David found the lame son of Jonathan and showed him favor (2 Samuel 9:2-3). But during Absalom's revolt, Ziba comes with donkeys loaded with provisions and accuses his master of betrayal; David gives him all his possessions (2 Samuel 16:1-4). Upon his return, Mephibosheth pleads his case; David divides the land (2 Samuel 19:24-29). The account warns us: a timely gift may conceal slander (Proverbs 18:17).

isch-boscheth.bio: Son of Saul, made king over Israel by Abner for two years, opposing David who reigned in Hebron. Assassinated in his bed.
isch-boscheth.histoire: After Saul's death, Abner makes him king at Mahanaim: Israel is divided in two (2 Samuel 2:8-10). A puppet king, he quarrels with Abner over Rizpah (2 Samuel 3:7-11), and Abner goes over to David. Two of his commanders assassinate him during his nap and bring his head to David, hoping for a reward; David has them executed, for "wicked men have murdered a righteous man in his own house and on his own bed" (2 Samuel 4:11).

agag.bio: King of Amalek spared by Saul against God's command. His survival cost Saul his kingdom.
agag.histoire: Saul was to devote Amalek to complete destruction; he spares Agag and the best of the livestock, "so we can sacrifice them to the Lord," he says (1 Samuel 15:9, 15). Samuel responds with words that have become proverbial: "Obedience is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22). It is Samuel himself who puts an end to Agag (1 Samuel 15:33). The book of Esther will present Haman as "the Agagite" — the enmity of Amalek resurges centuries later.

peninna.bio: Second wife of Elkanah, mother of several children, who humiliated the barren Hannah.
peninna.histoire: "Peninnah had children, but Hannah had none" (1 Samuel 1:2). Every year, at the festival in Shiloh, "her rival would provoke her harshly to irritate her" (1 Samuel 1:6). Yet it was from this pain that Hannah's prayer was born, and Samuel with it. God doesn't need our rivals to bless us, but He knows how to work through them.

hophni-phinees.bio: The sons of the priest Eli, priests at Shiloh, "wicked men who did not know the Lord." They died on the same day when the ark was captured.
hophni-phinees.histoire: They used force in the sacrifices before the fat was offered, and "despised the offerings of the Lord" (1 Samuel 2:12-17). Eli rebukes them weakly; a man of God announces to him: "you honor your sons more than me" (1 Samuel 2:29). At the battle of Aphek, they carry the ark like a good-luck charm; it is captured, and both of them die (1 Samuel 4:11). God will not be manipulated like an amulet.

ritspa.bio: Concubine of Saul. Her two sons were put to death for Saul's crime against the Gibeonites — and she kept vigil over their bodies for months.
ritspa.histoire: To atone for Saul's massacre of the Gibeonites, seven of his descendants are executed, including Rizpah's two sons (2 Samuel 21:8-9). Then "Rizpah daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it out for herself on the rock, from the beginning of harvest until rain fell on them from heaven," driving away the birds by day and the wild animals by night (2 Samuel 21:10). Moved by this vigil, David finally has Saul and Jonathan buried with dignity.

uzza.bio: He touched the Ark of God to steady it and was struck down. His death reminded David that the Ark was to be carried according to the Law.
uzza.histoire: The Ark travels on a new cart—in the manner of the Philistines. The oxen stumble, Uzzah reaches out to steady it,

schimei.bio: A Benjamite from Saul's family who cursed David in flight and threw stones at him. Though pardoned, he ultimately lost his life by breaking his word.
schimei.histoire: On the path of exile, he cries out: "Get away, man of blood!" while throwing stones. Abishai wants to kill him; David replies: "Leave him alone, and let him curse, for the Lord has told him to… Perhaps the Lord will look upon my affliction" (2 Samuel 16:5-12). Upon his return, Shimei throws himself at his feet and obtains mercy (2 Samuel 19:18-23). Solomon confines him to Jerusalem; when he leaves to retrieve two servants, he dies by his own broken word (1 Kings 2:36-46).

amasa.bio: Nephew of David, general of Absalom, then appointed by David as commander of the army. Joab assassinated him with a kiss.
amasa.histoire: Absalom appoints him commander of his army (2 Samuel 17:25). After the revolt, David, to win over Judah, promises him command in place of Joab (2 Samuel 19:13). Joab approaches: "Are you in good health, my brother?" and seizes him by the beard to kiss him—with the sword in his left hand (2 Samuel 20:9-10). David will charge Solomon not to leave this blood unpunished (1 Kings 2:5).

benaja.bio: One of David's mighty men: he killed a lion in a pit on a snowy day. Commander of the guard, then of the army under Solomon.
benaja.histoire: His exploits are told in two verses: he killed two heroes of Moab, an Egyptian armed with a spear using only a staff, and "went down into the middle of a pit and killed a lion on a snowy day" (2 Samuel 23:20-21). David put him in charge of his guard. During Adonijah's attempt to seize the throne, Benaiah sided with Solomon (1 Kings 1:36-38), who made him commander of the army (1 Kings 2:35).

achimaats.bio: Son of the priest Zadok, a runner and messenger for David during Absalom's revolt.
achimaats.histoire: With Jonathan, son of Abiathar, he carries news from Hushai to David; pursued, they hide in a well covered by a woman (2 Samuel 17:17-21). After the battle, he begs to run and announce the victory, outpaces the official messenger—but doesn't dare tell the king of Absalom's death (2 Samuel 18:19-29). A good messenger also knows that some news breaks a father's heart.

gad-prophete.bio: Prophet and "seer" of David, from his years of wandering to the end of his reign. He designated the threshing floor of Araunah, the future location of the temple.
gad-prophete.histoire: He appears at the very beginning of David's flight: "Do not stay in the stronghold; go away, and enter the land of Judah" (1 Samuel 22:5). After the prideful census, he brings to David the choice of three punishments (2 Samuel 24:11-14), then the command to build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah — where the temple would be built (2 Samuel 24:18; 2 Chronicles 3:1). He wrote part of the chronicles of the reign (1 Chronicles 29:29).

abijam.bio: King of Judah for three years, son of Rehoboam. His heart was not entirely devoted to God, but he won a victory by calling upon the Lord.
abijam.histoire: "He committed all the sins his father had done before him, and his heart was not entirely devoted to the Lord" (1 Kings 15:3) — yet God kept a lamp for David in Jerusalem. Chronicles records his speech on Mount Zemaraim, surrounded by Jeroboam's army: "Behold, God and His priests are with us, leading us" ; Judah cries out to the Lord and prevails (2 Chronicles 13:12-18).
