joram-juda.bio: Son of the godly Jehoshaphat, he married Athaliah, daughter of Ahab, and led Judah into idolatry. He died "unmourned."
joram-juda.histoire: "He walked in the way of the kings of Israel… for he had a wife who was a daughter of Ahab" (2 Kings 8:18): a political marriage alliance becomes an open door to Baal. He has all his brothers killed (2 Chronicles 21:4). Edom revolts. A letter from the prophet Elijah announces his judgment (2 Chronicles 21:12-15). He dies of a terrible disease and "departed without being mourned" (2 Chronicles 21:20).

achazia-juda.bio: Son of Jehoram and Athaliah, king of Judah for one year. While visiting his uncle Joram of Israel, he was killed by Jehu.
achazia-juda.histoire: "His mother encouraged him to do wrong" (2 Chronicles 22:3). He is at Jezreel with Israel's wounded king when Jehu rushes upon them; he flees, is struck in his chariot, and dies at Megiddo (2 Kings 9:27). Upon his death, Athaliah has the entire royal line massacred — except one baby hidden away, Joash (2 Kings 11:1-2).

amatsia.bio: King of Judah, son of Joash. He obeyed the law of Moses by sparing the children of his father's murderers, but pride destroyed him.
amatsia.histoire: He punished his father's assassins but spared their sons, "according to what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses… The fathers shall not be put to death for the children" (2 Kings 14:6; Deuteronomy 24:16). Victorious over Edom, he brought back their gods and bowed down to them (2 Chronicles 25:14). Intoxicated with pride, he challenged Joash of Israel, who answered him with the parable of the thistle and the cedar—then broke down the wall of Jerusalem (2 Kings 14:8-14).

achaz.bio: An ungodly king of Judah, son of Jotham. He refused the sign God offered him — and Isaiah announced to him the sign of Emmanuel.
achaz.histoire: He makes his son pass through the fire (2 Kings 16:3). Threatened by the coalition of Rezin and Pekah, his heart trembles "like the trees of the forest" (Isaiah 7:2). Isaiah tells him: "Ask for a sign from the Lord your God" (Isaiah 7:11). Ahaz refuses, preferring to call on Assyria and give them the temple's gold (2 Kings 16:7-8). God gives the sign anyway: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel" (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23).

amon-roi.bio: Son of Manasseh, king of Judah for two years. He resumed his father's idolatry without imitating his repentance, and was assassinated. Father of Josiah.
amon-roi.histoire: Manasseh humbled himself at the end of his life; Amon, however, "did not humble himself before the Lord, as his father Manasseh had humbled himself" (2 Chronicles 33:23). His servants killed him in his house; the people made his eight-year-old son, Josiah, king (2 Kings 21:23-24). From an ungodly father would come Judah's greatest reformer: lineage is not destiny.

joachaz-juda.bio: Son of Josiah, king of Judah for only three months, deposed and taken to Egypt by Pharaoh Neco.
joachaz-juda.histoire: The people anointed him king at the death of Josiah, who fell at Megiddo. Three months later, Pharaoh had him put in chains at Riblah, imposed a tribute on the land, and put his brother Eliakim—Jehoiakim—on the throne (2 Kings 23:31-34). Jeremiah, who calls him Shallum, weeps over him:

jojakim.bio: King of Judah appointed by Pharaoh, who burned the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies in the fire. The deportation to Babylon began during his reign.
jojakim.histoire: Jeremiah denounces him: "Woe to him who builds his house by injustice… who makes his neighbor work without paying him" (Jeremiah 22:13). When Jeremiah's scroll is read to him as he sits before the brazier in winter, he cuts the columns to pieces with his knife and throws them into the fire (Jeremiah 36:22-23). God has the scroll rewritten, this time longer. During his reign, Nebuchadnezzar takes away the first deportees, including Daniel (Daniel 1:1-6).

jojakin.bio: King of Judah for three months, deported to Babylon with the nation's elite. Released after thirty-seven years of captivity, he became a beacon of hope for David's line.
jojakin.histoire: At eighteen years old, he surrenders to Nebuchadnezzar and goes into exile with his mother, his officers, and ten thousand captives, among them the young Ezekiel (2 Kings 24:12-16; Ezekiel 1:2). Thirty-seven years later, Babylon's new king brings him out of prison, "spoke kindly to him" and had him eat at his table every day of his life (2 Kings 25:27-30). The book of Kings ends on this note: David's lamp is not extinguished. He is the ancestor of Zerubbabel and appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:12).

nadab-roi.bio: Son of Jeroboam, king of Israel for two years, assassinated by Baasha — end of Jeroboam's dynasty announced by the prophet Ahijah.
nadab-roi.histoire: "He did evil in the sight of the Lord; and he walked in the way of his father" (1 Kings 15:26). While he is besieging Gibbethon, Baasha conspires and kills him, then destroys the entire house of Jeroboam, "according to the word of the Lord which He spoke by His servant Ahijah of Shiloh" (1 Kings 15:27-29). The northern kingdom has just inaugurated a long series of coups d'état.

baescha.bio: King of Israel for twenty-four years, of the tribe of Issachar. He came to the throne through murder, then reproduced the very sins he had punished.
baescha.histoire: He destroyed the house of Jeroboam, executing a judgment that had been announced — but then walked in that same path himself. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani told him: "I lifted you up from the dust… but because you have walked in the way of Jeroboam" (1 Kings 16:2). He fortified Ramah to strangle Judah; Asa bought an alliance with Damascus to drive him out (1 Kings 15:16-22). His dynasty would not survive his son.

ela-roi.bio: Son of Baasha, king of Israel for two years, assassinated while drunk by Zimri, one of his officers.
ela-roi.histoire: "Elah was in Tirzah, drinking and getting drunk in the house of Arza, the steward of his house," when Zimri enters, strikes him down, and takes his place (1 Kings 16:9-10). The entire family of Baasha is destroyed, fulfilling the word of the prophet Jehu (1 Kings 16:12).

zimri-roi.bio: An officer who killed King Elah and reigned for seven days. Besieged by Omri, he set fire to the palace and died in the flames.
zimri-roi.histoire: His reign lasted just one week: when the army learned of the murder, they proclaimed Omri king and came to besiege Tirzah. Seeing the city about to fall, Zimri "went into the citadel of the king's house and burned the king's house down upon himself" (1 Kings 16:15-18). His name became an insult: Jezebel would greet Jehu with the words, "Is it peace, Zimri, you murderer of your master?" (2 Kings 9:31).

omri.bio: A general who became king of Israel, founder of Samaria, the new capital, and father of Ahab.
omri.histoire: Proclaimed king by the army, he prevailed after years of civil war against Tibni (1 Kings 16:21-22). He bought the hill of Samaria for two talents of silver and built there the capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 16:24). Politically shrewd, spiritually disastrous: he "did evil in the sight of the Lord more than all who were before him" (1 Kings 16:25). A century later, Micah would still speak of the "statutes of Omri" (Micah 6:16).

achazia-israel.bio: Son of Ahab and Jezebel, king of Israel for two years. Injured, he sought counsel from Baal-Zebub — and Elijah announced his death to him.
achazia-israel.histoire: After falling through the lattice of his chamber, he sends messengers to consult Baal-Zebub, god of Ekron. Elijah intercepts the messengers: "Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to consult Baal-Zebub?" (2 Kings 1:3). The captains sent to arrest the prophet are consumed by fire; the third begs for mercy, and Elijah himself comes down to announce the king's death (2 Kings 1:9-17).

joram-israel.bio: Son of Ahab, the last king of his dynasty. Contemporary of Elisha, he was killed by an arrow shot by Jehu in Naboth's field.
joram-israel.histoire: He removed the statue of Baal made by his father, but kept the golden calves of Jeroboam (2 Kings 3:2-3). On a campaign against Moab, the army dies of thirst; Elisha announces that the valley will be filled with water without wind or rain (2 Kings 3:16-20). Wounded, he rests at Jezreel when Jehu arrives: "Is it peace, Jehu?" Jehu's arrow pierces him, and his body is thrown into Naboth's field (2 Kings 9:22-26)—the stolen vineyard demanded justice.

joachaz-israel.bio: Son of Jehu, king of Israel for seventeen years, crushed by Syria. In his distress, he pleaded with the Lord—who answered him.
joachaz-israel.histoire: Hazael reduced his army to fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers, made "like the dust that is trampled underfoot" (2 Kings 13:7). Then "Jehoahaz pleaded with the Lord. The Lord answered him, for He saw the oppression by which the king of Syria oppressed Israel, and the Lord gave Israel a deliverer" (2 Kings 13:4-5). Even an unfaithful king is never too far away to be heard.

joas-israel.bio: King of Israel who wept at the bedside of dying Elisha. He struck the earth three times with arrows—and won only three victories.
joas-israel.histoire: Leaning over the sick Elisha, he cries out: "My father! My father! The chariots and horsemen of Israel!" (2 Kings 13:14). The prophet has him shoot "the arrow of deliverance," then strike the earth with the arrows. Joash strikes three times and stops. "You should have struck five or six times; then you would have defeated the Syrians until their destruction" (2 Kings 13:18-19). The measure of your faith sometimes limits the measure of your deliverance. He will also defeat Amaziah of Judah (2 Kings 14:11-14).

jeroboam-ii.bio: King of Israel for forty-one years, who restored the kingdom's borders according to the prophecy of Jonah. His prosperous reign was marked by the prophets Amos and Hosea.
jeroboam-ii.histoire: "He restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Arabah, according to the word of the Lord, the God of Israel, which He spoke by His servant Jonah the prophet, the son of Amittai" (2 Kings 14:25)—the Jonah of Nineveh was first a court prophet. But the wealth of his time conceals injustice: Amos denounces those who "have sold the righteous for silver" (Amos 2:6). Amaziah the priest of Bethel accuses Amos of conspiring against Jeroboam (Amos 7:10-11).

zacharie-roi.bio: Son of Jeroboam II, king of Israel for six months, assassinated in public. With him the dynasty of Jehu ended, at the fourth generation as announced.
zacharie-roi.histoire: Shallum struck him "before the people" and reigned in his place (2 Kings 15:10). The account emphasizes the fulfillment: "Thus Jehu's word to him was fulfilled when the Lord said to Jehu, 'Your sons shall sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation'" (2 Kings 15:12; 10:30). The final years of Israel unfold: five kings in twenty years.

schallum-roi.bio: He killed King Zechariah and reigned for one month, before being killed in turn by Menahem.
schallum-roi.histoire: "Shallum the son of Jabesh reigned... He reigned one month in Samaria. Menahem the son of Gadi went up from Tirzah and came to Samaria, and struck down Shallum" (2 Kings 15:13-14). One month: the northern kingdom consumed itself, as Hosea had seen it coming: "They set up kings, but not by me" (Hosea 8:4).

menahem.bio: King of Israel for ten years, known for his great cruelty. He paid a heavy tribute to Assyria to keep his throne.
menahem.histoire: He massacred the city of Tiphsah, which had closed its gates to him (2 Kings 15:16). When Pul, king of Assyria, invaded the land, Menahem paid him one thousand talents of silver, collected from all the wealthy men, "so that he might help him establish his kingdom firmly in his hand" (2 Kings 15:19-20). Buying security from Assyria: the policy that would ultimately destroy Israel.

pekachia.bio: Son of Menahem, king of Israel for two years, assassinated by his officer Pekah.
pekachia.histoire: "He did evil in the sight of the Lord; he did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam" (2 Kings 15:24). Pekah, his officer, strikes him down in the dungeon of the palace of Samaria, with fifty men of Gilead, and reigns in his place (2 Kings 15:25).

pekach.bio: King of Israel, allied with Damascus against Judah. During his reign, Assyria deported Galilee; he was killed by Hosea.
pekach.histoire: With Rezin, king of Syria, he marched against Jerusalem to dethrone Ahaz (Isaiah 7:1). Isaiah reassured Judah: these were only "two smoking stubs of firebrands" (Isaiah 7:4). Tiglath-Pileser, called by Ahaz, seized Galilee and deported its inhabitants (2 Kings 15:29)—"The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali" covered in disgrace, to whom Isaiah nevertheless promised a great light (Isaiah 8:23; 9:1).

osee-roi.bio: Last king of Israel. His betrayal of Assyria triggered the siege of Samaria and the deportation of the ten tribes in 722 BC.
osee-roi.histoire: A vassal of Shalmaneser, he stopped paying tribute and sought Egypt's support; he was arrested. Samaria was besieged for three years, then taken, and Israel was carried away captive to Assyria (2 Kings 17:3-6). Chapter 17 explains why, through a lengthy indictment:

jehojada.bio: High priest who hid the child Joash for six years, overthrew Athaliah, and restored David's line to the throne.
jehojada.histoire: While Athaliah reigns after massacring the royal family, the child Joash grows up hidden in the temple (2 Kings 11:2-3). In the seventh year, Jehoiada orchestrates everything: the guards, weapons from King David's armory, the coronation—"Long live the king!"—and Athaliah is put to death (2 Kings 11:4-16). He makes a covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people (2 Kings 11:17). At his death at one hundred thirty years old, he was buried among the kings, "because he had done good in Israel" (2 Chronicles 24:15-16).

abdias-intendant.bio: Chief of Ahab's palace who "greatly feared the Lord": he hid one hundred prophets, fifty by fifty, in a cave during Jezebel's persecution.
abdias-intendant.histoire: In the very heart of an idolatrous palace, a believer: "So it was, when Jezebel cut off the prophets of the Lord, that Obadiah took one hundred prophets and hid them, fifty to a cave, and fed them with bread and water" (1 Kings 18:4). Sent by Ahab to search for grass during the drought, he meets Elijah and trembles at bearing his message (1 Kings 18:7-16). God has His faithful even in hostile royal courts.

hilkija.bio: High priest under Josiah who discovered the Book of the Law in the temple—a spark that ignited a great reform.
hilkija.histoire: During the temple restoration work, Hilkijah declares: "I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the Lord" (2 Kings 22:8). The Word had been lost... in God's house. When read before the king, it triggers Josiah's repentance; Hilkijah then consults the prophetess Hulda (2 Kings 22:14) and purifies the temple of Baal's objects (2 Kings 23:4).

rabschake.bio: A high Assyrian official sent by Sennacherib to intimidate Jerusalem, to whom he spoke in Hebrew from the foot of the city walls.
rabschake.histoire: Standing by the aqueduct, he cries out in Hebrew so all the people can hear: "Do not let Hezekiah deceive you… Have the gods of the nations delivered each one his land from the hand of the king of Assyria?" (2 Kings 18:28-35). It's the old strategy of doubt: "In whom have you placed your trust…?" (2 Kings 18:20). The people remain silent, as the king has commanded, and Hezekiah will carry these words before the Lord.

sancherib.bio: King of Assyria who invaded Judah and besieged Jerusalem under Hezekiah. His army was struck down in one night; he was assassinated by his sons.
sancherib.histoire: He takes all the fortified cities of Judah (2 Kings 18:13) and sends Hezekiah a threatening letter. The king spreads it before the Lord in the temple and prays (2 Kings 19:14-19). Isaiah responds on behalf of God: "He shall not enter this city... I will protect this city to save it" (2 Kings 19:32-34). That night, the angel of the Lord strikes the Assyrian camp; Sennacherib returns to Nineveh, where his sons kill him while he is worshiping his god (2 Kings 19:35-37).

ben-hadad.bio: Name borne by several Aramean kings of Damascus, enemies of Israel in the time of Ahab, Elijah, and Elisha.
ben-hadad.histoire: One Ben-Hadad allied himself with Asa against Israel (1 Kings 15:18-20). Another besieged Samaria with thirty-two kings and boasted; Ahab answered him: "Let not him who puts on his armor boast like him who takes it off!" (1 Kings 20:11). He besieged Samaria again until famine struck (2 Kings 6:24), then, being ill, sent Hazael to consult Elisha—who announced his death and the rise of Hazael (2 Kings 8:7-15). A third, the son of Hazael, was defeated three times by Joash (2 Kings 13:24-25).

mescha.bio: King of Moab, a sheep breeder, who rebelled against Israel after the death of Ahab.
mescha.histoire: He paid Israel a tribute of one hundred thousand lambs and the wool of one hundred thousand rams; upon Ahab's death, he rebels (2 Kings 3:4-5). Besieged by the coalition of Israel, Judah, and Edom, he offers his firstborn son as a burnt offering on the wall, "and great indignation came upon Israel," and they withdraw (2 Kings 3:27). A stele of this king, discovered in 1868, tells of the same rebellion from the Moabite perspective.

hiel.bio: A man from Bethel who rebuilt Jericho under Ahab—and paid with the lives of his sons for the curse pronounced by Joshua.
hiel.histoire: Joshua had sworn: "Cursed be the man before the Lord who rises up and builds this city Jericho! He shall lay its foundation at the cost of his firstborn, and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son" (Joshua 6:26). More than five centuries later, under Ahab, "Hiel of Bethel built Jericho; he laid its foundation with the loss of Abiram his firstborn, and set up its gates with the loss of Segub his youngest son, according to the word of the Lord which He had spoken through Joshua" (1 Kings 16:34). God's Word does not grow old.

aschpenaz.bio: Chief of the eunuchs of Nebuchadnezzar: he received Daniel and his companions in Babylon and gave them Chaldean names.
aschpenaz.histoire:
The king commanded Ashpenaz, the chief of his eunuchs, "to bring some of the children of Israel of royal descent and of the noble families" to train them for three years in the letters and language of the Chaldeans (Daniel 1:3-5). It is he who renames the young captives: Daniel becomes Belteshazzar, Hananiah Shadrach, Mishael Meshach, Azariah Abed-Nego (Daniel 1:7).

When Daniel refuses to defile himself with the king's food, the chief of the eunuchs fears for his head; yet "God gave Daniel favor and compassion in the sight of the chief of the eunuchs" (Daniel 1:9). God prepares gracious hearts even in the palace of the oppressor.

arjoc.bio: Chief of the guards of Nebuchadnezzar, tasked with executing the wise men of Babylon; it was he who introduced Daniel to the king.
arjoc.histoire:
The king demands that he be told his dream and its interpretation; if not, all the wise men will die. Daniel speaks "with prudence and discernment to Arioch, the captain of the king's guard, who had gone out to put the wise men of Babylon to death" (Daniel 2:14). After prayer and nighttime revelation, Daniel tells him: "Do not destroy the wise men of Babylon! Take me before the king" (Daniel 2:24).

Arioch presents himself to the king, saying: "I have found a man among the captives from Judah who will give the interpretation to the king" (Daniel 2:25). Daniel's wisdom saves even those who do not worship his God.

nebuzaradan.bio: Captain of the guard under Nebuchadnezzar: he burned the temple and Jerusalem in 586 BC, deported the people, and released Jeremiah.
nebuzaradan.histoire:
"Nebuzaradan captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, came into Jerusalem. He burned the house of the Lord, the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem" (2 Kings 25:8-9). This marks the end of the First Temple. He takes the captives and leaves "some of the poorest of the land" as vinedressers and farmers (2 Kings 25:11-12).

By order of the king, he watches over Jeremiah: "Take him, and look after him well; do him no harm" (Jeremiah 39:12). He frees him from his chains at Ramah and even acknowledges: "The Lord your God declared this disaster against this place" (Jeremiah 40:1-4). A pagan confesses the fulfillment of God's word.

evil-merodac.bio: King of Babylon, son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar: he released Jehoiachin, king of Judah, from prison after thirty-seven years of captivity.
evil-merodac.histoire:
The last page of the books of Kings is a glimmer of hope. "In the thirty-seventh year of the captivity of Jehoiachin, king of Judah […] Evil-merodach, king of Babylon, in the first year of his reign, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and brought him out of prison" (2 Kings 25:27).

"He spoke kindly to him," had him change out of his prison clothes, "and Jehoiachin ate regularly at his table all the days of his life" (2 Kings 25:28-29). The line of David is not extinct: from Jehoiachin will descend Zerubbabel and then, according to Matthew's genealogy, the Messiah (Matthew 1:12).

neco.bio: Pharaoh of Egypt: he killed King Josiah at Megiddo, deposed Jehoahaz, and set up Jehoiakim in his place.
neco.histoire:
"Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, went up against the king of Assyria, toward the River Euphrates." King Josiah marches to meet him, and Neco kills him at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29). Chronicles records the striking warning from Neco: "Do not oppose God, who is with me"—words "that came from the mouth of God," but which Josiah did not heed (2 Chronicles 35:21-22).

Neco then binds Jehoahaz at Riblah, imposes on Judah a tribute of one hundred talents of silver, and "set up as king Eliakim son of Josiah [...] and changed his name to Jehoiakim" (2 Kings 23:33-34). Judah is no longer master of its own destiny.

achikam.bio: Son of Shaphan, a high official of King Josiah; he protected Jeremiah from death. Father of Gedaliah.
achikam.histoire:
When the book of the law is discovered in the temple, Josiah sends the priest Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, and others to consult the prophetess Huldah (2 Kings 22:12-14). Ahikam is among those men who seek God's will.

Years later, when the crowd wants Jeremiah's death, "the hand of Ahikam son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, so that he was not given over to the people to be put to death" (Jeremiah 26:24). His son Gedaliah, governor after Jerusalem's fall, will in turn welcome the prophet (Jeremiah 40:5-6). A faithful family across generations.

guemaria.bio: Son of Shaphan, secretary in the time of Jehoiakim: it was in his chamber that Baruch read the scroll of Jeremiah; he pleaded with the king not to burn it.
guemaria.histoire:
Baruch reads the words of Jeremiah to the people "in the chamber of Gemariah, son of Shaphan, the secretary, in the upper court" (Jeremiah 36:10). It is Micaiah, the son of Gemariah, who alerts the officials (Jeremiah 36:11-12).

When King Jehoiakim cuts up the scroll and throws it into the fire, "Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah urged the king not to burn the scroll, but he would not listen to them" (Jeremiah 36:25). The scroll was rewritten; the word of God does not burn.

jehudi.bio: Officer of King Jehoiakim: he went to fetch Jeremiah's scroll and read it to the king, who cut it up and threw it into the fire.
jehudi.histoire:
The officials send to Baruch "Jehudi son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi" to bring the book (Jeremiah 36:14). Then the king sends him to fetch it, and "he read it in the hearing of the king" (Jeremiah 36:21).

A chilling scene: the king is sitting before a fire; "When Jehudi had read three or four columns, the king cut up the book with a secretary's knife and threw it into the fire of the brazier" (Jeremiah 36:22-23). But God has all the words written again, and many more besides (Jeremiah 36:28, 32).

paschhur.bio: Priest, son of Immer and chief overseer of the temple: he struck Jeremiah and put him in stocks; the prophet changed his name to "Magor-Missabib."
paschhur.histoire:
"Pashhur, son of Immer, the priest and chief overseer in the house of the Lord" hears Jeremiah prophesying; he strikes him and puts him "in the prison that was at the upper gate of Benjamin" (Jeremiah 20:1-2). The next day, Jeremiah announces to him: "It is not the name Pashhur that the Lord gives you, but Magor-Missabib" (Jeremiah 20:3), that is, terror on every side.

He who had prophesied lies would himself go into captivity: "you will go to Babylon, and there you will die" (Jeremiah 20:6). Right after this, Jeremiah confides his distress—and his inner fire: "There is in my heart as a devouring fire" (Jeremiah 20:9).

hanameel.bio: Cousin of Jeremiah, son of his uncle Shallum: he sold the prophet his field in Anathoth during the siege of Jerusalem, a sign that the land would be revived.
hanameel.histoire:
Jerusalem is under siege, Jeremiah is in prison, and God announces to him: "Hanamel, the son of your uncle Shallum, will come to you and say, 'Buy my field that is in Anathoth'" (Jeremiah 32:7). Buying a field on the eve of deportation: human folly.

Jeremiah obeys, weighs out "seventeen shekels of silver," has the deed signed before witnesses, and entrusts it to Baruch (Jeremiah 32:9-12). The meaning is given at once: "Houses and fields and vineyards shall again be bought in this land" (Jeremiah 32:15). Faith invests in God's promises.

seraja.bio: Son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah — thus brother of Baruch —, chief chamberlain of King Zedekiah; Jeremiah entrusted him with the oracle against Babylon.
seraja.histoire:
In the fourth year of Zedekiah, Jeremiah charges "Seraiah, son of Neriah, son of Mahseiah" (Jeremiah 51:59), from the same lineage as Baruch, with carrying to Babylon a book containing all the calamities announced against it; "Now Seraiah was the chief chamberlain" (Jeremiah 51:59-60).

Once the reading is complete, he must attach a stone to it and throw it into the Euphrates, saying: "Thus Babylon will be overwhelmed; she will not rise again" (Jeremiah 51:63-64). The empire that seemed eternal is already judged.

ismael-nethania.bio: Officer of the royal line of Judah: he assassinated Governor Gedaliah at Mizpah, then fled to the Ammonites.
ismael-nethania.histoire:
After the fall of Jerusalem, Johanan warned Gedaliah: "Baalis, king of the Ammonites, has sent Ishmael, son of Nethaniah, to take your life"; but Gedaliah did not believe him (Jeremiah 40:14-16). In the seventh month, Ishmael, "of the royal line," came to dine with him at Mizpah, then struck him down with the sword (Jeremiah 41:1-2).

He also massacred the Jews and Chaldeans who were present, took the inhabitants of Mizpah captive including "the king's daughters"; caught up near the great waters of Gibeon, he escaped "with eight men" to the Ammonites (Jeremiah 41:10-15). The jealousy of a prince destroyed the small remnant that could have recovered.

jochanan-kareach.bio: Commander of Judah's forces after the fall of Jerusalem: he rescued Ishmael's captives, then led the remaining people to Egypt against Jeremiah's word.
jochanan-kareach.histoire:
He warned Gedaliah of Ishmael's plot—in vain (Jeremiah 40:13-16). After the murder, he pursues Ishmael and brings back the captives (Jeremiah 41:11-14). Then, with the people, he asks Jeremiah to pray: "Whether it is good or bad, we will obey the voice of the Lord" (Jeremiah 42:6).

But the answer—stay in the land—does not suit him: "You are telling a lie" (Jeremiah 43:2). He takes all the rest of Judah to Egypt, with Jeremiah and Baruch, as far as Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:5-7). Asking for God's will is not enough: you must be ready to accept it.

jonadab-recab.bio: Ally of Jehu against the worship of Baal and founder of the Rechabites, who kept his way of life for centuries: no wine, no houses.
jonadab-recab.histoire:
Jehu meets him on the road: "Is your heart right, as my heart is toward your heart?" And Jonadab answered: "It is." Jehu has him ride in his chariot: "Come with me, and see my zeal for the Lord" (2 Kings 10:15-16).

Two and a half centuries later, Jeremiah sets wine before his descendants, the Rechabites; they answer: "We do not drink wine; for Jonadab, son of Rechab, our father, commanded us" (Jeremiah 35:5-6). God holds up their faithfulness as an example to Judah who does not listen, and promises: "Jonadab, son of Rechab, shall never lack a descendant to stand before Me" (Jeremiah 35:19).

hegai.bio: Eunuch of King Ahasuerus, keeper of the women at Susa: Esther found favor in his eyes.
hegai.histoire:
The young women are gathered at Susa "under the care of Hegai, keeper of the women." Esther is brought there, and "the young woman pleased him and obtained his favor"; he gives her seven young women and the best quarters (Esther 2:8-9).

When her turn comes, Esther "asked for nothing except what Hegai advised" (Esther 2:15). Her humility and trust in the counsel of one who knew the king became part of the way God prepared the deliverance of His people.

hathac.bio: A eunuch placed in service to Queen Esther: messenger between her and Mordecai at the time of the massacre decree.
hathac.histoire:
When Mordecai puts on sackcloth and ashes, "Esther called Hathac, one of the king's eunuchs assigned to her" to find out what is happening (Esther 4:5). Hathac brings back a copy of the decree and Mordecai's request: that Esther go and plead with the king (Esther 4:7-9).

Through him passes the decisive word: "And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14). A simple faithful messenger in the service of a turning point in history.

zeresch.bio: Wife of Haman: she advised him to build a gallows to hang Mordecai on it, then predicted his downfall.
zeresch.histoire:
Haman cannot bear to see Mordecai at the king's gate. "Zeresh his wife and all his friends said to him, 'Let a gallows be made, fifty cubits high, and tomorrow morning ask the king to have Mordecai hanged on it'" (Esther 5:14).

But the next day, Haman must honor Mordecai before all the city. Zeresh's tone changes: "If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of the Jewish people, you will not be able to do anything against him, but you will fall before him" (Esther 6:13). Even enemies sense that God watches over His people.

scheschbatsar.bio: "Prince of Judah" to whom Cyrus entrusted the temple vessels; the first governor of the return, he laid the foundations of God's house.
scheschbatsar.histoire:
Cyrus brings out the temple vessels and entrusts them "to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah": 5,400 objects of gold and silver, which Sheshbazzar carries "from Babylon to Jerusalem, in the return from captivity" (Ezra 1:8-11).

The letter sent later to Darius recalls that Cyrus had appointed him governor, and that "this Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundation of the house of God in Jerusalem" (Ezra 5:14-16). The vessels profaned in Babylon find their place again: God restores what had been taken.

thathnai.bio: Persian governor of the province "beyond the River": he contested the rebuilding of the temple, but had to support it by order of Darius.
thathnai.histoire:
As Zerubbabel and Jeshua rebuild the temple, "Tattenai, governor of the province beyond the River, Shethar-Bozenai, and their associates" ask: "Who gave you a decree to build this house and to finish this wall?" (Ezra 5:3). But "the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews," and they are not stopped during the inquiry (Ezra 5:5).

Darius finds the decree of Cyrus and even orders the work to be financed. "Tattenai […] carried out the decree with all diligence" (Ezra 6:13). Opposition became the source of funding.

artaxerxes.bio: King of Persia: he sent Ezra to teach the Law in Jerusalem, then allowed his cupbearer Nehemiah to rebuild its walls.
artaxerxes.histoire:
He writes "Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra, the priest and scribe" a letter authorizing him to return and adorn the temple (Ezra 7:11-12); and Ezra blesses God "who has inclined the king's heart" (Ezra 7:27).

In the twentieth year of his reign, he notices the sadness of his cupbearer: "Why is your face so sad?" Nehemiah prays to the God of heaven and then asks to go rebuild Jerusalem. "The king gave me these letters, for the good hand of my God was upon me" (Nehemiah 2:1-8). The hearts of kings are in the hand of God (Proverbs 21:1).

tobija.bio: "The Ammonite servant," allied with Sanballat against the rebuilding of the walls; related to the priest Eliashib, he settled in the temple until Nehemiah drove him out.
tobija.histoire:
From the moment Nehemiah arrived, Sanballat and "Tobiah, the Ammonite servant" were "very displeased that someone had come to seek the well-being of the children of Israel" (Nehemiah 2:10). He mocked: "Let them build away! If a fox jumps on their stone wall, it will collapse!" (Nehemiah 4:3). He paid a false prophet to frighten Nehemiah (Nehemiah 6:12) and maintained a network of Judah's nobles connected to him through marriage (Nehemiah 6:17-19).

During one of Nehemiah's absences, the priest Eliashib had prepared a large room for him in the temple courts. When Nehemiah returned, he threw out all his belongings and had the rooms purified (Nehemiah 13:4-9). God's house is not a lounge for His enemies.

gueschem.bio: An Arab chief, the third enemy of Nehemiah alongside Sanballat and Tobijah; he attempted to lure Nehemiah into a trap in the Valley of Ono.
gueschem.histoire:
"Sanballat the Horonite, Tobijah the Ammonite servant, and Geshem the Arab" mock him: "Are you rebelling against the king?" Nehemiah answers: "The God of heaven will give us success. We His servants will arise and build" (Nehemiah 2:19-20).

When the wall is nearly complete, Sanballat and Geshem invite him to a meeting "in the villages of the Valley of Ono. They had planned to do me harm" (Nehemiah 6:2). Nehemiah refuses: he is doing a great work and cannot come down (Nehemiah 6:3).

eliaschib.bio: High priest in the time of Nehemiah: he rebuilt the Sheep Gate, but lodged Tobijah the Ammonite in the chambers of the temple.
eliaschib.histoire:
He opens the work: "Eliashib the high priest arose with his brothers, the priests, and they built the Sheep Gate" (Nehemiah 3:1). He is the grandson of Joshua, the great priest of the return (Nehemiah 12:10).

But, "relative of Tobijah," he provides for him a large chamber where offerings were stored (Nehemiah 13:4-5); and one of his grandsons becomes "son-in-law of Sanballat the Horonite" (Nehemiah 13:28). A good beginning does not guarantee a good ending: spiritual watchfulness must be guarded to the very end.

noadia.bio: A prophetess who, along with other false prophets, sought to frighten Nehemiah to stop the reconstruction of the wall.
noadia.histoire:
Nehemiah foiled the scheme of Shemaiah, paid by Sanballat and Tobiah to pressure him into hiding in the temple (Nehemiah 6:10–13). He then commits his adversaries to God's hands: "Remember, O my God, Tobiah and Sanballat, according to these works of theirs, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who wanted to make me afraid!" (Nehemiah 6:14).

A spiritual title does not guarantee God's word: every prophecy must be tested (1 John 4:1). Despite the intimidation, the wall was completed in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15).

hanani-nehemie.bio: Brother of Nehemiah: he brought to Susa the news of Jerusalem in ruins, then received with Hanania the guardianship of the rebuilt city.
hanani-nehemie.histoire:
It all began with his visit: "Hanani, one of my brothers, and some men came from Judah." They described the remnant "in great trouble and reproach; the walls of Jerusalem are broken down" (Nehemiah 1:2–3). Nehemiah sat down, wept, fasted, and prayed (Nehemiah 1:4).

Once the wall was completed, Nehemiah entrusted the city "to Hanani my brother, and Hanania the governor of the citadel of Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 7:2). The one who carried the burden of the news also carried the responsibility of guarding it.

auguste.bio: First Roman emperor: his census decree led Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem, where Jesus was to be born.
auguste.histoire:
"In those days a decree went out from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be registered" (Luke 2:1). The most powerful man in the world signs an administrative order; Joseph, "of the house and family of David," must go up from Nazareth to Bethlehem with Mary, who was pregnant (Luke 2:4-5).

Without knowing it, the emperor fulfills the prophecy: the Messiah will be born in Bethlehem (Micah 5:1). God directs the course of world history in service of His plan of salvation.

quirinius.bio: Roman governor of Syria at the time of the first census mentioned by Luke, at the birth of Jesus.
quirinius.histoire:
Luke, as a careful historian, dates the birth of Jesus: "This was the first census taken while Quirinius was governor of Syria" (Luke 2:2). He had announced that he had "carefully investigated everything from the beginning" (Luke 1:3).

The Gospel does not tell a myth outside of time: it anchors itself in real names, real functions, and real places. Christian faith is built on facts.

archelaus.bio: Son of Herod the Great, who ruled over Judea after him; fearing him, Joseph settled in Galilee, at Nazareth.
archelaus.histoire:
Upon returning from Egypt, Joseph learns "that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod"; he fears to go there and, "being divinely warned in a dream, he withdrew into the region of Galilee" (Matthew 2:22).

This is how Jesus grew up in Nazareth, "that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophets, 'He shall be called a Nazarene'" (Matthew 2:23). Even the fear of a tyrant serves God's purposes.

tibere.bio: Roman emperor and successor to Augustus: in the fifteenth year of his reign, the word of God was addressed to John the Baptist.
tibere.histoire:
Luke opens the ministry of John the Baptist with a solemn dating: "In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar" (Luke 3:1), when Pontius Pilate governs Judea and Herod Galilee. Then, after the emperors, tetrarchs, and high priests, comes what matters most: "the word of God came to John, the son of Zacharias, in the wilderness" (Luke 3:2).

The powerful occupy the scene; the word of God chooses a man in the desert.

lysanias.bio: Tetrarch of Abilene, northwest of Damascus, mentioned by Luke to date the beginning of John the Baptist's ministry.
lysanias.histoire:
In the list of rulers that opens Luke 3, we read: "Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene" (Luke 3:1). An obscure name that ancient inscriptions have confirmed: Luke's precision is verified even in the details.

Against this political backdrop, "the word of God came to John, the son of Zechariah, in the wilderness" (Luke 3:2).

claude-empereur.bio: Roman emperor: during his reign came the famine announced by Agabus, and he expelled the Jews from Rome, which brought Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth.
claude-empereur.histoire:
At Antioch, the prophet Agabus "announced through the Spirit that there would be a great famine over all the earth. And it happened under Claudius" (Acts 11:28). The disciples then send relief to the brothers in Judea, by Barnabas and Saul (Acts 11:29-30).

Later, Paul meets Aquila and his wife Priscilla at Corinth, who had come from Italy "because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome" (Acts 18:2). A decree of expulsion becomes the starting point of one of the most beautiful missionary partnerships.

berenice.bio: Sister of King Agrippa II: she was present with him at Paul's defense in Caesarea.
berenice.histoire:
"King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea to greet Festus" (Acts 25:13). The next day, they come "in great pomp" into the audience hall, and Paul is brought in (Acts 25:23).

Paul recounts his conversion; Agrippa says to him, "You almost persuade me to become a Christian!" Then the king, the governor, Bernice, and their entourage rise and conclude, "This man has done nothing deserving of death or imprisonment" (Acts 26:28-31). Hearing the Gospel up close is not enough: you must respond to it.

drusille.bio: Jewish wife of the governor Felix: with him, she heard Paul speak about faith in Christ.
drusille.histoire:
"Felix came with Drusilla, his wife, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul. He heard him concerning faith in Christ" (Acts 24:24).

But when Paul speaks "about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come," Felix, frightened, cuts him short: "Go away for now; when I find an opportunity, I will call for you" (Acts 24:25). The favorable moment postponed does not always return (2 Corinthians 6:2).

gallion.bio: Roman proconsul of Achaia in Corinth: he refused to judge Paul, deeming the matter purely religious.
gallion.histoire:
"When Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose up together against Paul" and brought him to the tribunal (Acts 18:12). Before Paul could even speak, Gallio made his ruling: "if it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, look to it yourselves; I do not wish to be a judge of such matters" (Acts 18:15).

This decision protected Paul's ministry in Corinth, where the Lord had told him: "no one will attack you to harm you" (Acts 18:10). An inscription from Delphi allows scholars to date this proconsulship to around 51–52.

claude-lysias.bio: Tribune of the Roman cohort in Jerusalem: he rescued Paul from the crowd, discovered that he was a Roman citizen, and sent him under escort to Caesarea.
claude-lysias.histoire:
When the crowd wants to kill Paul at the temple, the tribune rushes in with his soldiers and has him bound with two chains (Acts 21:31-33). About to have him flogged, he learns that Paul is a Roman citizen: "With a great sum I obtained this citizenship." And Paul said, "But I was born a citizen" (Acts 22:28).

Informed of a plot, he sends Paul by night to Caesarea with an escort of two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen (Acts 23:23-24), and writes: "Claudius Lysias, to the most excellent governor Felix, greetings!" (Acts 23:26). God keeps His promise: Paul will testify in Rome as well (Acts 23:11).

tertulle.bio: An orator hired by the high priest Ananias to accuse Paul before the governor Felix.
tertulle.histoire:
"Five days later the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman named Tertullus" (Acts 24:1). He begins by flattering the governor (Acts 24:3), then accuses: "We have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes" (Acts 24:5).

Paul responds calmly, without flattery, confessing his faith: "I serve the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the Law and in the Prophets" (Acts 24:14). Truth doesn't need hired eloquence.

ananias-grand-pretre.bio: High priest who ordered Paul struck on the mouth before the Sanhedrin, then went down to Caesarea to accuse him.
ananias-grand-pretre.histoire:
Paul begins his defense before the Sanhedrin; "The high priest Ananias ordered those standing near him to strike him on the mouth." Paul replies: "God will strike you, whitewashed wall!" Then, learning who he is addressing, he cites the law: "You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people" (Acts 23:2-5).

Five days later, Ananias goes down to Caesarea with the orator Tertullus to accuse Paul before Felix (Acts 24:1). Not to be confused with Ananias of Damascus, who laid hands on Paul, nor with the husband of Sapphira.

julius.bio: A centurion of the Augustan cohort tasked with escorting the prisoner Paul to Rome; he treated him with kindness and saved his life during the shipwreck.
julius.histoire:
Paul is handed over "to a centurion of the Augustan cohort named Julius"; from Sidon onward, "Julius, treating Paul kindly, allowed him to go to his friends and receive their care" (Acts 27:1-3). Yet he listens to the pilot rather than Paul's warning (Acts 27:11), and the storm breaks out.

During the shipwreck, the soldiers want to kill the prisoners, "But the centurion, wanting to save Paul, kept them from their purpose"; "and so it was that all were brought safely to land" (Acts 27:42-44). God had promised Paul the safety of all who sailed with him (Acts 27:24).

demetrius-orfevre.bio: A silversmith in Ephesus who made silver shrines of Diana; he stirred up a riot against Paul, whose preaching was ruining his business.
demetrius-orfevre.histoire:
"A man named Demetrius, a silversmith, made silver shrines of Diana." He gathers the craftsmen: "this Paul has persuaded and turned away a considerable number of people, saying that gods made by human hands are not gods" (Acts 19:24-26). The Gospel touches even wallets.

The entire city is in an uproar, crying out for nearly two hours: "Great is Diana of the Ephesians!" (Acts 19:34). The city clerk finally calms the crowd: "Therefore, if Demetrius and his craftsmen have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open" (Acts 19:38).

joseph-barsabbas.bio: A disciple who had followed Jesus from John's baptism; presented with Matthias to replace Judas, he was not chosen by casting of lots.
joseph-barsabbas.histoire:
To replace Judas, they needed a man who had been with the apostles "all the time the Lord Jesus lived among us," a witness of the resurrection. "They presented two men: Joseph called Barsabbas, surnamed Justus, and Matthias" (Acts 1:21-23).

They prayed, they cast lots, "and the lot fell on Matthias" (Acts 1:26). Barsabbas is mentioned no more—but he remains the one who followed Jesus from beginning to end. Being faithful does not depend on a title.

judas-barsabas.bio: Prophet of the Jerusalem church, sent to Antioch with Silas to deliver the letter from the council.
judas-barsabas.histoire:
After the Jerusalem Council, the church chose to send to Antioch, along with Paul and Barnabas, "Judas called Barsabas and Silas, leading men among the brothers" (Acts 15:22). They delivered the letter that freed believers of pagan origin from the burden of the law.

"Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, exhorted them and strengthened them with many words" (Acts 15:32). The gift of prophecy in service of the encouragement of the church (1 Corinthians 14:3).

sept-diacres.nom: The Seven (Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, Nicolas)
sept-diacres.bio: The seven men "full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom" chosen for the service of tables in Jerusalem, including Stephen and Philip.
sept-diacres.histoire:
The widows of the Hellenists are neglected in the daily distribution. The apostles ask to choose "seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom" (Acts 6:3). They elect "Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas, a proselyte of Antioch" (Acts 6:5).

After prayer and the laying on of hands, "the word of God continued to increase" (Acts 6:7). Practical service is a spiritual ministry: it sets the Word free.

simon-corroyeur.bio: A tanner in Joppa who lodged Peter; it was on his roof that Peter had the vision that opened the Gospel to the Gentiles.
simon-corroyeur.histoire:
After the resurrection of Dorcas, "Peter stayed for some time in Joppa with a tanner named Simon" (Acts 9:43). A trade considered unclean by the strictest — working with the skins of dead animals — and yet this is where Peter stays.

The angel tells Cornelius to send for Peter, lodged "with a certain Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the seaside" (Acts 10:6). On the roof of this house, Peter sees the sheet descending from heaven: "What God has declared clean, do not regard as unclean" (Acts 10:15).

prophetes-antioche.bio: Prophets and teachers of the Church at Antioch who, at the direction of the Holy Spirit, laid hands on Barnabas and Saul for their mission.
prophetes-antioche.histoire:
"Now in the church that was at Antioch there were certain prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manahen who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul" (Acts 13:1). A team that reflected the Gospel: a man surnamed Niger ("the Black"), a man from Cyrene, someone familiar with Herod's court, a Levite from Cyprus, and a Pharisee from Tarsus.

"As they ministered to the Lord and fasted, the Holy Spirit said, 'Now separate to Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.' Then, having fasted and prayed, and laid hands on them" (Acts 13:2-3): the first missionary journey was born from a time of praise and fasting.

sosthene.bio: Ruler of the synagogue in Corinth, beaten before the tribunal of Gallio; likely the same as "brother Sosthenes," co-author of 1 Corinthians with Paul.
sosthene.histoire:
After the complaint against Paul failed, the crowd seized "Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue," and beat him before the tribunal, "and Gallio was unconcerned about these things" (Acts 18:17). Before him, another synagogue ruler, Crispus, had believed in the Lord with all his household (Acts 18:8).

A few years later, Paul opens his letter to the Corinthians this way: "Paul, called to be an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God, and Sosthenes our brother" (1 Corinthians 1:1). If this is the same man, as many believe, the opponent who was beaten had become a brother.

hymenee.bio: A man from the church at Ephesus who shipwrecked his faith and taught that the resurrection had already occurred.
hymenee.histoire:
Paul writes to Timothy that some have lost a good conscience "and concerning the faith have suffered shipwreck. Of this sort are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme" (1 Timothy 1:19-20)—a discipline aimed at restoration.

In his second letter, Paul clarifies the error: "Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have strayed concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they overturn the faith of some" (2 Timothy 2:17-18). Yet "the solid foundation of God stands, having this seal" (2 Timothy 2:19).

alexandre-forgeron.bio: An opponent of Paul who did him "much harm"; possibly the same Alexander whom Paul had to hand over to Satan along with Hymenaeus.
alexandre-forgeron.histoire:
"Alexander the coppersmith did me much harm. May the Lord repay him according to his deeds. You also must watch out for him, because he has strongly resisted our message" (2 Timothy 4:14-15). Paul does not take revenge: he commits the case to God and warns Timothy.

An Alexander is already mentioned with Hymenaeus among those who have "shipwrecked their faith" (1 Timothy 1:19-20); it could be the same man, though we cannot be certain.

lois-eunice.bio: Timothy's grandmother and mother: believing Jewish women who passed on to him from childhood the faith and the Scriptures.
lois-eunice.histoire:
Paul reminds Timothy of "the genuine faith that is in you, which dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice" (2 Timothy 1:5). In Lystra, his mother is described as "a Jewish woman who believed," married to a Greek (Acts 16:1).

Their legacy is the Word: "from childhood you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus" (2 Timothy 3:15). Three generations of faith, and a great servant of the Church.

eraste.bio: A coworker of Paul sent to Macedonia with Timothy; an Erastus, treasurer of the city of Corinth, greets the Romans.
eraste.histoire:
From Ephesus, Paul "sent into Macedonia two of those who ministered to him, Timothy and Erastus" (Acts 19:22). In his letter to the Romans, written from Corinth, he conveys greetings from "Erastus, the city treasurer" (Romans 16:23)—a notable won to the Gospel. An inscription from Corinth mentions an aedile of this name.

In his final letter, Paul simply notes: "Erastus stayed in Corinth" (2 Timothy 4:20).

tertius.bio: Secretary who wrote the letter to the Romans at Paul's dictation and added his own greeting in it.
tertius.histoire:
In the midst of the final greetings, an unexpected voice: "I, Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord" (Romans 16:22).

The greatest exposition of the Gospel was written down by a scribe about whom we know nothing else. God honors the quiet hands that serve His Word.

rufus.bio: Son of Simon of Cyrene; possibly the same Rufus, "the chosen of the Lord," greeted by Paul in Rome along with his mother.
rufus.histoire:
Mark introduces Simon of Cyrene, who carried the cross, as the "father of Alexander and Rufus" (Mark 15:21)—names that must have been known to his readers, likely in Rome.

Paul writes precisely to the Romans: "Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to me as well" (Romans 16:13). If it's the same person, the cross carried by a passerby bore fruit in an entire family.

andronicus-junias.bio: Relatives of Paul and companions in captivity, highly respected among the apostles, and in Christ before him.
andronicus-junias.histoire:
"Greet Andronicus and Junia, my relatives and my fellow prisoners, who are outstanding among the apostles, and who also were in Christ before I was" (Romans 16:7).

Believers from the very beginning who had come to faith before Paul's conversion and shared his chains. A single line that opens a window onto the anonymous pioneers of the Gospel.

stephanas.bio: Head of the first converted household in Achaia, baptized by Paul; devoted to serving the saints, he joined Paul at Ephesus.
stephanas.histoire:
Paul baptized only a few Corinthians: "I also baptized the household of Stephanas" (1 Corinthians 1:16). This was a pioneering family: they "are the firstfruits of Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints" (1 Corinthians 16:15).

With Fortunatus and Achaicus, Stephanas came to find Paul: "they refreshed my spirit and yours. Therefore recognize such men" (1 Corinthians 16:17-18). There are servants whose very presence alone strengthens you.

chloe.bio: A woman of Corinth whose household informed Paul of the divisions tearing apart the church.
chloe.histoire:
"For it has been declared to me concerning you, my brethren, by those of Chloe's household, that there are contentions among you" (1 Corinthians 1:11). Some claimed to follow Paul, others Apollos, Cephas, or Christ.

Paul's first letter to the Corinthians is partly his response to this report: "Is Christ divided?" (1 Corinthians 1:13). A faithful household that had the courage to speak up about what was wrong.

archippe.bio: Leader of the Church of Colossae,
archippe.histoire:
Paul greets "Archippus our fellow soldier, and the church in your house" (Philemon 1:2)—likely a close associate of Philemon.

At the end of his letter to the Colossians, Paul gives a personal charge: "And tell Archippus, 'See that you fulfill the ministry you have received in the Lord'" (Colossians 4:17). A calling received must be carried through to completion.

apphia.bio: A Christian from Colossae greeted by Paul in his letter to Philemon, likely from his household.
apphia.histoire:
Paul's letter to Philemon is addressed "to our beloved sister Apphia, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church in your house" (Philemon 1:2).

Many believe she was Philemon's wife. Paul's request—to welcome the slave Onesimus as a brother—concerned the entire household, and she is mentioned by name to include her in this call.

nymphas.bio: A believer in the Laodicean region in whose home a church gathered.
nymphas.histoire:
"Greet the brethren who are in Laodicea, and Nymphas and the church that is in his house" (Colossians 4:15).

The early churches gathered in open homes. Paul also asks that the letter circulate: that it be read among the Laodiceans (Colossians 4:16).

clement.bio: A fellow worker with Paul at Philippi, whose name is
clement.histoire: Paul asks for help with Euodia and Syntyche,

phygelle-hermogene.bio: Believers from Asia who abandoned Paul during his final imprisonment.
phygelle-hermogene.histoire:
"You know that all those in Asia have abandoned me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes" (2 Timothy 1:15).

Paul immediately contrasts their defection with the faithfulness of Onesiphorus, who "was not ashamed of my chains" and searched for him in Rome until he found him (2 Timothy 1:16-17). In times of trial, true faithfulness is revealed.

zenas.bio: A Christian "teacher of the law," traveling with Apollos, whom Titus was to provide with everything he needed.
zenas.histoire:
"Make every effort to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way and see that they have everything they need" (Titus 3:13).

A jurist, perhaps trained in Jewish or Roman law, in the service of the Gospel. Paul shows that welcoming and materially supporting itinerant workers is part of ministry (3 John 1:5-8).

carpus.bio: A Christian in Troas with whom Paul had left his cloak, his books, and his parchments.
carpus.histoire:
In his final letter, Paul as a prisoner asks Timothy: "When you come, bring the cloak I left at Troas with Carpus, and my books, especially the parchments" (2 Timothy 4:13).

A tender, human detail: the apostle is cold, and to the very end he wants to study. Carpus is the trusted friend to whom you entrust what matters most to you.

crescens.bio: Paul's coworker who departed for Galatia during his final imprisonment.
crescens.histoire:
"Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world, and has departed for Thessalonica; Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me" (2 Timothy 4:10-11).

Crescens is not a deserter like Demas: he departs on mission. Two departures, two very different hearts.

mnason.histoire:
On their way up to Jerusalem, disciples from Caesarea brought Paul and Luke "to the home of Mnason, a man from Cyprus and an early disciple, with whom we were to stay" (Acts 21:16).

A believer from the very beginning, who opens his home to a man facing death. Hospitality is a form of courage.

tyrannus.bio: Owner or master of a school in Ephesus where Paul taught daily for two years.
tyrannus.histoire:
Driven out of the synagogue, Paul "separated the disciples and taught daily in the school of one named Tyrannus" (Acts 19:9).

Result: "This continued for two years, so that all who dwelt in Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord" (Acts 19:10). An ordinary classroom became the heart of the evangelization of an entire province.

sopater.bio: A Christian from Berea, son of Pyrrhus, who accompanied Paul on his journey to Jerusalem with the collection.
sopater.histoire:
"And these went ahead and waited for us at Troas. But we sailed away from Philippi after the Days of Unleavened Bread, and came to them at Troas in five days, where we stayed seven days. And Sopater of Berea accompanied him to Asia—also Aristarchus and Secundus of the Thessalonians, and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia" (Acts 20:4).

Berea was the city whose Jews "examined the Scriptures daily" (Acts 17:11): Sopater may well be a fruit of their sincere search.

marie-clopas.bio: One of the women standing near the cross of Jesus.
marie-clopas.histoire:
"Near the cross of Jesus stood His mother, and His mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene" (John 19:25). Where the disciples fled, these women remained.

Some identify her with "Mary, the mother of James the Less and Joses" who watched from afar and came to the tomb (Mark 15:40; 16:1), though this is not certain. Her silent presence at Calvary speaks the essential truth: love endures.

simon-pharisien.bio: A Pharisee who invited Jesus to his table and watched a sinful woman anoint Jesus' feet; Jesus taught him the parable of the two debtors.
simon-pharisien.histoire:
"A certain Pharisee asked Jesus to eat with him." A sinful woman comes, weeps at Jesus' feet, and anoints them with perfume. Simon thinks: "If this man were a prophet, he would know who and what kind of woman is touching him" (Luke 7:36-39). Jesus replies to him: "Simon, I have something to say to you"—and tells the story of the two debtors (Luke 7:40-43).

"Do you see this woman?" She did everything Simon neglected. "Therefore, I say to you, her many sins are forgiven, for she loved much. But he to whom little is forgiven loves little" (Luke 7:44-47).

simon-lepreux.bio: A resident of Bethany, probably healed by Jesus, in whose house a woman anointed Jesus with perfume before His Passion.
simon-lepreux.histoire:
"Now when Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came to him carrying an alabaster jar of very expensive perfume" (Matthew 26:6-7). John, who also places a meal in Bethany where Mary, the sister of Lazarus, anoints Jesus, appears to report the same event (John 12:1-3).

Simon still carries the name of his disease, yet he receives Jesus at his table; but a leper was required to live apart (Leviticus 13:46). He had therefore no doubt been healed. Jesus declares there: "Wherever this good news is proclaimed in the whole world, what this woman has done will also be told in memory of her" (Matthew 26:13).

haran.bio: Brother of Abram and Nahor, father of Lot and Milcah; he died at Ur before the family's departure.
haran.histoire:
"Terah fathered Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran fathered Lot" (Genesis 11:27). He dies young: "Haran died in the presence of Terah his father in the land of his nativity, in Ur of the Chaldeans" (Genesis 11:28).

His descendants remain central to the story: his son Lot accompanies Abram, and his daughter Milcah marries Nahor (Genesis 11:29, 31). Do not confuse him with the city of Haran, where the family later settles.

milca.bio: Daughter of Haran and wife of Nahor, brother of Abraham; grandmother of Rebekah.
milca.histoire:
"The name of Nahor's wife was Milcah, daughter of Haran" (Genesis 11:29). While Abraham waits for the promise, he is told: "Behold, Milcah has also borne children to Nahor, your brother"—eight sons, including Bethuel, who "fathered Rebekah" (Genesis 22:20-23).

When Abraham's servant prays at the well, Rebekah appears, "born to Bethuel, son of Milcah, wife of Nahor, brother of Abraham" (Genesis 24:15). The answer to prayer comes from Abraham's own family.

debora-nourrice.bio: Rebekah's nurse who departed with her from Mesopotamia; her death was mourned beneath "the Oak of Weeping" near Bethel.
debora-nourrice.histoire:
When Rebekah left her family to marry Isaac, she was allowed to go "and her nurse with her" (Genesis 24:59). This faithful woman followed her throughout her life, then remained in Jacob's household.

Decades later: "Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, died; and she was buried below Bethel, under the oak to which was given the name Oak of Weeping" (Genesis 35:8). The Bible takes time to name and honor a faithful servant.

er-onan.bio: Eldest sons of Judah, successive husbands of Tamar; both died for their wickedness.
er-onan.histoire:
"Judah took a wife for Er, his firstborn, whose name was Tamar. But Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord; and the Lord put him to death" (Genesis 38:6-7).

According to the custom of levirate marriage, Onan must raise up offspring for his brother; but, "knowing that the offspring would not be his," he refuses to do so, and "What he did displeased the Lord, who put him to death also" (Genesis 38:8-10). The line of Judah—the line of the Messiah—would continue through Tamar and Perez.

guerschom.bio: The two sons of Moses and Zipporah, whose names sum up their father's exile and deliverance.
guerschom.histoire:
In Midian, Zipporah bore a son, whom Moses "called Gershom, for he said, 'I have been a stranger in a foreign land'" (Exodus 2:22).

Jethro brought to Moses his wife and his two sons; the second "was named Eliezer, for he said, 'The God of my father was my help, and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh'" (Exodus 18:3-4). Two names, two stages of one life: exile, then God's rescue.

adoni-tsedek.bio: An Amorite king of Jerusalem who rallied five kings against Gibeon; defeated by Joshua on the day the sun stood still.
adoni-tsedek.histoire:
When Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, learned that Gibeon had made peace with Israel, he was "greatly alarmed" and called on the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon: "Come up to me and help me, so that we may strike Gibeon" (Joshua 10:1-4).

Joshua came to Gibeon's aid; it was the battle where he said, "Sun, stand still over Gibeon!" (Joshua 10:12). The five kings, hidden in a cave at Makkedah, were put to death (Joshua 10:16-26). His name means "my lord is righteousness"—a distant echo of Melchizedek, king of Salem.

jabin.bio: Name of Canaanite kings of Hazor: one was defeated by Joshua, another oppressed Israel for twenty years before Deborah and Barak's victory.
jabin.histoire:
The first Jabin gathers the northern kings against Joshua, "a people as numerous as the sand on the seashore"; Hazor is taken and burned (Joshua 11:1-11).

Later, "the Lord sold them into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor"; his commander is Sisera (Judges 4:2-3). After the victory at Tabor, "On that day God subdued Jabin, king of Canaan, before the children of Israel" (Judges 4:23).

adoni-bezek.bio: A Canaanite king defeated by Judah, who recognized that he himself suffered the cruelty he had inflicted on seventy kings.
adoni-bezek.histoire:
Judah and Simeon find "Adoni-Bezek at Bezek"; he flees, they catch up with him, "and they cut off his thumbs and big toes" (Judges 1:5-6).

He himself concludes: "Seventy kings with their thumbs and big toes cut off used to pick up scraps under my table. Now God has paid me back for what I did to them" (Judges 1:7). An ancient illustration of the principle: "Whatever a man sows, he will also reap" (Galatians 6:7).

eglon.bio: King of Moab who oppressed Israel for eighteen years; he was killed by Ehud, the left-handed judge.
eglon.histoire:
"The Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab against Israel, because they had done evil in the sight of the Lord." Allied with Ammon and Amalek, he took "the City of Palms," and Israel served him for eighteen years (Judges 3:12-14).

Ehud comes to bring him tribute, then returns: "I have a message from God for you." He strikes him with his sword hidden on his right side; "now Eglon was a very fat man," and the blade disappears (Judges 3:17-22). His servants wait a long time behind the locked door (Judges 3:24-25).

oreb-zeeb.bio: Two Midianite leaders captured and killed by the men of Ephraim during the rout caused by Gideon.
oreb-zeeb.histoire:
After the night of trumpets and jars, Gideon calls Ephraim to cut off the road to the fugitives. "They captured two leaders of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb; they killed Oreb at the Rock of Oreb, and they killed Zeeb at the Winepress of Zeeb" (Judges 7:25).

Their names—"raven" and "wolf"—will remain the symbol of God's enemies brought down (Psalms 83:11; Isaiah 10:26).

zebach-tsalmunna.bio: Kings of Midian pursued by Gideon beyond the Jordan River; they had killed his brothers at Tabor.
zebach-tsalmunna.histoire:
Gideon pursues them with three hundred exhausted men, then questions them: "What kind of men did you kill at Tabor?" They answered, "They were like you—each one looked like the son of a king." These were his own brothers (Judges 8:18-19).

His son Jether, still a child, dares not strike them; the kings say, "Rise up yourself, and kill us! For as the man is, so is his strength" (Judges 8:20-21).

jotham-gedeon.bio: Youngest son of Gideon and sole survivor of the massacre of his brothers; he told the parable of the trees from Mount Gerizim.
jotham-gedeon.histoire:
Abimelech kills his seventy brothers "on one stone. Only Jotham, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, escaped, for he hid himself" (Judges 9:5). From the top of Mount Gerizim, Jotham cries out to the people of Shechem the first parable in the Bible: the olive tree, the fig tree, and the grapevine refuse to reign; only the thornbush agrees (Judges 9:8-15).

The thornbush gives neither shade nor fruit, only fire. Jotham concludes: "Let a fire come out from Abimelech and consume the men of Shechem" (Judges 9:20). Three years later, his word comes to pass (Judges 9:56-57).

elimelec.bio: A man of Bethlehem, husband of Naomi, who departed with his family to Moab during a famine and died there.
elimelec.histoire:
"In the days when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land." A man leaves Bethlehem, whose name means house of bread, for Moab: "The name of the man was Elimelech, the name of his wife was Naomi, and the names of his two sons were Mahlon and Chilion" (Ruth 1:1-2). He dies there (Ruth 1:3).

His name means: My God is King. His inheritance will be redeemed by Boaz, his relative, who marries Ruth "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance" (Ruth 4:9-10).

machlon-kiljon.bio: Sons of Elimelech and Naomi, who married Moabite women, Ruth and Orpah, and died in Moab.
machlon-kiljon.histoire:
In Moab, they "took for themselves Moabite women; the name of the one was Orpah and the name of the other was Ruth." Ten years later, "both Mahlon and Chilion also died; so the woman was left of her two sons and her husband" (Ruth 1:4-5).

Boaz would clarify that Ruth was "the Moabite, the wife of Mahlon" (Ruth 4:10). Their death seemed to close the story; God made it the beginning of David's lineage.

obed.bio: Son of Boaz and Ruth, grandfather of King David; he appears in the genealogy of Jesus.
obed.histoire:
Naomi took the child and laid him on her lap, and she became his nurse. The women living there said, "Naomi has a son!" And they named him Obed. He was the father of Jesse the father of David (Ruth 4:15-17).

Matthew cites him: "Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth" (Matthew 1:5). Through him, a Moabite entered the lineage of the Messiah.

ikabod.bio: Grandson of the priest Eli, born on the day the ark was captured; his name means "the glory has departed."
ikabod.histoire:
On the day of the defeat at Aphek, the wife of Phinehas learns in quick succession of the capture of the ark, the death of her father-in-law, and the death of her husband; she gives birth and dies. "She called the child Ichabod, saying, 'The glory has departed from Israel!'" (1 Samuel 4:19-21).

"The glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured!" (1 Samuel 4:22). A name like a cry: without God's presence, nothing remains. His family will still serve in the time of Saul (1 Samuel 14:3).

kis.bio: Benjamite "mighty and valiant" man, father of King Saul; while searching for his donkeys that Saul met Samuel.
kis.histoire:
"There was a man of Benjamin named Kish […] He was a mighty man of power. He had a son whose name was Saul, a choice and handsome young man" (1 Samuel 9:1-2).

"The donkeys of Kish, Saul's father, had gone lost"; Saul sets out to search for them and encounters Samuel, who was waiting for him: "Do not worry about the donkeys […] they have been found" (1 Samuel 9:3, 20). A routine errand becomes a divine appointment. Saul was buried in the tomb of Kish (2 Samuel 21:14).

nachasch.bio: King of the Ammonites who threatened to gouge out the right eye of the inhabitants of Jabesh; his defeat strengthened Saul's kingship.
nachasch.histoire:
"Nahash the Ammonite came up and besieged Jabesh Gilead." When the inhabitants ask for a treaty, he replies: "I will gouge out all your right eyes, and bring reproach on all Israel" (1 Samuel 11:1-2).

The Spirit of God seized Saul, who gathered the people and delivered Jabesh (1 Samuel 11:6-11). Later, Nahash showed kindness to David, who wanted to honor his son Hanun (2 Samuel 10:2).

achimelec.bio: Priest of Nob who gave David the consecrated bread and the sword of Goliath; Saul had him killed along with all the priests.
achimelec.histoire:
David arrives alone at Nob; Ahimelech "came running to meet him in fear." Having only the consecrated bread, he gives it to him, along with the sword of Goliath (1 Samuel 21:1-9). Jesus will recall this episode to remind us that mercy comes first (Mark 2:25-26).

Betrayed by Doeg, Ahimelech defends himself with integrity: who is as faithful as David? Yet Saul has eighty-five priests massacred; only his son Abiathar escapes (1 Samuel 22:14-20). Psalm 52 bears the memory of this betrayal.

akisch.bio: A Philistine king of Gath, before whom David pretended to be insane, and with whom he later lived in exile for sixteen months.
akisch.histoire:
The first time, David fears Achish: he acts like a madman, "letting his spittle run down his beard." Achish is annoyed: "Am I lacking in madmen?" (1 Samuel 21:12-15).

Later, David settles with him with six hundred men; Achish gives him Ziklag and trusts him (1 Samuel 27:2-12). When the Philistine princes refuse David in the battle against Saul, Achish tells him: "You are as pleasing to me as an angel of God" (1 Samuel 29:9). God thus spares David from fighting against his own people.

femme-endor.bio: A woman who conjured the dead, secretly consulted by Saul on the eve of his death, despite the law's prohibition.
femme-endor.histoire:
God no longer answers Saul. He who had driven out the mediums says to his servants: "Find me a woman who conjures the dead." "Behold, there is a woman at En-Dor who conjures the dead" (1 Samuel 28:3-7). Saul goes there in disguise, by night.

When Samuel appears, the woman lets out "a loud scream"—a sign that this was not her usual power (1 Samuel 28:12). Samuel announces Saul's defeat and death for the next day (1 Samuel 28:19). Scripture clearly condemns such practices (Deuteronomy 18:10-12; 1 Chronicles 10:13).

jonadab-neveu.bio: Nephew of David, "a very shrewd man," who devised the scheme that led Amnon to abuse Tamar.
jonadab-neveu.histoire:
"Now Amnon had a friend, whose name was Jonadab the son of Shimeah, David's brother. And Jonadab was a very shrewd man." He whispers the plan to him: "Lie down on your bed and pretend to be ill" (2 Samuel 13:3-5). The crime against Tamar follows.

Two years later, when word spreads that all the king's sons have been killed, it's Jonadab again who knows the truth: "Only Amnon is dead; for by the appointment of Absalom this has been determined" (2 Samuel 13:32). Cleverness without the fear of God becomes complicity.

hanun.bio: King of the Ammonites, son of Nahash, who humiliated David's envoys of peace and provoked war.
hanun.histoire:
"David said, 'I will show kindness to Hanun the son of Nahash, as his father showed kindness to me'" (2 Samuel 10:2). But his advisors persuade him that these are spies.

"Then Hanun took David's servants, shaved off half their beards, and cut off their garments in the middle" (2 Samuel 10:4). This insult triggers war against Ammon—the very war during which David will remain in Jerusalem and fall into sin with Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:1).

scheba-bicri.bio: A Benjamite who led a rebellion against David following Absalom's revolt; his head was delivered to Joab by a wise woman.
scheba-bicri.histoire:
"Now there happened to be there a man of Belial, whose name was Sheba the son of Bichri, a Benjamite. And he blew a trumpet and said: 'We have no share in David […] Every man to his tents, O Israel!' " (2 Samuel 20:1).

Joab besieges him in Abel-Beth-Maachah; a wise woman negotiates from the wall and saves her city: "they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri, and threw it out to Joab" (2 Samuel 20:16-22). The wisdom of one person spares an entire city.

ornan.bio: A Jebusite from whom David purchased a threshing floor to build an altar; it was there that Solomon built the temple.
ornan.histoire:
After the census, plague strikes Israel. The prophet Gad tells David: "Raise an altar to the Lord in the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite." Araunah offers everything freely; David refuses: "I will not offer to the Lord my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing" (2 Samuel 24:18-24).

God answers "with fire from heaven falling on the altar" (1 Chronicles 21:26). This place will become the site of the temple: "on Mount Moriah [...] on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite" (2 Chronicles 3:1).

abischag.bio: A young woman chosen to care for King David in his old age; Adonijah asked for her in marriage, which cost him his life.
abischag.histoire:
"King David was old […] he could not keep warm." A search is made for "a young and beautiful girl, and they found Abishag, the Shunamite"; "She cared for the king and served him; but the king did not know her" (1 Kings 1:1-4).

After David's death, Adonijah asks Bathsheba to obtain Abishag as his wife. Solomon understands the scheme: "Then ask the kingdom for him" (1 Kings 2:17-22). Marrying a wife of the deceased king was to claim the throne.

schischak.bio: Pharaoh of Egypt (Sheshonq I) who welcomed the fleeing Jeroboam, then plundered Jerusalem under Rehoboam.
schischak.histoire:
Jeroboam, threatened by Solomon, "fled to Egypt to Shishak king of Egypt" (1 Kings 11:40). "In the fifth year of King Rehoboam's reign, Shishak king of Egypt attacked Jerusalem"; he took all the treasures and Solomon's gold shields (1 Kings 14:25-26).

The prophet Shemaiah explained: "You have abandoned me; I also abandon you"; the king and the leaders humbled themselves, and God spared the city (2 Chronicles 12:5-7). Rehoboam replaced the gold with bronze (1 Kings 14:27). An inscription at Karnak lists the cities taken during this campaign.

schemaeja-prophete.bio: Man of God under Rehoboam: he prevented fratricidal war against Israel and called Judah to humble themselves before Shishak.
schemaeja-prophete.histoire:
Rehoboam gathers one hundred eighty thousand men to reclaim Israel. God speaks through Shemaiah: do not make war against your brothers, "for this thing is from Me"; and they obey (1 Kings 12:21-24).

When Shishak invades Judah, he declares: "You have forsaken Me; therefore I also leave you." The leaders humble themselves: "The Lord is righteous!" — and God promises: "I will not destroy them" (2 Chronicles 12:5-7). A prophetic word that is heard prevents disaster.

hanani-voyant.bio: Father and son prophets: Hanani rebuked King Asa and was imprisoned; Jehu, son of Hanani, prophesied against Baasha and rebuked Jehoshaphat.
hanani-voyant.histoire:
"Hanani the seer came to Asa, king of Judah": "You have relied on the king of Aram and […] you have not relied on the Lord." Then this precious word: "the Lord's eyes range throughout the earth to strengthen those whose hearts are fully committed to him" (2 Chronicles 16:7-9). Asa throws him in prison (2 Chronicles 16:10).

His son takes over: "The word of the Lord came to Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha" (1 Kings 16:1). He will also rebuke Jehoshaphat for his alliance with Ahab (2 Chronicles 19:2). Not to be confused with King Jehu.

jehoscheba.bio: Princess of Judah, wife of the high priest Jehoiada: she saved young Joash from the massacre ordered by Athaliah, preserving the line of David.
jehoscheba.histoire:
Athaliah destroys the entire royal line. "But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah, took Joash son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the royal princes" and hid him with his nurse (2 Kings 11:1-2). He remained "hidden with Jehosheba in the house of the Lord for six years" (2 Kings 11:3).

Chronicles clarifies that she was "the wife of the priest Jehoiada" (2 Chronicles 22:11). Through the courage of one woman, the promise made to David—a descendant on his throne—was not extinguished.

zacharie-jehojada.bio: A priest filled with the Spirit who rebuked King Joash and the people; he was stoned in the courtyard of the temple.
