zacharie-jehojada.histoire:
After Jehoiada's death, the people return to idols. "Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest was clothed with the Spirit of God": "Why do you transgress the commandments of the Lord?" (2 Chronicles 24:20). He is stoned "at the command of the king, in the courtyard of the house of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 24:21).

"King Joash did not remember the kindness that Jehoiada had shown him"; Zechariah dies saying, "May the Lord see and bring justice!" (2 Chronicles 24:22). Many see in him the last martyr mentioned by Jesus, since the Hebrew Old Testament ends with Chronicles (Luke 11:51).

jachaziel.bio: A Levite, son of Asaph, upon whom the Spirit came in the midst of the assembly: he announced to Jehoshaphat that the battle belonged to God.
jachaziel.histoire:
Judah is threatened by an enormous coalition; Jehoshaphat prays: "we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you" (2 Chronicles 20:12). "Then the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jahaziel" (2 Chronicles 20:14).

"Do not be afraid or discouraged before this vast multitude, for the battle is not yours, but God's" (2 Chronicles 20:15); "stand firm, take your positions, and you will see the Lord's deliverance" (2 Chronicles 20:17). The next day, the singers march before the army, and the enemy destroys itself (2 Chronicles 20:21-23).

oded.bio: A prophet from Samaria who persuaded the army of Israel to release the captives from Judah.
oded.histoire:
Israel defeated Judah and brought back two hundred thousand captives. "There was a prophet of the Lord there, named Oded": "You have killed them with a rage that reaches to heaven […] return these captives whom you have taken from among your brothers" (2 Chronicles 28:9-11).

Leaders of Ephraim listen to him: the prisoners are clothed, fed, and the weakest are carried on donkeys to Jericho (2 Chronicles 28:12-15)—a scene that foreshadows the parable of the Good Samaritan.

tiglath-pileser.bio: King of Assyria who annexed Galilee and Damascus; King Ahaz of Judah bought his protection with the treasures of the temple.
tiglath-pileser.histoire:
"In the time of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-Pileser king of Assyria came and took […] Gilead and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and he carried captive their inhabitants to Assyria" (2 Kings 15:29)—the territories of Zebulun and Naphtali over which Isaiah announces a great light (Isaiah 8:23; 9:1).

Ahaz, threatened, writes to him: "I am your servant and your son; come up and deliver me" and sends him the gold of the temple (2 Kings 16:7-8). He returns from Damascus with the pattern of a pagan altar (2 Kings 16:10). Yet Isaiah had called him to trust in God alone (Isaiah 7:9).

salmanasar.bio: King of Assyria who besieged Samaria for three years; the city's fall in 722 BC ended the kingdom of Israel.
salmanasar.histoire:
"Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against him; and Hoshea became his servant." Discovering that Hoshea has turned to Egypt, he throws him into prison and besieges Samaria "for three years" (2 Kings 17:3-5).

"In the ninth year of Hoshea, the king of Assyria took Samaria and carried Israel away into Assyria" (2 Kings 17:6). The text explains why: Israel had rejected the warnings of all the prophets (2 Kings 17:13-14).

merodac-baladan.bio: King of Babylon who sent an embassy to Hezekiah; the king showed him all his treasures.

schebna.bio: Palace administrator under Hezekiah, arrogant, to whom Isaiah announced his removal in favor of Eliakim.
schebna.histoire:
"Go to this official, to Shebna, the palace administrator: [...] What are you doing here? Why are you carving out a tomb for yourself on the height?" (Isaiah 22:15-16). While Jerusalem is under threat, he tends to his own glory.

"I will remove you from your office" (Isaiah 22:19). During Sennacherib's siege, he is found serving as secretary, under Eliakim (2 Kings 18:18).

eliakim-hilkija.bio: Chief of the household of King Hezekiah, called by God "my servant"; he received "the key of the house of David."
eliakim-hilkija.histoire:
"In that day I will call My servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah"; "He will be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem"; "I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David: When he opens, no one will shut" (Isaiah 22:20-22). Jesus will use this image for Himself (Revelation 3:7).

During the Assyrian siege, it was he who negotiated with the Rabshakeh, then brought to Isaiah the message from Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:18, 26; 19:2).

enfants-esaie.bio: Isaiah's two sons, whose names were living prophecies:
enfants-esaie.histoire:
Isaiah went to meet King Ahaz with "Shear-Jashub, your son" (Isaiah 7:3)—"a remnant will return": even judgment leaves room for hope. Then a second son was born: "Name him Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz. For before the boy knows how to say 'My father' or 'My mother,' the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria will be carried off by the king of Assyria" (Isaiah 8:3-4).

Isaiah summed it up: "Here am I, and with me the children the Lord has given me. We are here, and with us the children the Lord has given us. We are here, and with us are the children God has given us as signs and wonders in Israel" (Isaiah 8:18). The prophet's own family was itself a message.

gomer.bio: Wife of the prophet Hosea, unfaithful, whom Hosea reclaimed through love: a living image of God's love for unfaithful Israel.
gomer.histoire:
"Go, take yourself a wife of harlotry and children of harlotry, for the land has committed great harlotry by departing from the Lord... So he went and took Gomer the daughter of Diblaim" (Hosea 1:2-3). Their children bear names of judgment and rejection (Hosea 1:4-9).

Then God said: "Go again, love a woman who is loved by a lover and is committing adultery; love her as the Lord loves the children of Israel." Hosea redeems her "for fifteen shekels of silver" (Hosea 3:1-2). The Gospel before the Gospel: love that redeems the unfaithful.

bigthan-theresch.bio: Two eunuchs who plotted against King Ahasuerus; Mordecai thwarted the plot, which was recorded in the Chronicles.
bigthan-theresch.histoire:
"Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs, doorkeepers, became furious and sought to lay hands on King Ahasuerus." Mordecai learns of it and informs Esther; the conspirators are hanged, "and it was written in the Book of the Chronicles" (Esther 2:21-23).

Years later, a sleepless night: the king has this passage read to him, and he asks, "What honor and distinction has been bestowed on Mordecai for this?" (Esther 6:1-3). What men forget, God does not.

elihu.bio: A young man who spoke after Job's three friends, insisting on God's greatness and the meaning of suffering.
elihu.histoire:
"Then the wrath of Elihu, the son of Barachel of Buz, was aroused" — against Job who claimed to be righteous, and against the three friends who condemned him without answering (Job 32:2-3). He had waited out of respect: "I am young, and you are aged" (Job 32:6).

But "in a man's heart is the spirit, and the breath of the Almighty gives him understanding" (Job 32:8). He shows that God also speaks through suffering to instruct (Job 33:14-30), preparing the response of the Lord from the midst of the storm (Job 38:1).

agur-lemuel.bio: Authors of the last two chapters of Proverbs: Agur's prayer and the teaching of King Lemuel's mother on the virtuous woman.
agur-lemuel.histoire:
"The words of Agur son of Jakeh." He is known for a prayer of rare wisdom: "Give me neither poverty nor riches, but give me only my daily bread. Otherwise, I may have too much and disown you" (Proverbs 30:1, 8-9).

"The words of King Lemuel—an oracle his mother taught him" (Proverbs 31:1). From her comes the famous portrait: "A wife of noble character who can find? She is worth far more than pearls" (Proverbs 31:10).

gabriel.bio: An angel who "stands before God": he explained his visions to Daniel, then announced the birth of John the Baptist to Zechariah and the birth of Jesus to Mary.
gabriel.histoire:
Daniel hears a voice: "Gabriel, explain the vision to him" (Daniel 8:16). Later, while Daniel is praying, "the man Gabriel [...] came near to me in swift flight": "I have come now to give you insight and understanding"; he reveals to him the seventy weeks until the Messiah (Daniel 9:21-27).

Six centuries later, in the temple: "I am Gabriel, who stands in the presence of God; I was sent to speak to you" (Luke 1:19). Then "the angel Gabriel was sent by God to a city of Galilee called Nazareth": "Greetings, you who are highly favored; the Lord is with you" (Luke 1:26-28). The messenger of the great announcements of salvation.

michel-archange.bio: Archangel, "one of the chief princes" and defender of God's people; he fights the dragon in Revelation.
michel-archange.histoire:
In Daniel, the Bible calls him Michael: "Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me" (Daniel 10:13); "At that time Michael, the great prince, the protector of your people, will arise" (Daniel 12:1). Daniel's prayer triggers an invisible battle.

Jude reports that "when the archangel Michael was disputing with the devil about the body of Moses, he did not dare to bring a slanderous accusation against him, but said, 'The Lord rebuke you!" (Jude 1:9). In Revelation: "Michael and his angels fought against the dragon [...] and they were no longer found in heaven" (Revelation 12:7-8).

mages.bio: Wise men from the East who followed a star to worship the newborn King of the Jews; they gave him gold, frankincense, and myrrh.
mages.histoire:
"Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem, saying, Where is he that is born King of the Jews? for we have seen his star in the east" (Matthew 2:1-2). The first foreign worshipers of the Messiah.

The star guides them; "And when they were come into the house, they saw the young child with Mary his mother, and fell down, and worshiped him" and offered "gold, and frankincense, and myrrh" (Matthew 2:11). The text does not say they were three, nor that they were kings. Warned in a dream, they depart "by another way" (Matthew 2:12).

bergers.bio: Shepherds watching their flocks by night: the first to receive the announcement of the Savior's birth, and the first to tell others about it.
bergers.histoire:
"There were shepherds living out in the fields nearby, keeping watch over their flocks at night"; an angel appears to them: "I bring you good news that will cause great joy for all the people. Today in the town of David a Savior has been born to you; he is the Messiah, the Lord" (Luke 2:8-11).

After the song of the heavenly host, "Glory to God in the highest," they go "in haste," find the child and tell everything (Luke 2:14-17). God chooses humble and despised people as first witnesses; they return "glorifying and praising God" (Luke 2:20).

centenier-capernaum.bio: Roman officer who asked for the healing of his servant; Jesus admired his faith: "I have not found such great faith even in Israel."
centenier-capernaum.histoire:
A centurion loves the Jewish people and built them a synagogue (Luke 7:5). His servant is dying. He sends word to Jesus: "Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only speak a word, and my servant will be healed" (Matthew 8:8). A man of authority, he understands the authority of Jesus' word (Matthew 8:9).

"Jesus marveled at him": "I have not found such great faith, not even in Israel"; and he announces that many will come "from east and west" to the feast of the kingdom (Matthew 8:10-11). "Go; let it be to you according to your faith" (Matthew 8:13).

centenier-croix.bio: A Roman officer who commanded the crucifixion and confessed, seeing Jesus die: "Surely, this man was the Son of God."
centenier-croix.histoire:
"The centurion, who stood facing Jesus, seeing that he had breathed his last in this way, said: Surely, this man was the Son of God" (Mark 15:39). Matthew specifies that he was seized with great fear after the earthquake (Matthew 27:54).

Luke adds: "The centurion, seeing what had happened, glorified God and said: Certainly, this man was righteous" (Luke 23:47). The first confession of faith at the foot of the cross came from a pagan—from the very officer of the execution.

femme-cananeenne.bio: A pagan mother from the region of Tyre and Sidon whose persistent faith obtained the healing of her daughter.
femme-cananeenne.histoire:
"A Canaanite woman from that region came and cried out, 'Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David! My daughter is severely tormented by a demon.' Jesus remained silent; the disciples wanted to send her away (Matthew 15:22-23). Mark clarifies that she was 'a Greek, a Syrophoenician by birth' (Mark 7:26).

Like the bread of the children, she replied: 'Yes, Lord, [...] but the little dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table.' 'Woman, your faith is great; let it be done for you as you wish' (Matthew 15:27-28). Persistent humility touches the Lord's heart.

legion.bio: A man possessed by a multitude of demons, living among the tombs, delivered by Jesus and became a witness in the Decapolis.
legion.histoire:
He lived among the tombs; no one could bind him. Seeing Jesus, he ran and fell at his feet, and the spirit cried out: "What have you to do with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?" — "What is your name? Legion is my name," he answered, "for we are many" (Mark 5:6-9).

Freed, he was found "sitting, clothed, and in his right mind" (Mark 5:15). He wanted to follow Jesus, who told him: "Go home to your own people, and tell them all that the Lord has done for you" (Mark 5:19). He became a missionary in the Decapolis.

aveugle-ne.bio: A blind beggar from birth who was healed by Jesus at the Pool of Siloam; questioned and cast out by the Pharisees, he confessed his faith in the Son of God.
aveugle-ne.histoire:
"Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents?" Jesus answered, "Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but that the works of God should be revealed in him." He made clay, applied it to his eyes: "Go, wash at the Pool of Siloam"; he returned "seeing clearly" (John 9:2-7).

When the Pharisees questioned him, he answered simply: "One thing I know: that though I was blind, now I see" (John 9:25). Cast out, he is found by Jesus: "Do you believe in the Son of God? […] I believe, Lord. And he worshiped him" (John 9:35-38).

theudas.bio: Two agitators whose movements had failed, cited by Gamaliel to advise the Sanhedrin to let the apostles go.
theudas.histoire:
Gamaliel reminds them: "Some time ago Theudas appeared, claiming to be somebody […] he was killed, and all his followers were scattered" (Acts 5:36), then "Judas the Galilean appeared in the days of the census […] he too was killed" (Acts 5:37).

His conclusion remains famous: "If their purpose or activity is of human origin, it will fail. But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them—you will only find yourselves fighting against God" (Acts 5:38-39).

blaste.bio: Chamberlain of King Herod Agrippa I, won over by the Tyrians and Sidonians to obtain peace, just before the king's death.
blaste.histoire:
The Tyrians and Sidonians, who depended on the king's grain, come to seek peace "after winning over Blastus, his chamberlain" (Acts 12:20).

During the audience, the people acclaim Herod: "The voice of a god, and not of a man!" "And immediately an angel of the Lord struck him down, because he did not give glory to God" (Acts 12:22–23). The historian Josephus also records this sudden death.

geolier-philippes.bio: Guard of the Philippi prison, converted along with his entire family the night an earthquake opened the doors.
geolier-philippes.histoire:
Paul and Silas, beaten, are thrown into the inner prison, their feet fastened in the stocks. "About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God." An earthquake opens all the doors; the jailer wants to kill himself, but Paul cries out: "Do not harm yourself, we are all here" (Acts 16:24-28).

Trembling, he asks: "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?" — "Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household." He washes their wounds, is baptized with his family, and "rejoiced with all his household that he had believed in God" (Acts 16:30-34).

fils-sceva.bio: Seven Jewish exorcists from Ephesus who invoked the name of Jesus without knowing Him and were routed by an evil spirit.
fils-sceva.histoire:
Traveling exorcists try the formula: "I adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preaches!" — "seven sons of Sceva, a Jew, chief of the priests" (Acts 19:13-14). The spirit answers: "I know Jesus, and I know who Paul is; but who are you?" and puts them to flight, "naked and wounded" (Acts 19:15-16).

The name of Jesus is not a magic formula: it works through relationship and faith. News of this causes "the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified," and many burn their books of magic (Acts 19:17-19).

fortunatus-achaicus.bio: Christians from Corinth who came with Stephanas to join Paul in Ephesus, and brought him comfort.
fortunatus-achaicus.histoire:
"I rejoice at the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, for what was lacking on your part they supplied. For they refreshed my spirit and yours" (1 Corinthians 16:17-18).

They likely carried the letter from the Corinthians to Paul (1 Corinthians 7:1), and perhaps his response as well. Faithful messengers whose arrival was a blessing to the soul.

artemas.bio: A trusted collaborator whom Paul planned to send to Crete to replace Titus.
artemas.histoire:
"When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make haste to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there" (Titus 3:12).

Just one verse, but great confidence: Paul judges him capable of continuing Titus's work among the churches of Crete.

eubulus-pudens-linus-claudia.bio: Christians in Rome who greet Timothy in Paul's final letter; tradition identifies Linus as the first leader of the Church in Rome after the apostles.
eubulus-pudens-linus-claudia.histoire:
"Make every effort to come before winter. Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers greet you" (2 Timothy 4:21).

Though abandoned by many, Paul is not alone: a small community surrounds him in Rome. In the second century, Irenaeus names Linus as the first entrusted with the leadership of the Church in Rome.

jannes-jambres.bio: Names given by Jewish tradition to Pharaoh's magicians who opposed Moses; Paul cites them as models of false teachers.
jannes-jambres.histoire:
Exodus does not name them: it speaks of the "magicians of Egypt" who imitated Moses' first signs (Exodus 7:11, 22). Paul uses their names known from tradition: "Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth" (2 Timothy 3:8).

But "they will make no further progress; for their folly will be evident to all, as was that of those two men" (2 Timothy 3:9). The magicians eventually had to confess: "This is the finger of God!" (Exodus 8:15).

antipas.bio: A Christian in Pergamum who was put to death for his faith, whom Jesus calls "my faithful witness."
antipas.histoire:
In the middle of the letter to Pergamum, Christ honors a name: "I know your works, and where you dwell, where Satan's throne is. And you hold fast to My name, and did not deny My faith even in the days in which Antipas was My faithful witness, who was killed among you, where Satan dwells" (Revelation 2:13).

Jesus Christ Himself is called "the faithful witness" (Revelation 1:5; 3:14). The Lord shares His own title with a martyr whose story has left us nothing else.

salues-romains.bio: The long list of believers whom Paul greets at Rome: Epaenetus, Amplius, Urbanus, Tryphena and Tryphosa, Persis, Herodion and many others—men and women, slaves and the freed.
salues-romains.histoire:
Paul greets "Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the firstfruits of Achaia for Christ," "Amplius, my beloved in the Lord," "Urbanus, our coworker in Christ, and Stachys," "Apelles, approved in Christ," those of the household of Aristobulus and Narcissus, "Herodion, my kinsman" (Romans 16:5-11).

Then: "Greet Tryphena and Tryphosa, who have labored in the Lord. Greet Persis the beloved, who has labored much in the Lord"; and also Asyncritus, Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympas (Romans 16:12-15). After the great doctrine of the epistle, a list of names: the Gospel is about loved people.

pharaon.bio: Title of the kings of Egypt: the Bible features several of them, from the one who raised Joseph to the one who refused to let Israel go.
pharaon.histoire:
Abram encounters a Pharaoh in Egypt (Genesis 12:15). Another raises Joseph to second in command of the kingdom: "I have set you over all the land of Egypt" (Genesis 41:40). But "a new king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph" and enslaved Israel (Exodus 1:8-10).

Facing Moses, Pharaoh declares: "Who is the Lord, that I should obey His voice?" (Exodus 5:2). Ten plagues and the Red Sea answer him: "Pharaoh and his chariots and his horsemen I will glorify" (Exodus 14:18). Paul sees God's sovereignty in this: "I have raised you up, that I may show My power in you" (Romans 9:17). Other pharaohs appear later: Solomon's father-in-law, Shishak, Necho, and Hophra.

satan.bio: The adversary, a fallen angel, accuser and liar; the ancient serpent of Genesis, defeated by the cross and destined for final defeat.
satan.histoire:
The "serpent" of Eden plants doubt: "Did God really say…?" (Genesis 3:1). God immediately announces his defeat: the offspring of the woman "will crush your head" (Genesis 3:15). In Job, he presents himself among the sons of God and accuses: "Does Job fear God for nothing?" (Job 1:9), but he can do nothing without God's permission (Job 1:12). Zechariah sees him accusing the high priest: "The Lord rebuke you, Satan!" (Zechariah 3:1-2).

Jesus rebukes him in the wilderness by Scripture: "Away from me, Satan!" (Matthew 4:10). He calls him "a murderer from the beginning" and the father of lies (John 8:44). Peter warns: "Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion" (1 Peter 5:8). His fate is sealed: "They overcame him by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony" (Revelation 12:11), and he will end up "in the lake of fire and brimstone" (Revelation 20:10).

tseruja.bio: David's sister and mother of his three formidable nephews: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel.
tseruja.histoire:
The Bible rarely names sons by their mother; here it is constant: "Joab, son of Zeruiah." Chronicles makes it clear: "Their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. Sons of Zeruiah: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, three" (1 Chronicles 2:16).

"There were the three sons of Zeruiah: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel" (2 Samuel 2:18). Faithful and fierce, they are David's strength and sometimes his burden—he sighs, "these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too powerful for me" (2 Samuel 3:39).

kehath-guerschon-merari.bio: The three sons of Levi, ancestors of the three families of Levites responsible for the tabernacle; Moses and Aaron descend from Kohath.
kehath-guerschon-merari.histoire:
"Here are the names of the sons of Levi, according to their generations: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari." Among the sons of Kohath: "Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel"—Amram is the father of Moses and Aaron (Exodus 6:16-20).

In the wilderness, each family had their responsibility: the Kohathites carried the most holy objects, the ark, the table, the lampstand (Numbers 4:4-15); the Gershonites, the curtains and coverings; the Merarites, the boards, the pillars, and the bases (Numbers 4:24-33). Each one their service, all for the presence of God in the midst of the people.

amalek.bio: Nomadic people descended from Esau, the first enemy to attack Israel after the Exodus from Egypt; a relentless adversary until the time of Esther.
amalek.histoire:
At Rephidim, Amalek attacks; Israel prevails as long as Moses holds up his hands. God commands: "Write this in a book […] I will completely blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven" (Exodus 17:14). Deuteronomy explains his sin: he struck "those who were lagging behind, all the stragglers," "without any fear of God" (Deuteronomy 25:18).

Saul spares their king Agag and loses the kingdom (1 Samuel 15). David will later recover from the Amalekites the plunder of Ziklag (1 Samuel 30). Haman, "the Agagite," is said to be a descendant of Amalek (Esther 3:1).

makir.bio: Firstborn son of Manasseh, grandson of Joseph; his descendants conquered Gilead.
makir.histoire:
Joseph lived to see his great-grandchildren: "the sons of Makir, son of Manasseh, were born on Joseph's knees" (Genesis 50:23).

Later, "The sons of Makir, son of Manasseh, went to Gilead and took possession of it"; "Moses gave Gilead to Makir" (Numbers 32:39-40). The daughters of Zelophehad, famous for their petition, belonged to his descendants (Numbers 27:1).

zerach.bio: Son of Judah and Tamar, twin of Perez, born with a scarlet thread on his wrist; ancestor of Achan.
zerach.histoire:
Tamar bears twins. One puts out his hand; the midwife ties a scarlet thread on it, but he withdraws it, and his brother is born first: Perez. "And afterward came out his brother that had the scarlet thread upon his hand: and his name was called Zerah" (Genesis 38:27-30).

It is Perez, not Zerah, who will be the ancestor of David and the Messiah (Matthew 1:3). Achan, who took forbidden things from Jericho, was from the family of Zerah (Joshua 7:1, 18).

heman-jeduthun.bio: Chiefs of the Levite singers established by David along with Asaph; their sons "prophesied" with the harp, lyre, and cymbals.
heman-jeduthun.histoire:
"David and the leaders of the army set apart for service those of the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun who prophesied with the harp, lyre, and cymbals" (1 Chronicles 25:1). Jeduthun "prophesied with the harp for praising and giving thanks to the Lord"; Heman "was the king's seer" (1 Chronicles 25:3-5).

Their names appear in the titles of several psalms (Psalms 39; 62; 88). Praise in the Bible is not merely an accompaniment: it can be a prophetic ministry.

achinoam.bio: Wife of David during his years of exile, mother of his firstborn son Amnon.
achinoam.histoire:
"David had also taken Ahinoam of Jezreel, and both became his wives" — alongside Abigail (1 Samuel 25:43). She shares his wandering life, even to Ziklag, where she is taken captive by the Amalekites and then rescued (1 Samuel 30:5, 18).

At Hebron, "His firstborn was Amnon, by Ahinoam of Jezreel" (2 Samuel 3:2). Do not confuse with Ahinoam, wife of Saul (1 Samuel 14:50).

retsin.bio: Last Aramean king of Damascus: allied with Pekah against Judah, he provoked the prophecy of Emmanuel; killed by the Assyrians.
retsin.histoire:
"Rezin king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah king of Israel, came up to Jerusalem to make war"; the heart of King Ahaz is troubled "as the trees of the woods are shaken by the wind" (Isaiah 7:1-2). God sends Isaiah: "do not fear [...] Before these two smoking stubs of torches"; "If you do not believe, you will not be established" (Isaiah 7:4, 9). It is in this context that the sign of Emmanuel is given (Isaiah 7:14).

Ahaz prefers Assyria; Tiglath-Pileser takes Damascus and puts Rezin to death (2 Kings 16:9).

ephron.bio: A Hittite from Hebron who sold Abraham the field and cave of Machpelah, the patriarch's only possession in Canaan.

heber-kenien.bio: A Kenite, descendant of Hobab, the father-in-law of Moses, settled near Kedesh; husband of Jael.
heber-kenien.histoire:
"Now Heber the Kenite had separated himself from the Kenites, from the sons of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses, and had pitched his tent near the Oak of Zaanannim, which is beside Kedesh" (Judges 4:11).

Sisera, defeated and fleeing, heads toward Heber's tent, for "there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the household of Heber the Kenite" (Judges 4:17). But Jael, his wife, chooses the side of Israel. Deborah sings: "Blessed above women shall Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, be!" (Judges 5:24).

jubal-tubal-cain.bio: Sons of Lamech, descended from Cain: the fathers of nomadic herders, musicians, and metalworkers.
jubal-tubal-cain.histoire:
The line of Cain invented civilization: "Ada bore Jabal; he was the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock. His brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who play the harp and flute" (Genesis 4:20-21).

"And Zillah also bore Tubal-Cain, an instructor of every craftsman in bronze and iron" (Genesis 4:22). Herding, music, metalworking: real gifts, in a line moving away from God. It is with Seth that people began to "call on the name of the Lord" (Genesis 4:26).

femme-lot.bio: She left Sodom with her family but looked back and became a pillar of salt; Jesus made her a warning.
femme-lot.histoire:
The angels urged the family: "do not look back" (Genesis 19:17). "Lot's wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt" (Genesis 19:26).

Jesus, speaking of His return, gives only one sentence: "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:32). You can leave Sodom and still keep your heart in Sodom.

echanson-panetier.bio: Two officers of Pharaoh imprisoned with Joseph, whose dreams he interpreted; the cupbearer forgot him for two years.
echanson-panetier.histoire:
"The cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt offended their master"; Pharaoh had them placed in prison where Joseph was imprisoned (Genesis 40:1-3). Joseph explains their dreams: one will be restored, the other hanged; which happens on the day of Pharaoh's birthday (Genesis 40:20-22).

"The chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph. He forgot him" (Genesis 40:23). Two years later, when Pharaoh dreams, he finally remembers: "I will call to mind my offense today" (Genesis 41:9). Man's delay serves God's timing.

fille-jephthe.bio: The only child of Jephthah, who came out first to meet him after his victory, victim of her father's rash vow.
fille-jephthe.histoire:
Jephthah had made a vow: to offer whatever came out first from his house. "And behold, his daughter came out to meet him with tambourines and dancing. She was his only child" (Judges 11:34). She responds with heartbreaking dignity: "My father, if you have made a vow to the Lord, deal with me according to what has come out of your mouth" (Judges 11:36).

She mourns her virginity for two months in the mountains; "It became a custom in Israel that the daughters of Israel went yearly to lament the daughter of Jephthah" (Judges 11:39-40). The tragic account reveals the spiritual confusion of the time of the judges; the law condemned human sacrifices (Deuteronomy 12:31).

levite-juges19.bio: A Levite from Ephraim whose concubine was abused and killed in Gibeah; this crime triggered a civil war against Benjamin.
levite-juges19.histoire:
"In those days when there was no king in Israel, a certain Levite […] took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem of Judah." He goes to win her back to speak to her heart (Judges 19:1-3). On the return, at Gibeah, no one welcomes them except an old man; the men of the city abuse the woman all night, and she dies (Judges 19:15-28).

The Levite sends her body in twelve pieces to all Israel: "Nothing like this has ever happened" (Judges 19:29-30). The Book of Judges closes with this reality: "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25).

femme-tekoa.bio: A wise woman sent by Joab to persuade David, through a fabricated story, to bring Absalom back from exile.
femme-tekoa.histoire:
Joab sees that the king's heart is drawn toward Absalom in exile; "he sent someone to Tekoa to bring a wise woman" and puts a story in her mouth (2 Samuel 14:1-3). Like Nathan before her, she leads David to judge himself through a parable.

She speaks words of great depth: "We will surely die [...] God does not take away life, but desires that the fugitive not remain banished from His presence" (2 Samuel 14:14). David recalls Absalom—without truly receiving him, which will fuel his rebellion.

homme-dieu-juda.nom: The Man of God from Judah
homme-dieu-juda.bio: A prophet who came from Judah to Bethel to announce the coming of Josiah; deceived by an old prophet, he disobeyed and was killed by a lion.
homme-dieu-juda.histoire:
"Behold, a man of God came from Judah to Bethel"; before Jeroboam, he cries out against the altar: "Behold, a son will be born to the house of David; his name will be Josiah" (1 Kings 13:1-2). The king's hand withers, the altar splits (1 Kings 13:4-5). Three centuries later, Josiah will fulfill this word (2 Kings 23:15-17).

But an old prophet from Bethel makes him return to eat at his house: "an angel spoke to me […] He was lying to him" (1 Kings 13:18). Having disobeyed the order he received, the man of God is killed by a lion (1 Kings 13:24). No word, even a "prophetic" one, overrides what God has clearly said.

veuve-sarepta.bio: A pagan widow who shared her last handful of flour with Elijah; the flour and oil did not run out, and her son was raised from the dead.
veuve-sarepta.histoire:
"Arise, go to Zarephath […] I have commanded a widow there to provide for you." She has only "a handful of flour in a jar and a little oil in a jug"; Elijah asks first for himself, with a promise: "The jar of flour will not be used up and the jug of oil will not run dry" (1 Kings 17:9-14).

Later, Elijah raises her son from the dead; she confesses: "Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the Lord from your mouth is the truth" (1 Kings 17:24). Jesus will cite her in Nazareth: Elijah was sent to a foreigner (Luke 4:25-26).

servante-naaman.bio: A young Israelite captive in Syria who, serving Naaman's wife, directed him to the prophet Elisha.
servante-naaman.histoire:
The Syrians had "taken captive a little girl from the land of Israel, and she served Naaman's wife. She said to her mistress, 'Oh, that my master were with the prophet who is in Samaria! He would heal him of his leprosy!' (2 Kings 5:2-3).

Torn from her homeland, without name or power, she keeps her faith and kindness toward her master. A single word from her leads a pagan general to healing and confession of the true God (2 Kings 5:15).

lepreux-samarie.bio: Lepers who discovered the abandoned Syrian camp during the siege of Samaria and went to announce the good news.
lepreux-samarie.histoire:
Samaria is dying of hunger. "There were four lepers at the entrance of the gate": "Shall we sit here until we die?" They go to the Syrian camp—empty: God made "the sound of a great army" heard there, and the Syrians fled (2 Kings 7:3-7).

After eating and hiding plunder, they stop: "We are not doing right! This day is a day of good news; if we keep silent [...] judgment will come upon us" (2 Kings 7:9). You don't keep good news that saves to yourself.

femme-job.bio: Job's wife who, in his trial, advised him to curse God; Job refused.
femme-job.histoire:
After losing his children and possessions, Job is struck with a disease. "His wife said to him, 'Do you still hold fast to your integrity? Curse God and die!'" (Job 2:9). She too had lost everything.

Job replied, "Shall we indeed accept good from God, and shall we not accept adversity?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips" (Job 2:10). In the end, God gave Job seven sons and three daughters (Job 42:13).

baal.bio: Canaanite deities of storm and fertility; their worship became Israel's great snare, from Judges through the exile.
baal.histoire:
Already in the generation after Joshua, "they forsook the Lord and served Baal and the Ashtoreths" (Judges 2:13). Samuel calls to repentance: "Put away the foreign gods and the Ashtoreths from among you" (1 Samuel 7:3). Even Solomon himself would follow "Ashtoreth, the goddess of the Sidonians" (1 Kings 11:5).

Under Ahab and Jezebel, Elijah challenges the prophets of Baal at Carmel: "How long will you falter between two opinions?" They cry from morning till noon, "But there was no voice nor any who answered"; the fire of the Lord falls on Elijah's altar (1 Kings 18:21-38). A god who does not answer is not God.

dagon.bio: God of the Philistines; Samson caused his temple to collapse, and his statue fell face-down before the Ark.
dagon.histoire:
The Philistine rulers celebrate Samson's capture: "Our god has delivered our enemy Samson into our hands" (Judges 16:23). Samson, blind, prays one last time and brings down the temple upon them (Judges 16:28-30).

Later, the Ark is placed "in the house of Dagon" at Ashdod. The next morning, Dagon is "lying face-down on the ground before the Ark of the Lord"; the following morning, "Dagon's head and both his hands had been broken off on the threshold" (1 Samuel 5:2-4).

moloc-kemosch.bio: Gods of the Ammonites (Moloch, also called Milcom) and the Moabites (Chemosh), whose worship involved child sacrifice.
moloc-kemosch.histoire:
The law strictly forbade offering children to Moloch (Leviticus 18:21). Yet Solomon built "a high place for Chemosh, the abomination of Moab, and for Moloch, the abomination of the sons of Ammon" (1 Kings 11:7).

King Josiah "defiled Topheth in the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, so that no one could make his son or daughter pass through the fire to Moloch" (2 Kings 23:10). Stephen would later recall this idolatry (Acts 7:43).

diane.bio: Great goddess of Ephesus (Artemis), whose temple was one of the wonders of the world; her worship was shaken by Paul's preaching.
diane.histoire:
Demetrius the silversmith grew concerned: not only his business, but "the temple of the great goddess Diana be regarded as nothing" (Acts 19:27). The whole city cried out for nearly two hours: "Great is Diana of the Ephesians!" (Acts 19:34).

The town clerk reminded them that the city is "the keeper of the temple of the great Diana and of her image which fell down from Jupiter" (Acts 19:35). The Gospel had not attacked the temple; it had changed hearts.

femme-adultere.bio: A woman caught in adultery and brought to Jesus to be stoned; He saved her and told her:
femme-adultere.histoire:
"The scribes and Pharisees brought to Him a woman caught in adultery": the law commanded to stone her, "So what do you say?" Jesus wrote on the ground, then: "He who is without sin among you, let him throw a stone at her first" (John 8:3-7). They withdrew one by one, "from the oldest even to the last" (John 8:9).

"Woman, where are those accusing you? [...] Neither do I condemn you; go and sin no more" (John 8:10-11). Grace that lifts up, and holiness that calls.

hemorroisse.nom: The Woman Healed of a Hemorrhage
hemorroisse.bio: A woman sick for twelve years, impoverished by physicians, healed by touching Jesus' garment.
hemorroisse.histoire:
"There was a woman who had been subject to bleeding for twelve years." She "had spent all she had," without result. She said to herself, "If I just touch his clothes, I will be healed"—and she is (Mark 5:25-29).

Jesus stops: "Who touched my clothes?" She confesses trembling. "Daughter, your faith has healed you; go in peace and be freed from your suffering" (Mark 5:30-34). Unclean by the law, isolated for twelve years, she is publicly called "daughter."

pauvre-veuve.bio: A widow who gave two small coins, all she had, to the temple treasury; Jesus said she had given more than everyone else.
pauvre-veuve.histoire:
Jesus observes the offerings: "Many rich people threw in large amounts. But a poor widow came and put in two very small copper coins, worth only a few cents" (Mark 12:41-42).

"This poor widow has put in more than all the others. All these people gave their gifts out of their wealth; but she out of her poverty put in all she had to live on" (Mark 12:43-44). God does not measure the gift by its amount, but by what it costs the giver.

jeune-homme-riche.bio: A wealthy and devout man who asked Jesus how to inherit eternal life, but left sorrowfully, unable to let go of his possessions.
jeune-homme-riche.histoire:
"A man ran up to him, and kneeling before him asked him, 'Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?'" He had kept the commandments since his youth (Mark 10:17-20). Matthew notes that he was young; Luke notes that he was a ruler.

"Jesus, looking at him, loved him, and said to him, 'You lack one thing; go, sell all that you have [...] Then come, follow me.' This man went away sorrowful; for he had great possessions" (Mark 10:21-22). Jesus's look of love precedes the demanding call.

brigands-croix.nom: The Two Criminals Crucified with Jesus
brigands-croix.bio: Two condemned men crucified on either side of Jesus; one mocked him, while the other repented and received the promise of paradise.
brigands-croix.histoire:
Jesus is crucified between two criminals, fulfilling Isaiah: "he was numbered with the transgressors" (Isaiah 53:12). "One of the criminals who hung there hurled insults at him: 'Aren't you the Messiah? Save yourself and us!'" (Luke 23:39).

The other rebuked him: "this man has done nothing wrong. And he said to Jesus, 'Remember me when you come into your kingdom.'" "I tell you the truth, today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:40-43). Salvation by grace, in the final hour, without any works.

servante-python.nom: The Fortune-Telling Slave Girl of Philippi
servante-python.bio: A young enslaved woman possessed by a spirit of divination, exploited by her masters; Paul cast out the spirit, which led to his imprisonment.
servante-python.histoire:
"A certain slave girl possessed with a spirit of divination met us, who brought her masters much profit by fortune-telling" and followed Paul, crying out: "These men are the servants of the Most High God" (Acts 16:16-17). Truth from the mouth of an evil spirit.

After many days, Paul said to the spirit, "I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her. And he came out that very hour" (Acts 16:18). Her masters, seeing their profit gone, had Paul and Silas thrown into prison—from which the jailer's conversion would arise.

titius-justus.bio: A God-fearing man from Corinth whose house, next door to the synagogue, welcomed Paul and the new believers.
titius-justus.histoire:
Rejected by the synagogue, Paul "entered the house of a man named Justus, a worshiper of God, whose house was next door to the synagogue" (Acts 18:7). Right after, Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed along with his entire household (Acts 18:8).

A pagan sympathizer opens his home at the very moment a door closes: this is where the Church of Corinth takes root, and where God says to Paul, "I have many people in this city" (Acts 18:10).

bon-samaritain.bio: Character in Jesus's parable: a Samaritan, despised by the Jews, who cared for an injured man whom the priest and the Levite had ignored.
bon-samaritain.histoire:
To the question "Who is my neighbor?" Jesus responds with a story: "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves." A priest passes by, a Levite as well; "But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was; and when he saw him, he was moved with compassion" (Luke 10:30-33).

He tends his wounds with oil and wine, brings him to an inn, and pays in advance (Luke 10:34-35). "Which of these three do you think was neighbor to him who fell among the thieves? [...] Go and do likewise" (Luke 10:36-37). Your neighbor is not someone you choose—it's someone you reach.

fils-prodigue.bio: Character in the parable: the younger son who squandered his inheritance, returned in repentance, and was welcomed by his father with a celebration.
fils-prodigue.histoire:
"A man had two sons." The younger one demands his share, goes to a distant country and "squandered his wealth in wild living"; reduced to tending pigs, "he came to his senses" and said to himself: "I will set out and go back to my father" (Luke 15:11-18).

"While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him"; the finest robe, the ring, the fattened calf: "this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found" (Luke 15:20-24). The older son refuses to join the celebration (Luke 15:28-32): the parable also speaks to the religious.

riche-lazare.bio: Characters in Jesus' account: a wealthy, indifferent man and a poor man named Lazarus, whose fortunes are reversed after death.
riche-lazare.histoire:
"There was a certain rich man who was clothed in purple and fine linen [...] A certain beggar named Lazarus was laid at his gate, full of sores" (Luke 16:19-20). The poor man dies "and was carried by the angels to Abraham's bosom"; the rich man, in torment, pleads (Luke 16:22-24).

Abraham responds that "between us and you there is a great gulf fixed," and then: "If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they be persuaded though one rise from the dead" (Luke 16:26, 31). Do not confuse with Lazarus of Bethany, whom Jesus raised from the dead.

cesar-neron.bio: The Roman emperor to whom Paul, a Roman citizen, appealed; Acts does not name him by name, but it was Nero who reigned at that time.
cesar-neron.histoire:
Before Festus, Paul refuses to be tried in Jerusalem: "It is before Caesar's tribunal that I must appear"; Festus concludes: "You have appealed to Caesar; you will go before Caesar" (Acts 25:10-12). Agrippa will say: "This man could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar" (Acts 26:32).

In the storm, the angel confirms: "Paul, do not be afraid; you must appear before Caesar" (Acts 27:24). From Rome, Paul writes to the Philippians: "All the saints greet you, and especially those of Caesar's household" (Philippians 4:22)—the Gospel had entered even into the palace. Tradition reports that Paul was executed under Nero.

henoc-cain.bio: Firstborn son of Cain. His father built a city and gave it his name: the first city in the Bible bears the name of a child.
henoc-cain.histoire:
Cast out from the Lord's presence, Cain settled in the land of Nod. "Cain made love to his wife, and she became pregnant and gave birth to Enoch. Cain was then building a city, and he named it after his son Enoch" (Genesis 4:17).

Do not confuse him with the other Enoch, a descendant of Seth, who "walked with God" (Genesis 5:24): two men with the same name, two family lines, two paths.

irad.bio: Son of Enoch and grandson of Cain, a link in the line of Cain.
irad.histoire: The Bible tells us just one thing about him: he belongs to the descendants of Cain who multiply, generation after generation: "Enoch begat Irad, and Irad begat Mehujael" (Genesis 4:18). These brief genealogies show that humanity grows, even far from God.

mehujael.bio: Son of Irad, in the line of Cain.
mehujael.histoire: He is mentioned only once: "Irad fathered Mehujael, and Mehujael fathered Methuselah" (Genesis 4:18). He is the link between the earliest generations and Lamech, the first man in the Bible to take two wives.

metuschael.bio: Son of Mehujael and father of Lamech, in the line of Cain. Not to be confused with Methuselah, from the line of Seth.
metuschael.histoire: "Mehujael fathered Methushael" (Genesis 4:18). His name resembles that of Methuselah, the grandfather of Noah, but he belonged to the other branch: that of Cain, who turned away from God.

ada-lemec.bio: One of Lamech's two wives, mother of Jabal and Jubal, the fathers of herders and musicians.
ada-lemec.histoire:
"And Lamech took for himself two wives: the name of one was Adah, and the name of the second was Zillah" (Genesis 4:19). Adah bore Jabal, "the father of those who dwell in tents and have livestock," and Jubal, "the father of all those who play the harp and flute" (Genesis 4:20–21).

It is to her and to Zillah that Lamech addresses his song of vengeance: "Adah and Zillah, hear my voice!" (Genesis 4:23).

tsilla.bio: Second wife of Lamech, mother of Tubal-Cain the blacksmith and of Naamah.
tsilla.histoire: "And Zillah also bore Tubal-Cain, an instructor of every craftsman in bronze and iron. And the sister of Tubal-Cain was Naamah" (Genesis 4:22). Along with Adah, she hears the boastful song of her husband, who brags about having killed a man (Genesis 4:23-24).

naama-lemec.bio: Daughter of Lamech and Zillah, sister of Tubal-Cain: one of the very first women named in the Bible.
naama-lemec.histoire: The account simply mentions: "And the sister of Tubal-Cain was Naamah" (Genesis 4:22). It is rare for a daughter to be named in these genealogies: her name means "pleasant."

enosch.bio: Son of Seth and grandson of Adam. In his time, men began to call upon the name of the Lord.
enosch.histoire:
"Seth also had a son, and he called his name Enosh. At that time people began to call upon the name of the Lord" (Genesis 4:26). While the line of Cain built cities and forged weapons, the line of Seth turned toward God in prayer.

"When Enosh had lived ninety years, he fathered Kenan"; he lived a total of nine hundred and five years (Genesis 5:9-11). Luke names him Enos in the genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:38).

kenan.bio: Son of Enosh, the fourth generation after Adam; he lived nine hundred and ten years.
kenan.histoire:
"Enosh, being ninety years old, fathered Kenan"; "Kenan, being seventy years old, fathered Mahalalel", and "all the days of Kenan were nine hundred and ten years; and he died" (Genesis 5:9-14).

Luke calls him Cainan in the genealogy that traces from Jesus back to Adam (Luke 3:37).

mahalaleel.bio: Son of Kenan and father of Jared, in the line of Seth; his name means
mahalaleel.histoire: "When Mahalaleel had lived 65 years, he fathered Jared"; "all the days of Mahalaleel were 895 years, and he died" (Genesis 5:15-17). The refrain "and he died" echoes through Genesis 5: since the Fall, death reigns—until Enoch, his great-grandson, is taken up by God.

jered.bio: Son of Mahalaleel and father of Enoch, the man who "walked with God." He lived nine hundred sixty-two years.
jered.histoire:
"Jared was one hundred sixty-two years old when he fathered Enoch"; "all the days of Jared were nine hundred sixty-two years, and he died" (Genesis 5:18-20).

His son Enoch did not experience death: "Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24).

cusch.bio: Eldest son of Ham, ancestor of the peoples of the south (ancient Ethiopia) and father of Nimrod.
cusch.histoire:
"The sons of Ham were Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan" (Genesis 10:6). The name Cush later designated the region south of Egypt.

"Cush also fathered Nimrod; he was the first on earth to be a mighty man" (Genesis 10:8): the founder of Babel and the earliest great cities of Mesopotamia.

mitsraim.bio: Son of Ham, ancestor of the Egyptians: in Hebrew, Mizraim is the very name of Egypt.
mitsraim.histoire: Second son of Ham (Genesis 10:6), he is the ancestor of several peoples, including the Philistines who descended from him (Genesis 10:13-14). His name will become that of the land where Joseph will be sold and where Israel will be enslaved: Egypt.

puth.bio: Son of Ham, ancestor of a people of North Africa (ancient Libya, according to many).
puth.histoire: Third son of Ham (Genesis 10:6). His descendants appear later among the prophets as soldiers allied with Egypt (Jeremiah 46:9).

canaan-fils.bio: Son of Ham and grandson of Noah, cursed by his grandfather; ancestor of the peoples of the land that would bear his name.

elam-sem.bio: Eldest son of Shem, ancestor of the Elamites, a people of eastern Mesopotamia (modern-day Iran).
elam-sem.histoire: "The sons of Shem were Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram" (Genesis 10:22). His descendants would form the kingdom of Elam, whose capital, Susa, would later serve as the setting for the books of Esther and Nehemiah.

assur-sem.bio: Son of Shem, ancestor of the Assyrians, the people who would make Israel tremble.
assur-sem.histoire: Second of the sons of Shem (Genesis 10:22). His name would become that of Assyria, the empire that destroyed Samaria in 722 B.C. (2 Kings 17:6).

arpacschad.bio: Son of Shem, born two years after the Flood, ancestor of Heber and Abraham.
arpacschad.histoire:
"Shem was one hundred years old when he begot Arphaxad, two years after the Flood" (Genesis 11:10). "Arphaxad lived thirty-five years, and begot Salah" (Genesis 11:12).

Through him runs the lineage leading to Abraham, then to David and to Jesus: Luke calls him Arphaxad (Luke 3:36).

lud.bio: Son of Shem, ancestor of a people of Asia Minor, possibly the Lydians.
lud.histoire: Fourth son of Shem (Genesis 10:22). The name of Lud would reappear among the prophets among the distant peoples to whom God would announce His glory (Isaiah 66:19).

aram-sem.bio: Son of Shem, ancestor of the Arameans (the Syrians of the Bible).
aram-sem.histoire: Fifth son of Shem (Genesis 10:22). His descendants, the Arameans, would populate Syria and upper Mesopotamia: it was in Aram that Laban, Rebekah, Leah, and Rachel would live. Aramaic would become the common language in the time of Jesus.

schelach.bio: Son of Arphaxad and father of Eber, in the line of Shem toward Abraham.
schelach.histoire: "And Arphaxad begot Shelah; and Shelah begot Eber" (Genesis 10:24). "Shelah, when he was thirty years old, begot Eber" (Genesis 11:14). Luke names him Sala in the genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:35).

heber.bio: Son of Shelah, ancestor of Abraham; many connect his name to that of the "Hebrews."
heber.histoire:
The Bible presents Shem as the "father of all the children of Heber" (Genesis 10:21): Heber therefore holds a special place. "Two sons were born to Heber; the name of one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided, and his brother's name was Joktan" (Genesis 10:25).

"Heber was thirty-four years old when he fathered Peleg" (Genesis 11:16). Luke calls him Eber (Luke 3:35).

peleg.bio: Son of Eber; his name means "division" because "in his days the earth was divided."
peleg.histoire: His name recalls an event: "in his days the earth was divided" (Genesis 10:25) — often connected with the scattering of peoples after Babel. "Peleg lived thirty years, and begot Reu" (Genesis 11:18). Luke names him Phalec (Luke 3:35).

jokthan.bio: Son of Heber and brother of Peleg, ancestor of many Arabian tribes.
jokthan.histoire: Brother of Peleg (Genesis 10:25), he fathered thirteen sons whose names—Sheba, Ophir, Havilah…—designate tribes of southern Arabia (Genesis 10:26–30). Ophir will become famous for its gold in the time of Solomon.

rehu.bio: Son of Peleg and father of Serug, in the line of Shem toward Abraham.
rehu.histoire: "Reu lived thirty-two years, and begot Serug. After he begot Serug, Reu lived two hundred and seven years, and begot sons and daughters" (Genesis 11:20-21). Luke calls him Ragau (Luke 3:35).

serug.bio: Son of Reu and great-grandfather of Abraham.
serug.histoire: "When Serug was thirty years old, he fathered Nahor" (Genesis 11:22). Three generations later, Abram would be born. Luke calls him Serug in the genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:35).

nachor-ancien.bio: Son of Serug and father of Terah: the grandfather of Abraham, whose grandson Nahor bore the same name.
nachor-ancien.histoire:
"When Nahor had lived 29 years, he fathered Terah" (Genesis 11:24). His name was borne by one of his grandsons, Abraham's brother, who married Milcah (Genesis 11:26-29).

He appears in the genealogy of Jesus according to Luke: "son of Terah, son of Nahor" (Luke 3:34).

jisca.bio: Daughter of Haran, sister of Lot and Milcah, niece of Abraham.
jisca.histoire: The Bible mentions her only once: Haran is "the father of Milcah and the father of Jisca" (Genesis 11:29). Her father died young in Ur of the Chaldees, "in the presence of Terah, his father" (Genesis 11:28).

moab-fils.bio: Eldest son of Lot, born after the destruction of Sodom; ancestor of the Moabites, the people of Ruth.
moab-fils.histoire:
Taking refuge in a cave after the ruin of Sodom, Lot became a father through his own daughters. "And the firstborn bore a son and called his name Moab; he is the father of the Moabites to this day" (Genesis 19:37).

From this troubled beginning would come a people often hostile to Israel—and yet from Moab came Ruth, the great-grandmother of David (Ruth 1:4).

ben-ammi.bio: Youngest son of Lot, ancestor of the Ammonites.
ben-ammi.histoire: "The younger also bore a son and called his name Ben-Ammi; he is the father of the Ammonites to this day" (Genesis 19:38). The Ammonites would often oppose Israel; yet Naamah the Ammonite became the mother of King Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:21).

fille-schua.nom: The Daughter of Shua (wife of Judah)
fille-schua.bio: A Canaanite woman and wife of Judah, mother of Er, Onan, and Shelah. The Bible does not give her name, only that of her father.
fille-schua.histoire: "There Judah saw the daughter of a certain Canaanite whose name was Shua; and he took her and went in to her" (Genesis 38:2). She bears him three sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah (Genesis 38:3-5). The two eldest die, and Judah's line is ultimately continued through Tamar.

schela.bio: Third son of Judah, promised to Tamar but never given to her; ancestor of the Shelanite family.
schela.histoire:
After the deaths of Er and Onan, Judah sends Tamar away: "Remain a widow in your father's house until Shelah my son is grown" (Genesis 38:11); he feared "that he also would die like his brothers" (Genesis 38:11). But Tamar sees "that Shelah had grown up, and she had not been given to him as a wife" (Genesis 38:14).

Judah would eventually acknowledge: "She is more righteous than I am, since I did not give her to Shelah my son" (Genesis 38:26). Shelah founded the family of the Shelanites (Numbers 26:20).

hetsron.bio: Son of Perez and grandson of Judah, who went down to Egypt with Jacob; ancestor of David and Jesus (Esrom in the Gospels).
hetsron.histoire:
He was one of the seventy members of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt: "The sons of Perez were Hezron and Hamul" (Genesis 46:12).

The genealogy of Ruth makes him a link in the royal line: "Perez begot Hezron; Hezron begot Ram" (Ruth 4:18-19). Matthew calls him Esrom (Matthew 1:3).

ram.bio: Son of Hezron, ancestor of David and Jesus, during the time of Israel's sojourn in Egypt (Aram in Matthew).
ram.histoire: "Hezron fathered Ram; Ram fathered Amminadab" (Ruth 4:19). Nothing else is told of his life: he belongs to the silent generations of Egypt, between Joseph and Moses, through whom God nonetheless kept His promise. Matthew calls him Aram (Matthew 1:3-4).

amminadab.bio: Son of Ram, of the tribe of Judah: father of Nahshon, leader of Judah in the wilderness, and of Elisheba, the wife of Aaron.
amminadab.histoire: His family connected two great lineages: his daughter Elisheba married Aaron, the first high priest (Exodus 6:23), and his son Nahshon was the prince of Judah in the wilderness —

m.v: for Judah, Nahshon the son of Amminadab

(Numbers 1:7).

He is an ancestor of David:
Ram fathered Amminadab, and Amminadab fathered Nahshon
(Ruth 4:19-20). Matthew and Luke call him Aminadab.

elischeba.bio: Wife of Aaron, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon: the mother of the priestly line.
elischeba.histoire:
"Aaron took as his wife Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab, sister of Nahshon; and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar" (Exodus 6:23).

Through her, the tribe of Judah—the tribe of kings—and the tribe of Levi—the tribe of priests—are united. All the high priests of Israel descend from her.

salmon.bio: Son of Nahshon and husband of Rahab, according to Matthew: the father of Boaz.
salmon.histoire: "Nahshon fathered Salmon; Salmon fathered Boaz" (Ruth 4:20-21). Matthew adds an unexpected detail: "Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab" (Matthew 1:5)—Rahab, the Canaanite woman of Jericho saved by her faith, thus enters into the family of David and the Messiah. Chronicles calls him Salma (1 Chronicles 2:11).

zabdi.bio: Descendant of Zerah, son of Judah, and grandfather of Achan.
zabdi.histoire: When the drawing of lots exposed Achan's sin, Joshua "brought his household near by men, and Achan the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, from the tribe of Judah, was taken" (Joshua 7:18). A genealogy recalled at the moment of judgment: each person belongs to a family, yet each answers for his own actions.

carmi.bio: Son of Zabdi and father of Achan, from the tribe of Judah.
carmi.histoire: He is known only as the father of Achan, who took things devoted to God during the capture of Jericho: "Achan son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things" (Joshua 7:1).

jitsehar.bio: Son of Kohath and uncle of Moses and Aaron; father of Korah, who rebelled against them.
jitsehar.histoire:
"The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel"; "The sons of Izhar: Korah, Nepheg, and Zichri" (Exodus 6:18-21).

His son Korah would lead the great rebellion in the wilderness: "Korah, the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, took men" (Numbers 16:1). Two first cousins: Moses the servant, Korah the challenger.

hebron-fils.bio: Son of Kohath and uncle of Moses, ancestor of the Levitical family of the Hebronites. Not to be confused with the city of Hebron.
hebron-fils.histoire: Third son of Kohath (Exodus 6:18). His descendants, the Hebronites, were among the families of Kohath responsible for carrying the most holy objects of the tabernacle (Numbers 3:27-31).

uziel.bio: Son of Kohath and uncle of Aaron; his sons carried the bodies of Nadab and Abihu out of the camp.
uziel.histoire: The youngest of the sons of Kohath (Exodus 6:18). When Nadab and Abihu were consumed for offering unauthorized fire, "Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Uzziel, the uncle of Aaron, and said to them: 'Come here, carry your brothers out from the sanctuary, out of the camp'" (Leviticus 10:4).

abinadab-isai.bio: Second son of Jesse, older brother of David; he was in Saul's army facing Goliath.
abinadab-isai.histoire:
When Samuel comes to anoint a king from among Jesse's sons, "Jesse called Abinadab and had him pass in front of Samuel; and Samuel said, 'The Lord has not chosen this one either'" (1 Samuel 16:8).

He then goes to war against the Philistines with his older brothers: "his firstborn was Eliab, his second son Abinadab, and the third Shammah" (1 Samuel 17:13). It is the youngest, David, who will face Goliath.

schimea.bio: Third son of Jesse, brother of David; also called Shamma. His sons Jonadab and Jonathan appear in the history of David.
schimea.histoire:
"Then Jesse made Shimea pass by. And Samuel said, 'The Lord has not chosen this one either'" (1 Samuel 16:9). Chronicles names him Shimea, "the third" of Jesse's sons (1 Chronicles 2:13).

His two sons marked the history of their uncle David: Jonadab, the shrewd friend who counsels Amnon (2 Samuel 13:3), and Jonathan, who killed a Philistine giant: "Jonathan son of Shimea, David's brother, killed him" (2 Samuel 21:21).

nethaneel.bio: The fourth son of Jesse, brother of David.
nethaneel.histoire: He is mentioned only in the genealogy of Chronicles: "Jesse begat Eliab his firstborn, and Abinadab the second, and Shimea the third, and Nethanel the fourth" (1 Chronicles 2:13-14). A brother in the shadow of the youngest, chosen by God.

raddai.bio: Fifth son of Jesse, brother of David.
raddai.histoire: Only mention: "Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth" (1 Chronicles 2:14). Chronicles lists seven sons of Jesse, with David being "the seventh"; 1 Samuel speaks of eight sons (1 Samuel 17:12), one of whom may have died young.

otsem.bio: The sixth son of Jesse, David's brother just above him in birth order.
otsem.histoire: "Otsem the sixth, David the seventh" (1 Chronicles 2:15). He is the last of David's older brothers named in Scripture.

abigail-soeur.bio: Sister of David and Zeruiah, mother of Amasa, commander of Absalom's army and then of David's army. Not to be confused with Abigail, David's wife.
abigail-soeur.histoire:
"Their sisters were: Zeruiah and Abigail"; "Abigail bore Amasa" (1 Chronicles 2:16-17).

The book of Samuel calls her Abigal and says she was "the daughter of Nahash and sister of Zeruiah" (2 Samuel 17:25): she may have been David's half-sister, through their mother. Her son Amasa would command Absalom's rebellious army before being pardoned by David and then killed by his cousin Joab.

kileab.bio: David's second son, born in Hebron to Ahinoam; Chronicles calls him Daniel.
kileab.histoire: "The second, Chileab, born of Ahinoam of Jezreel" (2 Samuel 3:3). Chronicles calls him Daniel (1 Chronicles 3:1). Nothing else is known of him: he disappears from the narrative, perhaps dying young, while his brothers Amnon, Absalom, and Adonijah would later struggle for the throne.

maaca-david.bio: An Aramean princess, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur; wife of David and mother of Absalom and Tamar.
maaca-david.histoire:
"The third, Absalom, son of Maaca, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur" (2 Samuel 3:3). A marriage alliance with a neighboring small kingdom.

After having Amnon killed, Absalom would flee to his maternal grandfather: "he went to Talmai son of Ammihur, king of Geshur" (2 Samuel 13:37).

haggith.bio: Wife of David and mother of Adonijah, the prince who wanted to make himself king in place of Solomon.
haggith.histoire: "The fourth was Adonijah, son of Haggith" (2 Samuel 3:4). The book of Kings returns to this mother's name at the moment of the drama: "Adonijah, son of Haggith, exalted himself, saying, I will be king!" (1 Kings 1:5).

nathan-fils-david.bio: Son of David and Bathsheba, brother of Solomon. Through him, Luke traces the genealogy of Jesus.
nathan-fils-david.histoire:
Born in Jerusalem: "Now these were the sons born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon" (2 Samuel 5:14); Chronicles further specifies that all four were born to Bathshua, that is, Bathsheba (1 Chronicles 3:5). Not to be confused with the prophet Nathan.

Matthew traces Jesus' descent from David through Solomon; Luke, through Nathan: "son of Mattatha, son of Nathan, son of David" (Luke 3:31).

naama-ammonite.bio: Ammonite wife of Solomon and mother of Rehoboam: a foreigner in the line of Judah's kings.
naama-ammonite.histoire: The book of Kings mentions her twice, with emphasis:

schealthiel.bio: Son of King Jehoiachin born in exile in Babylon, father of Zerubbabel: the link connecting the kings of Judah to the return from exile.
schealthiel.histoire:
He was born in captivity: "The sons of Jehoiachin: Assir, whose son was Shealtiel" (1 Chronicles 3:17). His name appears each time Zerubbabel is introduced: "Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah" (Haggai 1:1).

Matthew names him Salathiel: "And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zerubbabel" (Matthew 1:12). The line of David, which exile seemed to have broken, continues.

achinoam-saul.bio: Daughter of Ahimaaz, wife of King Saul. Not to be confused with Ahinoam of Jezreel, wife of David.
achinoam-saul.histoire: Only one sentence names her: "The name of Saul's wife was Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz" (1 Samuel 14:50). She is probably the mother of Jonathan, Merab, and Michal, but the text does not specify this.

joses.bio: One of four brothers of Jesus named by the Gospels; Matthew calls him Joseph.
joses.histoire:
In Nazareth, people were amazed at Jesus' wisdom: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, and brother of James, Joses, Jude, and Simon?" (Mark 6:3). Matthew calls him Joseph (Matthew 13:55).

Protestants see in him a son of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus; other traditions view him as a cousin or half-brother.

simon-frere.bio: One of four brothers of Jesus named in Nazareth. Not to be confused with Simon Peter or Simon the Zealot.
simon-frere.histoire:
He appears only in the question of the people of Nazareth: "Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not His mother called Mary? And His brothers James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas?" (Matthew 13:55).

The brothers of Jesus did not believe in Him during His ministry (John 7:5), but after the resurrection they are found praying with the disciples (Acts 1:14).

soeurs-jesus.bio: Jesus' sisters, mentioned in Nazareth but not named.
soeurs-jesus.histoire:
"And are not all His sisters with us?" (Matthew 13:56). The Gospels tell us neither their number nor their names: at least two, since the text says "all."

As with His brothers, Protestants understand them as children of Mary and Joseph; other traditions view them as cousins.

salome-herodias.bio: Daughter of Herodias, whose dance cost John the Baptist his life. The Bible does not name her; the historian Flavius Josephus calls her Salome.
salome-herodias.histoire:
At Herod's birthday banquet, "the daughter of Herodias came in and danced, and pleased Herod and those who sat with him" (Mark 6:22). The king promises her anything she wants; she consults her mother, then returns: "At her mother's prompting, she said, 'Give me here the head of John the Baptist on a platter'" (Matthew 14:8).

The guard beheads John in prison and brings the head "on a platter. He gave it to the young girl, and the young girl gave it to her mother" (Mark 6:28).

aristobule.bio: Son of Herod the Great, whom his father had executed; father of Herod Agrippa I and Herodias. The Bible does not name him: he is known through the historian Flavius Josephus.
aristobule.histoire:
Aristobulus does not appear in the Bible, but he connects several personalities of the New Testament. According to Flavius Josephus, a Jewish historian of the 1st century, he was the son of Herod the Great and Mariamne; suspected of conspiracy, he was executed by order of his own father, around 7 BC.

His children left their mark on the Gospels and Acts: his daughter Herodias, who obtained the head of John the Baptist (Mark 6:24), and his son Herod Agrippa I, who had the apostle James put to death (Acts 12:1-2).

herode-antipas.bio: Son of Herod the Great, tetrarch of Galilee in the time of Jesus. He had John the Baptist beheaded and mocked Jesus at his trial.
herode-antipas.histoire:
He ruled Galilee, the region where Jesus grew up and carried out most of his ministry: "Herod the tetrarch of Galilee" (Luke 3:1). He marries Herodias, his brother's wife; John the Baptist rebukes him for this, and he has John imprisoned (Luke 3:19-20) and then beheaded at a banquet (Mark 6:27).

Jesus knows him: "Go, and tell that fox" (Luke 13:32). At his trial, Pilate sends Jesus to him; "Herod, with his guards, treated him with contempt" (Luke 23:11), and on that day he became friends with Pilate (Luke 23:12).

herode-agrippa.bio: Grandson of Herod the Great, king of Judea around 41–44. He had the apostle James put to death, imprisoned Peter, and died struck by an angel.
herode-agrippa.histoire:
Acts calls him simply "King Herod." "About that time King Herod stretched out his hand to harm some who belonged to the church. He had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword" (Acts 12:1-2). Seeing that this pleased the Jews, he also had Peter arrested, but an angel delivers him from prison (Acts 12:7).

At Caesarea, dressed in his royal robes, he allows himself to be acclaimed as a god: "Immediately, because Herod did not give praise to God, an angel of the Lord struck him down, and he was eaten by worms and died" (Acts 12:23). Yet, "the word of God continued to spread and flourish" (Acts 12:24).

philippe-tetrarque.bio: Son of Herod the Great, tetrarch of the regions northeast of the Sea of Galilee; he rebuilt the city that would become Caesarea Philippi.
philippe-tetrarque.histoire:
Luke mentions him to date the beginning of John the Baptist's ministry: "Herod, tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip, tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis" (Luke 3:1).

The city he enlarged at the foot of Mount Hermon bears his name: at Caesarea Philippi, Peter confessed, "You are the Christ" (Mark 8:27-29).

herode-philippe.bio: Son of Herod the Great and first husband of Herodias, who left him for his brother Herod Antipas.
herode-philippe.histoire:
The Gospels mention him only in connection with his wife: Herod Antipas had arrested John "on account of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because he had married her" (Mark 6:17).

He was probably a different son of Herod the Great than Philip the tetrarch: the historian Josephus presents him as a man without official position, having lived as a private citizen.

eden.bio: The garden planted by God himself, where mankind walked with their Creator. Lost through the fall — recovered, more beautiful still, in the new creation of Revelation.
eden.histoire:
Garden planted by God himself "on the east side" (Genesis 2:8), Eden is the place of perfect communion: the tree of life in the midst, a river that waters it, and God walking in the cool of the day (Genesis 3:8).

After the fall, mankind is driven out and cherubim guard the way to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24). But the Bible ends as it began: in the new Jerusalem, the tree of life reappears, and "there shall be no more curse" (Revelation 22:3). All of salvation's history is the path home to Eden — and better.

ararat.bio: The mountains where Noah's ark came to rest when the floodwaters receded — the first solid ground of the world after, the covenant of the rainbow.
ararat.histoire:
It is "on the mountains of Ararat" that the ark stops when the floodwaters recede (Genesis 8:4). From there, Noah releases the raven and then the dove, which returns with an olive leaf — the earth is alive again (Genesis 8:11).

At the foot of the mountain, the first act of the new world is an altar (Genesis 8:20), and the first word from heaven, a covenant: the bow in the cloud, a promise that the waters will never again destroy all flesh (Genesis 9:15). Ararat is the mountain of new beginnings.

canaan.bio: The promised land given to Abraham and his descendants,
canaan.histoire: Promised to Abraham at his very calling —

egypte.bio: A land of refuge for Joseph and for the child Jesus, a land of slavery for Israel.
egypte.histoire:
The granary of the ancient world, Egypt was both refuge and furnace. Joseph is sold there and then exalted to save his family from famine (Genesis 45:7); the sons of Israel become a people there—and slaves (Exodus 1:11).

Through ten plagues and a Passover, God brings His people out "with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm" (Exodus 12:51): the Exodus becomes throughout the Bible THE foundational memory of deliverance. Centuries later, another child finds refuge there: "Out of Egypt I called My Son" (Matthew 2:15).

mer-rouge.bio: The sea that parted in two before Israel and closed over Pharaoh's army. The most famous dry passage in history—proof that God makes a way where there is no way.
mer-rouge.histoire:
With the sea at their back and Pharaoh's army pressing forward: it's the ultimate dead end. "Do not be afraid… the Lord will fight for you" (Exodus 14:14). Moses raises his staff, an east wind blows all night, and Israel passes through on dry ground between two walls of water (Exodus 14:22).

At dawn, the sea closes its waters over Egypt's chariots, and from the shore rises the first great song of the Bible: "I will sing to the Lord, for He has triumphed gloriously" (Exodus 15:1). The Red Sea remains the name of every impossible passage that God opens.

sinai.bio: The mountain ablaze where God gave the Ten Commandments and made a covenant with Israel. Moses spoke with the Lord there — and his face shone with His glory.
sinai.histoire:
Three months after leaving Egypt, Israel camps at the foot of Mount Sinai: thunder, lightning, a thick cloud, and the sound of a trumpet — "the mountain was all in smoke because the Lord had descended upon it in fire" (Exodus 19:18).

There the Ten Commandments are given (Exodus 20:1), the covenant, and the plan of the tabernacle. Moses stays there forty days, and comes down with his face shining (Exodus 34:29). It is also the mountain where, centuries later, the exhausted Elijah will hear a gentle whisper (1 Kings 19:12). Sinai speaks of holiness; the Gospel speaks of grace (John 1:17).

jourdain.bio: The river of crossings: Israel crossed it dry-shod behind the ark, Naaman was cleansed of his leprosy in it, and Jesus was baptized in it under the open sky.
jourdain.histoire:
A river of crossings, the Jordan opens before the ark of the covenant to let Israel enter Canaan (Joshua 3:17); twelve stones will guard its memory. Elijah crosses it dry before being taken up; Elisha returns by striking it with his mantle (2 Kings 2:14). Naaman dips himself in it seven times and his flesh becomes like that of a child (2 Kings 5:14).

It is in its waters that John baptizes—and that Jesus himself comes down: the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove (Matthew 3:16). The ancient river of crossings becomes the door of heaven opened.

jericho.bio: The city with impenetrable walls, which fell at the sound of trumpets and a cry of faith. Centuries later, Jesus restored sight to Bartimaeus there and invited himself to Zacchaeus' home.
jericho.histoire:
The first city facing Israel, locked behind its walls, Jericho falls without a single sword stroke: seven days of silent marches, seven trumpets, one cry—"and the wall collapsed" (Joshua 6:20). Rahab and her family, clinging to the scarlet cord, are spared (Joshua 6:25).

In Jesus' time, the city of palms is a stop on the way to Jerusalem: He restores sight to the blind Bartimaeus there (Mark 10:52) and invites Himself to Zacchaeus' house (Luke 19:5). And it's "from Jerusalem down to Jericho" that the man in the parable of the Good Samaritan travels (Luke 10:30).

jerusalem.bio: The city of David, of the Temple, and of the cross. The beating heart of the entire Bible: Jesus died and rose again there, the Church was born there — and the New Jerusalem will descend from heaven, adorned as a bride.
jerusalem.histoire:
Captured by David who made it his capital (2 Samuel 5:7), Jerusalem received the ark, then Solomon's temple where his glory descended (1 Kings 8:11). City of the songs of ascent — "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem" (Psalm 122:6) — destroyed by Babylon, rebuilt by Nehemiah.

Jesus went there with resolve: acclaimed on Palm Sunday (Matthew 21:9), he wept over it (Luke 19:41), was crucified outside its walls and rose again there. Pentecost gave birth to the Church there (Acts 2:5); the council there set the Gospel free for the nations (Acts 15:28).

And the story ends with it: "I saw the holy city, the New Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven" (Revelation 21:2).

sion.bio: The hill of Jerusalem that became a name of love for God's people. "The Lord loves the gates of Zion": in the Psalms and the prophets, it is the place where God reigns and comforts.
sion.histoire:
First the name of the fortress taken by David — "the city of David" (2 Samuel 5:7) — Zion becomes in the psalms and the prophets far more than a hill: the mountain that God loves (Psalm 87:2), the place of His dwelling, "the perfection of beauty" from which God shines forth (Psalm 50:2).

The prophets attach their hope to it: "Out of Zion shall go forth the law" (Isaiah 2:3); "Behold, I lay in Zion a cornerstone" (Isaiah 28:16). The New Testament fulfills it: "You have come to Mount Zion, to the heavenly Jerusalem" (Hebrews 12:22).

bethlehem.bio: "You, Bethlehem, small among the thousands of Judah..." — the city of Ruth and David, where the Savior was born in a manger, to the song of angels.
bethlehem.histoire:
Small among the thousands of Judah, Bethlehem — "house of bread" — witnesses Rachel die at its gates, Ruth gleaning in its fields (Ruth 2:4), and Samuel anointing David there, the shepherd who became king (1 Samuel 16:13).

Micah points to it the most precise of prophecies: "Out of you shall come forth for Me the One who will be Ruler over Israel, whose goings forth are from of old, from everlasting" (Micah 5:2).
