Seven centuries later, a census brings Joseph and Mary there: the Bread of Life is born in the house of bread, laid in a manger (Luke 2:7), greeted by shepherds whom the angel found in the same fields where Ruth gleaned.

babylone.bio: The empire of exile, where Israel wept with her harps hung upon the willows—and where Daniel prayed with windows open. In Revelation, she becomes the symbol of all pride that opposes God.
babylone.histoire:
From Babel and its tower—"let us make ourselves a name" (Genesis 11:4)—Babylon embodies human pride organized against God. Nebuchadnezzar's empire destroyed Jerusalem and deported Judah (2 Kings 25:9); on her rivers, the exiles hung their harps (Psalms 137:1).

Yet God reigns in the very heart of Babylon: Daniel serves and prays there, the furnace and the lions lose their power (Daniel 6:22), and writing appears on the wall of the final feast (Daniel 5:5). Revelation will make her the ultimate symbol of the seductive world: "Babylon the great has fallen!" (Revelation 18:2).

ninive.bio: away. At Jonah's preaching, from king to least, it covered itself in sackcloth — and God turned from His anger.
ninive.histoire:
Capital of Assyria, immense — "three days' journey" (Jonah 3:3) — Nineveh is the enemy city par excellence, "the bloodthirsty city" (Nahum 3:1). Yet it is to her that God sends Jonah.

Against all expectations, the preaching of a single message transforms the city: a general fast, from king to livestock, "and God saw... that they turned from their evil way" (Jonah 3:10). Jesus will cite its inhabitants as an example: "The men of Nineveh will stand up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it; for they repented at the preaching of Jonah" (Matthew 12:41).

nazareth.bio: The village in Galilee where Jesus grew up, worked as a carpenter, and was first rejected. "Can anything good come from Nazareth? Come and see."
nazareth.histoire:
A town in Galilee never mentioned in the Old Testament, Nazareth receives the greatest announcement in history: Gabriel visits a young girl named Mary there (Luke 1:26). Jesus grows up in the carpenter's workshop, obedient to his parents (Luke 2:51) — thirty years of hidden life.

"Can anything good come from Nazareth?" asks Nathanael (John 1:46). In his synagogue, Jesus unrolls the scroll of Isaiah — "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me" (Luke 4:18) — and his townspeople want to throw him down the cliff (Luke 4:29). He will remain forever "Jesus of Nazareth."

galilee.bio: The region of Jesus' first ministry steps: calls by the lakeshore, the Sermon on the Mount, the stilled storm. "Galilee of the nations, the people sitting in darkness have seen a great light."
galilee.histoire:
"Galilee of the nations" despised by Jerusalem, yet it was Galilee that Isaiah had designated: "The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light" (Isaiah 9:1). Around its lake, Jesus calls fishermen (Matthew 4:18), teaches in parables, stills the storm (Mark 4:39), and walks on water.

The Mount of the Beatitudes, the feeding of the five thousand, the Transfiguration: the essence of His ministry unfolds here. And it is in Galilee that the Risen One meets with His followers for the final commission: "Go and make disciples of all nations" (Matthew 28:19).

capernaum.bio: "His city": the fishing port that became Jesus's headquarters in Galilee. He healed the centurion's servant there, the paralyzed man lowered through the roof, and Peter's mother-in-law.
capernaum.histoire:
Situated on the shore of the lake, Capernaum becomes "his city" (Matthew 9:1): Jesus settles there at the beginning of his ministry (Matthew 4:13). In its synagogue, he teaches with authority and delivers a demon-possessed man (Mark 1:27); at Peter's house, he heals his fevered mother-in-law (Mark 1:31); they pierce a roof to lower a paralyzed man to him (Mark 2:4).

It is there that a Roman centurion amazes Jesus with his faith (Matthew 8:10) and where his discourse on the bread of life causes the crowds to flee (John 6:59). So much light received creates so much responsibility: "And you, Capernaum..." (Matthew 11:23).

judee.bio: The southern province, centered around Jerusalem — the land of the kings of Judah, of John the Baptist's desert, and of Jesus's final weeks.
judee.histoire:
The mountainous heart of the land, around Jerusalem, Judea bears the name of Judah, the royal tribe. It is "Judea" of the censuses and kings: Bethlehem of Judea sees the Messiah born (Matthew 2:1), its desert hears John the Baptist cry out (Matthew 3:1) and shelters forty days of temptation (Matthew 4:1).

Jesus went up there for the feasts, taught there, died there, and rose again there. The Great Commission places it as the first step after the city: "in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and in Samaria, and to the end of the earth" (Acts 1:8); persecution scattered the first witnesses there (Acts 8:1).

samarie.bio: The region that Jews avoided — yet Jesus went through it on purpose, for a woman at a well's edge. Philip preached there afterward, and the city was filled with joy.
samarie.histoire:
Capital of the Northern Kingdom and then the name of its entire region, Samaria was to the Jews the land of the "half-brothers" you avoid — you'd take the long way around rather than pass through it. Yet Jesus "had to go through Samaria" (John 4:4): at the well of Sychar, he offers living water to a woman married five times, and the whole city believes (John 4:39).

He makes a Samaritan the hero of his most famous parable (Luke 10:33) and notices the only grateful leper — a Samaritan (Luke 17:16). After Pentecost, Philip preaches there, and "there was great joy in that city" (Acts 8:8).

bethanie.bio: The village of Martha, Mary, and Lazarus, on the slope of the Mount of Olives — the house where Jesus loved to stay, the place of the poured perfume and His ascension.
bethanie.histoire:
A village of friends, fifteen stadia from Jerusalem, on the side of the Mount of Olives: at the home of Martha, Mary, and Lazarus, Jesus has a house waiting for Him (Luke 10:38). There He weeps before a tomb and cries out "Lazarus, come forth!" (John 11:43); there Mary breaks her alabaster jar of costly perfume on His feet (John 12:3); there He spends the nights of that final week (Matthew 21:17).

And it is "toward Bethany" that He takes His own to bless them one last time before ascending into heaven (Luke 24:50). Bethany speaks one thing: Jesus loves to have friends.

damas.bio: The oldest city in the world still inhabited—and the site of the most dramatic conversion in history: on his way there, Saul encountered the light of the Risen One.
damas.histoire:
The oldest inhabited city in the world and capital of Syria, Damascus runs through the Old Testament via its kings at war with Israel—and through Naaman, its general healed in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:14).

But its finest hour is a road: at the gates of Damascus, light struck down Saul of Tarsus (Acts 9:3). On the street called Straight, Ananias laid hands on the blind persecutor who became the apostle Paul (Acts 9:17); in a basket along the wall, he escaped death (Acts 9:25). "The Damascus road" has become, in every language, the name for sudden, transformative conversions.

antioche.bio: The great city of Syria where the Gospel first overflowed to the Gentiles—and where the disciples were called "Christians" for the first time. The launching base for Paul's missionary journeys.
antioche.histoire:
The third city of the empire, Antioch of Syria became the Gospel's laboratory for the nations: anonymous believers proclaimed Jesus to the Greeks, and "the hand of the Lord was with them" (Acts 11:21). Barnabas rejoiced in this and went to find Saul; it was there that "the disciples were called Christians for the first time" (Acts 11:26).

The first missionary Church in history: during a fast, the Spirit said, "Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul" (Acts 13:2)—all of Paul's journeys departed from here and returned here (Acts 14:27). Jerusalem saw the Church born; Antioch saw it launch into the world.

chypre.bio: The birthplace of Barnabas, first stop of the first missionary journey: the Gospel crossed the sea for the first time there.
chypre.histoire:
The birthplace of Barnabas (Acts 4:36), Cyprus was the first stop of the first missionary journey: in Salamis and then Paphos, Barnabas and Saul traveled across the island proclaiming the Word (Acts 13:5).

In Paphos, facing the sorcerer Elymas, the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed, "astonished at the teaching about the Lord" (Acts 13:12)—the first Roman official won to the Gospel; it was also there that Saul began to be called Paul. Barnabas would return there with Mark for a second chance (Acts 15:39): the island of the encourager.

phenicie.bio: The coast of Tyre and Sidon, north of Israel. Jesus honored the faith of a foreign mother there, and the first scattered Christians brought the Word to it.
phenicie.histoire:
Coastal region of Tyre and Sidon, land of the cedars that built the temple (1 Kings 5:9), Phoenicia saw Elijah lodged with the widow of Zarephath whose flour never ran out (1 Kings 17:16).

Jesus withdrew there and met the Canaanite woman whose faith-filled wit amazed him: "Woman, your faith is great" (Matthew 15:28). Believers scattered by persecution proclaimed the Word there (Acts 11:19), and Paul passed through "reporting the conversion of the Gentiles, and bringing great joy to all the brothers" (Acts 15:3).

cilicie.bio: Paul's native province—Tarsus was its capital. Its churches received the letter from the Jerusalem Council and strengthening visits from the apostle.
cilicie.histoire:
A province in southeast Asia Minor, Cilicia had Tarsus as its capital—a "great city" whose citizenship Paul claimed: "I am a Jew from Tarsus in Cilicia" (Acts 21:39). It was there that Barnabas came to find him for the work in Antioch (Acts 11:25).

The letter from the Jerusalem Council was addressed to the brothers "in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia" (Acts 15:23), and Paul passed through there again to strengthen the churches at the beginning of his second journey (Acts 15:41): the apostle's native province was also his first quiet field of ministry.

pamphylie.bio: The coast of Asia Minor on the first missionary journey — where John Mark turned back, a painful memory that temporarily separated Paul and Barnabas.
pamphylie.histoire:
A coastal plain in southern Asia Minor, Pamphylia welcomed the missionaries on their first journey: after landing at Perga, they experienced a wound there — young Mark abandoned them and returned to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13), a desertion that would later divide Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:38).

On the way back, though, they stopped to "proclaim the word at Perga" (Acts 14:25) before setting sail again: the place of failure became a place of Gospel. Pamphylians were already in the crowd at Pentecost (Acts 2:10).

macedoine.bio: "Come over to Macedonia and help us!" — the vision that brought the Gospel into Europe. Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea — churches born in joy amid trials.
macedoine.histoire:
In the night vision at Troas, a Macedonian pleads with Paul: "Come over to Macedonia and help us!" (Acts 16:9). The Gospel enters Europe: Lydia baptized by the riverside at Philippi (Acts 16:14), the jailer converted after the earthquake, then Thessalonica and Berea with their "noble-minded" people who examined the Scriptures every day (Acts 17:11).

The churches of Macedonia would remain Paul's joy: poor yet overflowing with generosity — "their deep poverty welled up in rich generosity" (2 Corinthians 8:2).

philippes.bio: The first church in Europe, born of a purple merchant, a delivered servant, and a jailer converted at midnight. Paul will write to it his most joyful letter — from a prison.
philippes.histoire:
A proud Roman colony known for its rights, Philippi is the first Church in Europe: a purple merchant by the water's edge (Acts 16:14), an enslaved woman set free, and a jail cell that becomes a baptistry — "Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household" (Acts 16:31).

Ten years later, from his prison, Paul writes to this beloved Church the letter of joy: "Rejoice in the Lord always" (Philippians 4:4), the hymn of Christ who humbled Himself even to the cross (Philippians 2:8), and the secret of contentment in all circumstances (Philippians 4:12).

corinthe.bio: A vast and corrupt port where Paul stayed eighteen months: "I have many people in this city." The church there was brilliant and turbulent — it received the hymn of love.
corinthe.histoire:
A cosmopolitan port between two seas, wealthy and dissolute, Corinth saw Paul settle for eighteen months with Aquila and Priscilla, making tents and teaching (Acts 18:3). In a vision, the Lord encourages him: "Do not be afraid… I have many people in this city" (Acts 18:10).

To this gifted and turbulent Church, Paul would write his most personal letters: unity against divisions (1 Corinthians 1:13), the hymn of love (1 Corinthians 13:4), resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20), and grace that is sufficient in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9).

athenes.bio: The capital of philosophers and idols, where Paul, his heart burning with passion, proclaimed "the Unknown God" before the Areopagus — the God who does not dwell in temples made by human hands.
athenes.histoire:
The intellectual capital of the ancient world, bristling with idols, Athens stirred Paul's spirit as he reasoned daily in the marketplace (Acts 17:17). Before the Areopagus, he began with their altar "To an Unknown God" to proclaim the God "who made the world and everything in it" (Acts 17:24) — even quoting their own poets: "In him we live and move and have our being" (Acts 17:28).

When he mentioned the resurrection, some mocked, others put it off—but Dionysius the Areopagite and a few believed (Acts 17:34). The wisdom of God had visited the city of the wise.

ephese.bio: The city of great Diana, where God's Word grew with power: three years of Paul's ministry, magic books burned in the public square, and later one of the seven churches of Revelation.
ephese.histoire:
Metropolis of Asia, guardian of the temple of Artemis, one of the wonders of the world: Ephesus becomes Paul's longest stay — three years (Acts 20:31). God's Word wins all of Asia (Acts 19:10), magic books burn publicly (Acts 19:19), and the silversmith Demetrius sparks a riot to save his idol business (Acts 19:28).

To the elders of Ephesus, Paul says tearful goodbye at Miletus (Acts 20:37); to the Church, the letter of heavenly riches "in Christ" (Ephesians 1:3) and the armor of God (Ephesians 6:11). Revelation will address her with the first of seven letters: "You have left your first love" (Revelation 2:4).

rome.bio: The capital of the world then—and Paul's destination: "I must also see Rome." He arrived in chains, preached with complete freedom there, and sent it the densest of his letters.
rome.histoire:
Capital of the world, the secret destination of all roads: "I must also see Rome" (Acts 19:21). Paul first writes to the believers in that city his most masterful letter—the Gospel, "the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes" (Romans 1:16).

He arrives in chains, after a shipwreck; the Lord had promised it to him: "You must also testify about me in Rome" (Acts 23:11). For two years, in his rented quarters under guard, he receives visitors and preaches "with all boldness and without hindrance"—the closing words of the book of Acts (Acts 28:31). From the heart of the empire, the Gospel radiates "even in Caesar's household" (Philippians 4:22).

ur.bio: "Ur of the Chaldees," a great Mesopotamian city from which God brought Abram out. The starting point of the entire story of faith.
ur.histoire:
It was from Ur of the Chaldees that Terah took his son Abram, Sarai, and Lot toward Canaan (Genesis 11:31). God Himself would remind Abram of this: "I am the Lord, who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldees, to give you this land to possess" (Genesis 15:7).

A brilliant city, wealthy and idolatrous—and left at a word. Nehemiah would make it the first article of Israel's creed: "You are the Lord God, who chose Abram and brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees" (Nehemiah 9:7). Faith often begins by leaving.

bethel.bio: "House of God": the place where Jacob, a fugitive, saw a ladder set up between earth and heaven. Later, sadly, one of the two sanctuaries of Jeroboam's golden calf.
bethel.histoire:
Jacob, fleeing from Esau, fell asleep with a stone for a pillow and saw a ladder reaching to heaven, with angels ascending and descending on it, and the Lord promising: "I am with you and will keep you wherever you go." Upon waking: "This is none other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven!" — he names the place Bethel (Genesis 28:10-19). He would return there at God's command to build an altar (Genesis 35:1-7).

Centuries later, Jeroboam set up a golden calf there to turn the people away from Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:28-29); the prophets Amos and Hosea denounced this corrupted sanctuary (Amos 4:4). The place of visions can become the place of idols — it all depends on whom you worship there.

sichem.bio: Abram's first stop in Canaan, the place where Joshua renewed the covenant—"As for me and my household, we will serve the Lord"—and where the well of the Samaritan woman was located at its gates.
sichem.histoire:
Abram travels through the land "to the place of Shechem"; the Lord appears to him—"I will give this land to your offspring"—and he builds his first altar in Canaan there (Genesis 12:6-7). Jacob buys a field there (Genesis 33:18-19), and the bones of Joseph will be buried there (Joshua 24:32).

It is at Shechem, between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, that Joshua gathers all the tribes for the great choice: "Choose for yourselves this day whom you will serve… As for me and my household, we will serve the Lord" (Joshua 24:14-15). Near there, at Jacob's well, Jesus will speak of living water to the Samaritan woman (John 4:5-14).

hebron.bio: City of the patriarchs: Abraham pitched his tents there and bought the cave of Machpelah, the tomb of Sarah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. David was anointed king there and reigned seven years.
hebron.histoire:
Abraham comes to "dwell by the oaks of Mamre, which are near Hebron," and builds an altar there (Genesis 13:18). At Sarah's death, he purchases the cave of Machpelah—the only parcel of the promised land he ever possessed—to bury his own there (Genesis 23:17-20); Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob rest there (Genesis 49:29-31).

Caleb, at eighty-five years old, claims and conquers this promised mountain (Joshua 14:12-14). It is at Hebron that the men of Judah come to anoint David as king (2 Samuel 2:1-4), and all the tribes consecrate him over all Israel (2 Samuel 5:1-5). A city of memory: the promises sleep there like seeds.

sodome.histoire:
Lot had chosen the fertile plain and pitched his tents toward Sodom — and "Now the men of Sodom were wicked and great sinners against the Lord" (Genesis 13:10-13). When the cry of the city rises up, Abraham bargains with God: "Perhaps there will be ten righteous found there?" (Genesis 18:20-32). But ten righteous were not found.

The angels snatch Lot, his wife, and his two daughters; sulfur and fire fall, and Lot's wife, who looked back, became a pillar of salt (Genesis 19:15-26). Jesus will make it a warning — "remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:28-32) — and the prophets, the standard of sin: pride, abundance and carelessness, without sustaining the poor (Ezekiel 16:49).

silo.bio: Israel's first sanctuary in Canaan: the tabernacle remained there for centuries. It was here that Hannah prayed in silence and that young Samuel heard God calling him in the night.
silo.histoire:
After the conquest, "the whole assembly of the children of Israel gathered together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of meeting there" (Joshua 18:1). Each year, Elkanah and Hannah went up there to worship; and it was at its gates that Hannah, in tears, moved her lips silently—and the priest Eli promised her that her prayer would be answered (1 Samuel 1:3-17).

The child she had asked for was brought there and dedicated: "I will lend him to the Lord; as long as he lives, he shall be lent to the Lord" (1 Samuel 1:24-28). And it was at Shiloh, in the night of the temple, that the Lord called three times: "Samuel! Samuel!" (1 Samuel 3:1-10). After the Philistines captured the ark, the glory departed from Shiloh (1 Samuel 4:21-22; Jeremiah 7:12)—a sanctuary stands only by the presence it houses.

carmel.bio: Mountain of the great showdown: Elijah alone against four hundred fifty prophets of Baal. Fire fell from heaven, and the people cried out: "The Lord is God!"
carmel.histoire:
After three and a half years of drought, Elijah calls all Israel to Mount Carmel: "How long will you falter between two opinions? If the Lord is God, follow Him; but if Baal, follow him!" (1 Kings 18:19-21). The prophets of Baal cry out, dance, and cut themselves from morning until evening—"there was no voice; no one answered, nor was there any regard" (1 Kings 18:26-29).

Elijah rebuilds the altar with twelve stones, drenches everything with water, then prays a thirty-second prayer. The fire of the Lord falls, consuming the burnt offering, the stones, and even the water in the trench; the people fall on their faces: "The Lord is God!" (1 Kings 18:36-39). On that same mountain, his servant later watches for the small cloud, as small as a man's hand, which signals the coming rain (1 Kings 18:42-45).

moab.bio: A highland country east of the Dead Sea, a people related to Israel descended from Lot. The homeland of Ruth, and the land where Moses died facing the Promised Land.
moab.histoire:
The Moabites descended from Lot (Genesis 19:36-37). Their king Balak hired Balaam to curse Israel — and the curse turned into a blessing (Numbers 22:1-6; 23:11-12). It was in the plains of Moab that Moses recited all the law (Deuteronomy 1:5), and on Mount Nebo, "in the land of Moab," that he died after seeing the land with his own eyes (Deuteronomy 34:1-5).

In the time of the judges, a famine drove Elimelech and Naomi to Moab; they returned with Ruth the Moabite — "your people will be my people, and your God will be my God" (Ruth 1:1-16). The foreigner from Moab became the great-grandmother of David (Ruth 4:13-17) and entered into the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).

madian.bio: Desert and people of the southeast: Moses' refuge while fleeing for forty years — it was while tending Midian's flocks that he saw the burning bush — then an oppressor defeated by Gideon.
madian.histoire:
Moses, fleeing Pharaoh, stops in the land of Midian, sits by a well, defends the daughters of the priest Jethro, and marries Zipporah (Exodus 2:15-21). Forty years of desert and flocks — until the day when, beyond the desert at Horeb, the bush burns without being consumed (Exodus 3:1-10). God shapes His servants far from the world's gaze.

Centuries later, Midian oppresses Israel "like locusts"; God raises up Gideon and reduces his army to three hundred men, because the people "might take the glory for themselves against Me" — trumpets, broken jars, torches: Midian flees (Judges 6:1-6; 7:2-22). Isaiah will remember "the day of Midian" as the model of God's deliverances (Isaiah 9:3).

tyr.bio: Opulent Phoenician port, island fortress of the seas. Its king Hiram supplied the cedars for the temple; his prophecies of ruin made merchants tremble; Jesus passed through its territory.
tyr.histoire: Hiram, king of Tyre, friend of David and then of Solomon, provided the cedars of Lebanon and craftsmen to build the temple (1 Kings 5:1-10). But the merchant city grew proud: Ezekiel dedicated a funeral song to it—

sidon.bio: Phoenician port city, twin of Tyre. It was near Sidon, in Zarephath, that a pagan widow fed Elijah with her last handful of flour—an example Jesus would cite in Nazareth.
sidon.histoire:
During the famine, God sends Elijah "to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon": a widow at the end of her resources shares her last cake, and "the jar of flour was not used up and the jug of oil did not run dry" (1 Kings 17:8-16). Yet Jezebel, the scourge of Israel, was the daughter of the king of the Sidonians (1 Kings 16:31): from the same shore come both the worst influence and the most beautiful faith.

Jesus would remind Nazareth that there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah—and that he was sent only to the one at Zarephath (Luke 4:25-26). Crowds from Tyre and Sidon would follow him (Luke 6:17), and Paul, a prisoner on his way to Rome, would be allowed to visit his friends there (Acts 27:3).

gaza.bio: One of the five cities of the Philistines. Samson tore off its gates and carried them on his shoulders; on its desolate road, the Ethiopian eunuch was baptized.
gaza.histoire: A stronghold of the Philistines, Gaza witnesses Samson carrying the city gates on his shoulders to the top of a mountain (Judges 16:1-3). Yet it is there he returns, betrayed by Delilah, his eyes gouged out, grinding grain as a prisoner (Judges 16:21). In the temple of Dagon, between two pillars, he prays one last time—

gethsemane.bio: "The oil press": a garden of olive trees at the foot of the Mount of Olives where Jesus, in anguish, surrendered His will to the Father—and where He was arrested with a kiss.
gethsemane.histoire:
After the Last Supper, Jesus goes "to a place called Gethsemane" with His disciples. He takes Peter, James, and John: "My soul is exceedingly sorrowful, even to death. Stay here and watch with Me" (Matthew 26:36-38). Falling on His face, He prays three times: "O My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as You will" (Matthew 26:39-44). Luke adds: His sweat became like great drops of blood, and an angel strengthened Him (Luke 22:43-44).

The disciples sleep; Judas arrives with the mob and betrays Him with a kiss (Mark 14:43-46). Jesus rises from prayer determined: "Rise, let us go" (Matthew 26:46). The battle of the cross was won first in a garden—where the first Adam gave in, the second one said yes (Romans 5:19).

golgotha.bio: "The place of the skull," outside the gates of Jerusalem: the hill of the cross. The darkest and most luminous place in all of Scripture.
golgotha.histoire:
"Jesus, bearing his cross, came to the place of the skull, which is called in Hebrew Golgotha. There they crucified Him" (John 19:17-18), between two criminals, under the inscription "Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews" written in three languages (John 19:19-20). They offer Him wine mixed with gall, and they cast lots for His garments (Matthew 27:33-35)—the Psalms are fulfilled word for word (Psalm 22:17-19).

From noon until three in the afternoon, darkness covered the land; then the cry—"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?"—the veil of the temple torn from top to bottom, and the centurion who confesses: "Surely this was the Son of God" (Matthew 27:45-54). His last word in John: "It is finished" (John 19:30). Nearby, a garden and a new tomb awaited the third day (John 19:41-42).

emmaus.bio: Village about two hours' walk from Jerusalem. On the evening of Easter, the Risen Lord joined two discouraged disciples on the road there — recognized at the breaking of bread.
emmaus.histoire:
On the evening of Easter, two disciples are heading back to Emmaus, "about seven miles from Jerusalem," their hearts heavy with grief: "We were hoping that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel" (Luke 24:13-21). A traveler joins them — their eyes are kept from recognizing him — and, "beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he explained to them what was said in all the Scriptures concerning himself" (Luke 24:25-27).

They urge him: "Stay with us, for it is getting late." At the table, he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it — their eyes are opened, and he disappears. "Were not our hearts burning within us while he talked with us on the road?" At that very hour, they retrace their steps to announce it to the Eleven (Luke 24:28-35). Discouragement, too, is a road where Jesus meets his own.

cana.bio: Village in Galilee where Jesus performed His first miracle: turning water into wine at a wedding. He also healed from a distance the son of a royal official from Capernaum.
cana.histoire:
At a wedding in Cana, the wine runs out. Mary gives the servants an instruction that applies to all generations: "Do whatever he tells you." Six stone jars filled with water to the brim—and the master of the banquet is amazed that they've saved the good wine for last. "This, the first of his miraculous signs, Jesus performed at Cana in Galilee. He thus revealed his glory, and his disciples believed in him" (John 2:1-11).

Returning to Cana, he receives a royal official whose son is dying in Capernaum: "Go... your son will live." The man believes the word and leaves; on the way, he is told of the healing—at that very hour (John 4:46-53). Cana was also the hometown of Nathanael (John 21:2). Two miracles, one lesson: His word is enough.

joppe.bio: A port of Judea on the Mediterranean Sea. Jonah embarked there to flee from God; Peter raised Tabitha there and received, on a rooftop, the vision that opened the Gospel to the Gentiles.
joppe.histoire: (Acts 10:9-16). From that same port, one fled from the Gentiles of Nineveh; the other set out toward the Gentile Cornelius. Joppa, or the turning point of the mission.

cesaree.bio: Roman port built by Herod, residence of the governors. City of Cornelius and Philip the evangelist; Paul was imprisoned there for two years and defended his faith before kings and governors.
cesaree.histoire:
Capital of the Roman province, Caesarea was home to the centurion Cornelius: it was in his house that Peter sees the Spirit fall upon Gentiles (Acts 10:24-48). Philip the evangelist settled there with his four daughters who prophesied, and welcomed Paul (Acts 21:8-9); it was also there that the prophet Agabus bound Paul's hands with his belt, announcing his chains (Acts 21:10-11).

Words fulfilled: Paul, arrested, spent two years in Herod's praetorium at Caesarea (Acts 23:33-35; 24:27). Before Felix he speaks of justice and judgment, before Festus he appeals to Caesar, before Agrippa he recounts the Damascus road (Acts 24-26). From the port of Caesarea, in chains, he finally embarks for Rome (Acts 27:1-2) — the very prison served God's plan. (Caesarea Philippi, at the foot of Mount Hermon, is the other Caesarea: that of Peter's confession, Matthew 16:13-16.)

lystre.bio: A city in Lycaonia where Paul was mistaken for a god and then stoned the same day. It was also the hometown of Timothy, his spiritual son.
lystre.histoire:
Paul healed a man crippled in his feet there, and the crowd cried out: "The gods have come down to us!" They called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercury; the priest brought bulls and garlands. The apostles tore their clothes: "We also are men of like nature with you... to turn you from these useless things to the living God" (Acts 14:8-18).

The incense quickly turned to stones: Jews from Antioch and Iconium turned the crowd around, Paul was stoned and dragged outside the city, thought to be dead. Surrounded by the disciples, he got up—and went back into the city (Acts 14:19-20). Timothy lived in Lystra: "The brothers at Lystra and Iconium spoke well of him"; Paul, passing through again, took him with him (Acts 16:1-3). From the place of his stoning, God gave him a son.

thessalonique.bio: A major port city in Macedonia. Three Sabbaths of preaching, a riot—yet a model church was born, the recipient of Paul's two earliest letters.
thessalonique.histoire:
Paul preaches there for three Sabbaths in the synagogue, demonstrating "that the Christ had to suffer and rise again." Jews, many Greeks, and women of high standing believe; the others stir up the city: "These men who have turned the world upside down have come here too... saying that there is another king, Jesus" (Acts 17:1-7). At night, the brothers send Paul away to Berea (Acts 17:10).

A few weeks of sowing, and what a harvest: "you became a model to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia... you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven" (1 Thessalonians 1:7-10). It is to them that Paul will write his clearest words about the return of the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:13-18).

beree.bio: A small city in Macedonia known for its listeners who became proverbial: they "examined the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so."
beree.histoire:
Driven out of Thessalonica, Paul arrives at night in Berea and enters the synagogue, as always. An unprecedented welcome: "These Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures daily to see if what Paul said was true. Many of them believed" (Acts 17:10-12).

Neither gullible nor closed: open and discerning. The agitators from Thessalonica eventually stir up trouble there too, and Paul departs for Athens (Acts 17:13-15) — but Berea has given its name to an attitude: receive with joy, verify with the Bible.

troas.bio: A port in Asia Minor facing Europe. This is where Paul saw a vision of the Macedonian—
troas.histoire: Prevented by the Spirit from going to Asia and then to Bithynia, Paul comes down to Troas, at the end of his routes. At night, a vision: a Macedonian standing pleads with him —

tarse.bio: "A famous city of Cilicia," a Greek and Roman crossroads: the birthplace of Saul — a Roman citizen by birth, a Pharisee by training, an apostle by calling.
tarse.histoire:
"I am a Jew… from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no unimportant city" (Acts 21:39): Paul carries his city like an identity card. Born there a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25-28), raised in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel (Acts 22:3), he embodies three worlds — Jewish, Greek, Roman — that the Gospel would soon traverse.

After his conversion, threatened in Jerusalem, he is sent back by the brothers to Tarsus (Acts 9:29-30): years of silence in his native city, until Barnabas comes to find him for Antioch (Acts 11:25-26). God had prepared in Tarsus the exact instrument his mission would need — he also knew to let it mature there.

colosses.bio: A small city in the Lycus Valley in Phrygia. Paul never visited it—yet he wrote to it one of the highest portraits of Christ in all of Scripture.
colosses.histoire:
The church at Colossae was born from the ministry of Epaphras, a "faithful minister of Christ" and fellow countryman of the Colossians who battled for them in his prayers (Colossians 1:7; 4:12-13). Paul writes to believers "who have not seen my face in the flesh" (Colossians 2:1), threatened by a piety of philosophies, visions, and prohibitions.

His answer: Christ is enough. "He is the image of the invisible God… all things were created through Him and for Him… He is the head of the body, the Church" (Colossians 1:15-18); "in Him dwells all the fullness of the Godhead bodily" and "you have been made complete in Him" (Colossians 2:9-10). It was also at Colossae that Philemon and Onesimus lived (Philemon 1:1-2; Colossians 4:9): the letter of fullness arrived with the letter of forgiveness.

malte.bio: Island of Shipwreck: After fourteen nights of storm, all two hundred seventy-six passengers reached shore safe and sound. Paul shook a viper into the fire there and healed the sick of the island.
malte.histoire:
After fourteen days of storm and a ship broken on a sandbar, "all came safely to land" — as the angel had promised to Paul (Acts 27:21-44). "After we had escaped, we learned that the island was called Malta. The natives showed us unusual kindness" (Acts 28:1-2).

Around the fire, a viper fastens on Paul's hand; the islanders wait for him to swell up and fall dead — he shakes the creature into the fire without any harm (Acts 28:3-6). The father of Publius, the chief of the island, is healed of a fever by prayer and the laying on of hands; then all the sick of the island come and are healed (Acts 28:7-9). Three months of forced stay become a visitation: God's detours are still missions.

patmos.bio: A rocky island in the Aegean Sea where John was exiled "because of the word of God." It was there, "on the Lord's Day," that the Revelation was opened to him.
patmos.histoire:
"I, John, your brother and companion in the suffering and kingdom and patient endurance that are ours in Jesus, was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus" (Revelation 1:9). Exile sought to silence the last apostle; instead, it made him the greatest seer.

"On the Lord's Day I was in the Spirit, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet" (Revelation 1:10). John turns around and sees the Risen One standing among the golden lampstands, His face like the sun: "Do not be afraid. I am the First and the Last. I am the Living One; I was dead, and now look, I am alive for ever and ever" (Revelation 1:12-18). From that island of exile came the letters to the seven churches and the vision of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:1-4): no exile can isolate you from heaven.

sychar.bio: A city of Samaria, near the field that Jacob gave to Joseph and his well. It was there that Jesus, weary from his journey, meets the Samaritan woman.
sychar.histoire: Jesus "had to go through Samaria" (John 4:4) — what every devout Jew avoided. At Jacob's well, at the hottest hour of the day, he asks a woman to give him a drink, someone everyone else avoided too. From the well's water, the conversation rises toward "a spring of water welling up to eternal life" (John 4:14), and the woman leaves her water jar to run to the village: "Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did" (John 4:29). Many Samaritans from Sychar believed — the first fruits of a harvest that Jesus already saw ripening white (John 4:35-42).

cesaree-philippe.bio: A pagan city at the foot of Mount Hermon, at the sources of the Jordan River. It was there that Peter confessed: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."
cesaree-philippe.histoire: At the foot of a cliff covered with pagan sanctuaries, Jesus asks the question that echoes through the centuries: "Who do you say that I am?" Peter answers: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God" (Matthew 16:15-16). Jesus declares him blessed—"flesh and blood has not revealed this to you"—and announces: "on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades will not prevail against it" (Matthew 16:17-18). It was also there that He began to foretell His cross (Matthew 16:21).

mont-thabor.bio: An isolated mountain that dominates the Plain of Jezreel. Site of Deborah and Barak's victory—and, according to ancient tradition, the location of the Transfiguration.
mont-thabor.histoire: It was from Tabor that Barak rushed down with ten thousand men at Deborah's word: "Does not the Lord go before you?" (Judges 4:14)—and Sisera's army was swept away. The psalmist makes it sing: "Tabor and Hermon rejoice in Your name" (Psalm 89:13). An ancient tradition also places there the "high mountain" where Jesus was transfigured before Peter, James, and John: "His face shone like the sun" (Matthew 17:1-2).

mont-oliviers.bio: The hill overlooking Jerusalem, on the far side of the Kidron Valley. Jesus prayed there, wept over the city there, was arrested there—and from there he ascended into heaven.
mont-oliviers.histoire: David went up it weeping, fleeing from Absalom (2 Samuel 15:30); Jesus came there to pray "according to his custom" (Luke 22:39). On its slope, he wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:37-41), delivered his great discourse on the end times there (Matthew 24:3), experienced the agony of Gethsemane there. After his resurrection, it was from this mountain that he was taken up into heaven (Acts 1:9-12)—and Zechariah announces that "his feet will stand on the Mount of Olives" (Zechariah 14:4).

mer-galilee.bio: The lake of Jesus' ministry: calling fishermen, stilling the storm, walking on water, the miraculous catch on Easter morning.
mer-galilee.histoire: On its shores, Jesus calls Peter, Andrew, James, and John: "Follow Me, and I will make you fishers of men" (Matthew 4:18-19). On its waters, He sleeps in the storm and then silences it: "Peace, be still!" (Mark 4:39); He walks toward exhausted disciples (Matthew 14:25); He fills their nets to overflowing, twice—at His first calling (Luke 5:4-11) and on the morning of the resurrection, when He waits for His own on the shore, a charcoal fire and bread ready (John 21:4-13).

bethsaida.bio: Fishing village north of the lake, birthplace of Peter, Andrew, and Philip. Jesus healed a blind man there and multiplied the loaves nearby.
bethsaida.histoire: "Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter" (John 1:44): at least three apostles grew up in this fishing village. It was near there that Jesus fed five thousand men (Luke 9:10-17), and it was there that He healed a blind man in two stages—the men "like trees walking," then clear sight (Mark 8:22-25): Jesus does not abandon a healing halfway through. Yet the city heard so many miracles without repenting that Jesus weeps over it: "Woe to you, Bethsaida!" (Matthew 11:21)—privilege heard, responsibility engaged.

nain.bio: A small village in Galilee where Jesus, moved with compassion, restores to a widow her only son, stopping the funeral procession at the city gates.
nain.histoire: Two processions meet at the gate of Nain: the crowd following Jesus, and the one carrying to the grave the only son of a widow. "When the Lord saw her, He was moved with compassion for her, and said to her, 'Do not weep.'" (Luke 7:13). He touches the coffin—a gesture that makes one unclean according to the law, but with Him, life is contagious: "Young man, I say to you, arise!" And He "gave him to his mother" (Luke 7:14-15). The crowd understands: "God has visited His people."

beer-scheba.bio: "The well of the oath," the southern gateway of the land: Abraham plants a tamarisk tree there, Isaac digs wells there, and an exhausted Elijah collapses beneath a broom tree.
beer-scheba.histoire: It was the great crossroads of the patriarchs: Abraham made a covenant there and "called on the name of the Lord, the God of eternity" (Genesis 21:33); God spoke to Isaac there—"Do not fear, for I am with you" (Genesis 26:24)—and to Jacob as he departed for Egypt (Genesis 46:1-4). Centuries later, it was at Beersheba that Elijah, in the depths of depression, asked for death beneath a broom tree—and an angel woke him with a cake baked on hot coals and a jar of water (1 Kings 19:3-8). The expression "from Dan to Beersheba" designated all of Israel.

guilgal.bio: Israel's first camp after crossing the Jordan: twelve memorial stones, circumcision of the new generation, first Passover in Canaan.
guilgal.histoire: Twelve stones taken from the Jordan's riverbed were set up there, "that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, saying, 'What do these stones mean to you?'" (Joshua 4:6). At Gilgal, God "rolled away" the reproach of Egypt—this is what the name means (Joshua 5:9)—the manna ceased, and the Commander of the Lord's army appeared to Joshua (Joshua 5:13-15). Saul was confirmed as king there (1 Samuel 11:14-15)… and there lost the kingdom through his hasty sacrifice (1 Samuel 13:8-14).

gabaon.bio: A cunning city that secured a covenant from Joshua, sky of the
gabaon.histoire: The Gibeonites, disguised as distant travelers with stale bread and worn-out skins, deceive Israel, whose men

sarepta.bio: A small Phoenician town near Sidon where a widow on the brink of famine feeds Elijah — and watches her flour never run out and her son come back to life.
sarepta.histoire: In the midst of famine, God sends Elijah not to a wealthy woman in Israel but to a pagan widow gathering wood for one last meal. "The jar of flour will not be used up and the jug of oil will not run dry" (1 Kings 17:14) — and each day the promise holds. When her son dies, Elijah raises him back to life for his mother (1 Kings 17:22-23). Jesus himself will cite Zarephath to show that God's grace crosses all boundaries (Luke 4:25-26).

dothan.bio: Plain with pastures where Joseph was sold by his brothers — and where, centuries later, Elisha showed his servant the mountain full of chariots of fire.
dothan.histoire: It was at Dothan that Joseph's brothers threw him into a pit and then sold him for twenty shekels of silver (Genesis 37:17-28) — the beginning of God's long detour to save his family. At that same place, the Syrian army surrounds Elisha one night. His servant panics; the prophet prays: "Lord, open his eyes so he may see." And the mountain appears "full of horses and chariots of fire" (2 Kings 6:15-17). Two stories, one lesson: at Dothan, what you see is never the whole reality.

mont-nebo.bio: Peak in Moab facing Jericho, from which Moses beheld all the promised land before his death — "and no one has known his burial place."
mont-nebo.histoire: "Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo…and the Lord showed him all the land" (Deuteronomy 34:1). At one hundred twenty years old, his eye still sharp, the liberator beholds what he will not walk upon — because of Meribah — but he dies "according to the word of the Lord," who buries him himself in the valley: "no one has known his burial place to this day" (Deuteronomy 34:5-7). Yet the promise was not finished for him: centuries later, Moses stands in the land, on the Mount of Transfiguration, speaking with Jesus (Matthew 17:3).

siloe.bio: The pool south of Jerusalem, fed by Hezekiah's tunnel. Jesus sends the man born blind there to wash his eyes —

garizim.bio: The mountain of blessings, facing Mount Ebal, above Shechem. It became the holy place of the Samaritans — "our fathers worshiped on this mountain."
garizim.histoire: Moses had commanded it: six tribes on Gerizim "to bless the people," six on Ebal for the curses (Deuteronomy 27:12-13) — and Joshua read all the law between the two mountains (Joshua 8:33-35). The Samaritans built their rival temple there; it is the mountain the Samaritan woman shows to Jesus: "Our fathers worshiped on this mountain" (John 4:20). His answer shifts the question forever: "the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth" (John 4:23).

ai.bio: Canaanite city near Bethel: Israel's defeat there revealed Achan's sin, before Joshua conquered it.
ai.histoire:
Abram already pitched his tent between Bethel and Ai (Genesis 12:8). After Jericho, Israel thought Ai would be easy to take; but "they fled before the men of Ai," and thirty-six men fell: "The people's heart melted and became like water" (Joshua 7:4-5). The cause was hidden: Achan had taken some of the devoted things (Joshua 7:20-21).

Once the sin was removed, God gave victory through an ambush: "Joshua burned Ai and made it a permanent heap of ruins" (Joshua 8:28). Hidden sin weakens an entire people; repentance reopens the way.

hatsor.bio: A great Canaanite city in Upper Galilee, capital of King Jabin; taken by Joshua, then fortified by Solomon.
hatsor.histoire:
"Hazor was formerly the capital of all these kingdoms": Joshua takes it and sets it on fire (Joshua 11:10-11). Later, another Jabin rules there and oppresses Israel through his general Sisera, until the victory of Deborah and Barak (Judges 4:2).

Solomon rebuilt it as a fortified city, along with Megiddo and Gezer (1 Kings 9:15). Excavations there have uncovered a vast lower city and gates from the royal period.

lakis.bio: Powerful fortified city of Judah, in the Shephelah: besieged by Sennacherib, then by Nebuchadnezzar.
lakis.histoire:
In 701 BC, Sennacherib besieged Lachish; it was there that Hezekiah sent word to him: "I have done wrong! Withdraw from me" (2 Kings 18:14). The king of Assyria had the siege of Lachish carved on the walls of his palace in Nineveh.

A century later, under Nebuchadnezzar, Lachish and Azekah were the last strong cities of Judah still holding out (Jeremiah 34:7). Letters on potsherds found there echo those days of anguish.

meguiddo.bio: Strategic city guarding the passage to the Plain of Jezreel: site of decisive battles, where King Josiah died.
meguiddo.histoire:
Deborah sings of the defeat of the kings of Canaan "At Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo" (Judges 5:19). Solomon made it one of his fortified cities (1 Kings 9:15). King Ahaziah dies there while fleeing Jehu (2 Kings 9:27), and it is there that Pharaoh Neco kills King Josiah (2 Kings 23:29).

Its name, combined with the Hebrew word for "mountain" (har), gives Armageddon, the place of the great gathering of Revelation (Revelation 16:16).

jizreel.bio: Royal city of Ahab and a great fertile valley in northern Israel: Naboth's vineyard, Jezebel's death, and the prophetic name of Hosea's son.
jizreel.histoire:
"Naboth of Jezreel had a vineyard in Jezreel, beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria" (1 Kings 21:1). Jezebel has him stoned to give it to the king. Elijah announces judgment, and Jehu executes it in Jezreel itself: Joram dies there and Jezebel is thrown from a window (2 Kings 9:24, 33).

A century later, God asks Hosea to name his son Jezreel: "I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood shed at Jezreel" (Hosea 1:4). Jehu's zeal had become violence; God also judges His instruments.

beth-schemesch.bio: Levitical city of Judah, on the border of the Philistines: it was there that the Ark of the Covenant returned, drawn by two cows.
beth-schemesch.histoire:
The Philistines, struck by the Ark, sent it back on a cart pulled by two nursing cows: "The cows went straight toward the road to Beth Shemesh and stayed on that road, lowing as they went" (1 Samuel 6:12). The harvesters "looked up and saw the Ark, and they rejoiced at seeing it" (1 Samuel 6:13).

But some of the people look inside the Ark and are struck down: "Who is able to stand in the presence of the Lord, before this holy God?" (1 Samuel 6:19-20). Joy in God's presence does not exempt us from reverence for His holiness.

mitspa.bio: City of Benjamin ("watchpost"): gathering place of Israel under Samuel, where Saul was designated as king; residence of Gedaliah after the fall of Jerusalem.
mitspa.histoire:
Samuel summons the people: "Gather all Israel to Mizpah, and I will pray to the Lord for you." Water is poured out before the Lord, they fast and confess: "We have sinned against the Lord!" (1 Samuel 7:5-6). After the victory, Samuel sets up a stone: "Thus far the Lord has helped us" (1 Samuel 7:12). It is also at Mizpah that Saul is designated by lot (1 Samuel 10:17-24).

After the destruction of Jerusalem, Mizpah becomes the residence of Governor Gedaliah, where Jeremiah comes to dwell (Jeremiah 40:6), until Gedaliah's assassination by Ishmael (Jeremiah 41:1-3). Do not confuse with Mizpah of Gilead (Genesis 31:49).

rama.bio: "Height": a city of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, linked to Samuel and to Rachel's weeping; Samuel's native Ramah is sometimes located elsewhere, in Ephraim.
rama.histoire:
Samuel, after his circuit as judge, "returned to Ramah, where his home was; and there he judged Israel, and he built an altar to the Lord" (1 Samuel 7:17). It was there that the elders came to ask him for a king (1 Samuel 8:4-5). Several cities bore this name; Samuel's Ramah (Ramathaim-Zophim, 1 Samuel 1:1) has not been identified with certainty.

Jeremiah hears "weeping in Ramah": "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and bitter weeping, Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted" (Jeremiah 31:15) — the deportees were gathered there (Jeremiah 40:1). Matthew sees this word fulfilled in the massacre of the children of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:18); but Jeremiah immediately announced their return (Jeremiah 31:16-17).

gath.bio: One of the five Philistine cities, homeland of Goliath; David feigned madness before King Achish there, then found refuge in it.
gath.histoire:
The giant who defied Israel "was named Goliath, from Gath" (1 Samuel 17:4). Later, David in flight takes refuge with Achish, king of Gath, and must feign madness to save his life (1 Samuel 21:10-15); he returns there later with six hundred men (1 Samuel 27:2-3).

At Saul's death, David sings: "Tell it not in Gath, Proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon" (2 Samuel 1:20). The site of Tell es-Safi has yielded an inscription bearing names similar to "Goliath".

ekron.bio: The northernmost Philistine city, where the ark was sent; the city's god, Baal-Zebub, was consulted by King Ahaziah.
ekron.histoire:
The ark, having passed from Ashdod to Gath, arrives at Ekron, whose inhabitants cry out that they want to be put to death; they ask for it to be sent back (1 Samuel 5:10-11).

Later, King Ahaziah, wounded, sends messengers to consult "Baal-Zebub, god of Ekron." Elijah intercepts the messengers: "Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to consult Baal-Zebub, god of Ekron?" (2 Kings 1:2-3). The name of this god, "Beelzebul," will designate Satan in the Gospel (Matthew 12:24).

asdod.bio: Philistine city where the ark was placed in the temple of Dagon; called Azotus in the time of Acts.
asdod.histoire:
The Philistines bring the ark to Ashdod, into the house of Dagon. The next day, Dagon is "fallen on his face to the ground before the ark of the Lord"; the day after, his head and hands are broken off at the threshold (1 Samuel 5:1-4). Idols cannot stand before the true God.

Centuries later, after the baptism of the Ethiopian eunuch, "Philip was found at Azotus, and passing through, he preached the gospel to all the cities till he came to Caesarea" (Acts 8:40).

askalon.bio: Philistine port on the Mediterranean, one of the five cities of the Pentapolis; targeted by several oracles of the prophets.
askalon.histoire:
Samson goes down there and kills thirty men to pay for the lost riddle (Judges 14:19). David mourns Saul, wishing that the news not be announced "in the streets of Ashkelon" (2 Samuel 1:20).

The prophets announce its ruin (Amos 1:8; Zephaniah 2:4; Zechariah 9:5). According to tradition, Herod the Great was born there.

tsiklag.bio: A town in the Negev given to David by the Philistine king Achish; plundered by the Amalekites, then recovered. The exact site remains disputed.
tsiklag.histoire:
"And Achish gave him Ziklag that same day" (1 Samuel 27:6). David lived there a year and four months with his men.

One day, they find the city burned, women and children taken away. His men speak of stoning him; "But David strengthened himself in the Lord his God" (1 Samuel 30:6). He pursues the raiders and recovers everything (1 Samuel 30:18-19). At his lowest point, he finds strength in God—just days before becoming king.

en-guedi.bio: Oasis and spring on the western shore of the Dead Sea, with its caves: David spared Saul there.
en-guedi.histoire:
"From there David went up to the strongholds of En-gedi, where he stayed" (1 Samuel 24:1). Saul pursued him and entered alone into a cave where David and his men were hiding. David "cut off the corner of Saul's robe" secretly, then his heart struck him: "May the Lord keep me from doing such a thing to my master, the Lord's anointed, as to lay my hand on him!" (1 Samuel 24:4-7).

The beauty of the place inspired the Song of Solomon, which speaks of the vineyards of En-gedi (Song of Solomon 1:14), and Ezekiel saw the waters of the temple heal the Dead Sea all the way to En-gedi (Ezekiel 47:10).

adullam.bio: City in the Shephelah of Judah: its cave served as a refuge for David and the distressed men who joined him.

mahanaim.bio: "The Two Camps": a place in Gilead where angels met Jacob; David's refuge during Absalom's revolt.
mahanaim.histoire:
Jacob, returning to Canaan, sees angels: "This is God's camp! And he called that place Mahanaim" (Genesis 32:1-2). He does not walk alone toward the meeting he dreads with Esau.

Ish-Bosheth reigns there for a time after Saul (2 Samuel 2:8). Later, David fleeing Absalom is welcomed there by Shobi, Makir, and Barzillai, who bring beds, provisions, and honey, because "This people must have suffered from hunger, weariness, and thirst in the desert" (2 Samuel 17:27-29).

ramoth-galaad.bio: A city of refuge in Gilead, disputed between Israel and Syria: Ahab was killed there, and Jehu was anointed king there.
ramoth-galaad.histoire:
A city of refuge in the tribe of Gad (Joshua 20:8). Despite the warning of the prophet Micaiah, Ahab and Jehoshaphat go up against Ramoth in Gilead. Ahab disguises himself; but "a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the joints of his armor"; he dies in the evening (1 Kings 22:29-35).

It is again at Ramoth that a disciple of Elisha comes to anoint Jehu, in the midst of a council of the army's commanders (2 Kings 9:1-6). God's word reaches its target, even "at random."

galaad.bio: Mountainous and forested region east of the Jordan, known for its balm; territory of Gad, Reuben, and part of Manasseh.
galaad.histoire:
Jacob and Laban sealed their covenant there (Genesis 31:21-25). Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh requested this pastoral land for their livestock (Numbers 32:1, 33). Jephthah and the prophet Elijah, "the Tishbite," were sons of Gilead (Judges 11:1; 1 Kings 17:1).

Its caravans of spices passed toward Egypt (Genesis 37:25). Jeremiah drew from it a lament that became famous: "Is there no balm in Gilead? Is there no physician?" (Jeremiah 8:22).

basan.bio: Fertile plateau northeast of the Jordan River, famous for its oak trees and cattle; kingdom of Og, conquered by Moses.
basan.histoire:
Og, king of Bashan, comes out to meet Israel; God delivers him into the hands of Moses (Numbers 21:33-35). His iron bed remained legendary (Deuteronomy 3:11).

His fattened herds become images: the psalmist, a figure of the suffering Messiah, says: "The bulls of Bashan surround me" (Psalms 22:12), and Amos addresses the wealthy women of Samaria: "cows of Bashan […] You who oppress the poor" (Amos 4:1).

hermon.bio: The highest peak in the region (over 9,200 feet), on Israel's northern border; its snows feed the sources of the Jordan River.
hermon.histoire:
It marks the northern limit of Moses' and Joshua's conquests (Deuteronomy 3:8; Joshua 11:17).

Its abundant dew becomes an image of the blessing of unity: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is For brethren to dwell together in unity! […] Like the dew of Hermon, Descending upon the mountains of Zion" (Psalms 133:1-3). Many believe that the Transfiguration took place on its slopes, near Caesarea Philippi.

ebal.bio: Mountain facing Gerizim, above Shechem: Joshua built an altar there and read the entire law, blessings and curses.
ebal.histoire:
Moses commands: "you shall set up these stones on Mount Ebal" where the law will be written (Deuteronomy 27:4). The curses will be pronounced there, and the blessings from Gerizim (Deuteronomy 11:29).

Joshua obeys: he builds an altar of uncut stones and writes on the stones a copy of the law; then "There was not a word of all that Moses had commanded which Joshua did not read in the presence of all the assembly of Israel, with the women, the little ones, and the strangers" (Joshua 8:30-35). Entering the promise begins with listening to God's Word.

guilboa.bio: A range of hills overlooking the Plain of Jezreel: Saul and his three sons, including Jonathan, perished there at the hands of the Philistines.
guilboa.histoire:
The day before, Saul had consulted the medium of En Dor (1 Samuel 28:4-7). The next day, the men of Israel "fell slain on Mount Gilboa"; Jonathan dies, and Saul, wounded, throws himself on his sword: "So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men, that same day together" (1 Samuel 31:1-6).

David sings his lament: "O mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew or rain upon you […] For there the shield of the mighty was cast away" (2 Samuel 1:21).

kison.bio: A watercourse in the plain of Jezreel toward the Bay of Haifa: it swept away Sisera's army; Elijah caused the prophets of Baal to perish there.
kison.histoire:
God defeats Sisera's chariots, which became mired in the waterlogged plain: "The stream of Kishon swept them away, The ancient stream, the stream of Kishon" (Judges 5:21).

After fire fell from heaven on Mount Carmel, Elijah brought the prophets of Baal down to the stream of Kishon, where they were put to death (1 Kings 18:40). The Kishon flows at the foot of Carmel, witness to both victories.

cedron.bio: A valley east of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives; David crossed it while fleeing Absalom, and Jesus crossed it on the night of his arrest.
cedron.histoire:
David, betrayed by his son, leaves Jerusalem in tears: "The king also crossed over the Brook Kidron" (2 Samuel 15:23). The reforming kings Asa, Hezekiah, and Josiah burn idols there (1 Kings 15:13; 2 Kings 23:6).

A thousand years later, the Son of David walks the same path: "Jesus went out with his disciples across the Brook Kidron, where there was a garden" (John 18:1). Like David, he is betrayed by someone close to him; but he goes freely toward the cross.

kades.bio: Desert oasis south of Canaan, Israel's main camp during the wilderness years: refusal to enter the land, death of Miriam, waters of Meribah.
kades.histoire:
It was at Kadesh that the twelve spies returned to show the fruits of the land (Numbers 13:26). But the people believed the report of the ten and refused to enter: they would wander forty years (Numbers 14:33-34).

Years later, "the people stayed at Kadesh. There Miriam died" (Numbers 20:1). Lacking water, the people complained; Moses "struck the rock twice with his staff" instead of speaking to it, and God said to him: "you shall not bring this assembly into the land" (Numbers 20:11-12).

mara.bio: "Bitterness": Israel's first stop after the Red Sea, where bitter waters were made sweet.
mara.histoire:
Three days without water, then disappointment: "they could not drink the water of Mara, for it was bitter" (Exodus 15:23-24); the people complained: "What shall we drink?" (Exodus 15:23-24).

"Moses cried out to the Lord; and the Lord showed him a tree, which he threw into the water. And the water became sweet." There, God revealed Himself: "I am the Lord, who heals you" (Exodus 15:25-26). Just after comes Elim with its twelve springs (Exodus 15:27).

elim.bio: An oasis in the Sinai Desert with twelve springs and seventy palm trees, where Israel camped after Marah.
elim.histoire:
After the bitterness of Marah, God leads His people to rest: "Then they came to Elim, where there were twelve wells of water and seventy palm trees. So they camped there by the waters" (Exodus 15:27).

Twelve springs for twelve tribes. God's way alternates between trials and refreshment; He knows what His people need. Next, Israel enters the Desert of Sin, where manna will fall (Exodus 16:1).

rephidim.bio: A stopping place before Sinai: God made water flow from the rock there, and Israel defeated Amalek while Moses prayed with his hands raised.
rephidim.histoire:
The people, lacking water, contend: "Is the Lord among us, or is He not?" God says to Moses: "you shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it"; the place is named Massah and Meribah (Exodus 17:6-7).

Then Amalek attacks. Joshua fights in the plain, while Moses holds his hands raised on the hill, supported by Aaron and Hur; Moses builds an altar afterward "and gave it the name: The Lord Is My Banner" (Exodus 17:11-15).

gosen.bio: Fertile region in the eastern Nile Delta where Jacob and his sons settled; spared from several plagues of Egypt.
gosen.histoire:
Joseph tells his father: "You will dwell in the land of Goshen, and you will be near me" (Genesis 45:10). Pharaoh establishes them "in the best of the land," and they "were fruitful and increased greatly" (Genesis 47:6, 27).

During the plagues, God makes a distinction: "I will set apart the land of Goshen, where My people dwell" (Exodus 8:22), and "Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, there was no hail" (Exodus 9:26).

charan.bio: City in Upper Mesopotamia where Terah's family stopped; Abram departed from there for Canaan, and Jacob served Laban there for twenty years.
charan.histoire:
Terah left Ur with Abram and Lot: "They came to Haran and settled there" (Genesis 11:31). After his father's death, "Abram departed, as the Lord had told him […] Abram was seventy-five years old when he went out from Haran" (Genesis 12:4).

The family remained connected to Haran: Rebekah came from there (Genesis 24:10), and Jacob fled to escape Esau, married Leah and Rachel there, and saw nearly all his sons born there (Genesis 28:10; 29:4).

assyrie.bio: Empire of northern Mesopotamia, capital Nineveh: it destroyed the kingdom of Israel (722 BC) and besieged Jerusalem under Hezekiah.
assyrie.histoire:
The king of Assyria takes Samaria and deports Israel, "because the children of Israel sinned against the Lord" (2 Kings 17:6-7). Sennacherib then invades Judah; but after Hezekiah's prayer, the angel of the Lord strikes the Assyrian camp (2 Kings 19:35).

Isaiah cries out: "Woe to the Assyrian, the rod of my anger!" — an instrument that thinks itself master and will be judged in turn (Isaiah 10:5-12). Nineveh will fall in 612 BC, as Nahum had announced.

suse.bio: Persian capital, royal residence: the setting of the book of Esther and the place where Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, learned of the destruction of Jerusalem.
suse.histoire:
Nehemiah writes: "As I was in Susa, the capital," he receives news of Jerusalem (Nehemiah 1:1-3). Daniel sees himself in a vision "in Susa, the capital" (Daniel 8:2).

It is in Susa that Esther, facing the decree of death, asks Mordecai: "Go, gather all the Jews who are in Susa, and fast for me [...] and if I must perish, I will perish" (Esther 4:16). The palace of the most powerful king becomes the stage for God's faithfulness.

tarsis.bio: A distant port in the West, possibly Tartessos in Spain: a symbol of the end of the known world, and the destination of Jonah's flight.

edom.bio: A mountainous country southeast of the Dead Sea, populated by the descendants of Esau (called Edom); brother and often enemy of Israel.
edom.histoire:
"Esau is Edom" (Genesis 36:8). When Israel asks to pass through its territory, Edom refuses and comes out in arms (Numbers 20:14-21). David subdues it; Edom rebels later (2 Kings 8:20).

When Jerusalem falls, Edom rejoices and plunders. Obadiah addresses his entire book to it: "The pride of your heart has deceived you, You who dwell in the clefts of the rocks"; "Because of your violence against your brother Jacob, You will be covered with shame" (Obadiah 1:3-10). The Herods were Idumeans, descendants of Edom.

anathoth.bio: A priestly city of Benjamin, northeast of Jerusalem: birthplace of Jeremiah, who bought a field there during the siege.
anathoth.histoire:
City of the priests: Solomon exiles the high priest Abiathar there (1 Kings 2:26). Jeremiah is "the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests of Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin" (Jeremiah 1:1). His own townspeople conspire against him (Jeremiah 11:21).

As Jerusalem is about to fall, God commands him to buy the field of his cousin Hanamel in Anathoth: "Houses and fields and vineyards shall yet be bought in this land" (Jeremiah 32:7-15). Among the exiles who returned, there were "the men of Anathoth, one hundred and twenty-eight" (Ezra 2:23).

kirjath-jearim.bio: A Gibeonite city west of Jerusalem, where the ark remained for twenty years in the house of Abinadab.
kirjath-jearim.histoire:
After Beth-shemesh, "The men of Kiriath-jearim came and took up the ark of the Lord; they brought it into the house of Abinadab, on the hill" (1 Samuel 7:1). "Twenty years had passed. Then all the house of Israel groaned toward the Lord" (1 Samuel 7:2).

David came to fetch it there to bring it to Jerusalem — first on a new cart, and Uzzah died (1 Chronicles 13:5-10). It was also the city of the prophet Uriah, put to death by Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 26:20).

nob.bio: "Priestly city" near Jerusalem, where David received consecrated bread; Saul had its priests massacred there.
nob.histoire:
David on the run arrives "at Nob, to Ahimelech the priest." Without other bread, Ahimelech gives him "the consecrated bread" and Goliath's sword (1 Samuel 21:1-9). Jesus will cite this episode: mercy takes precedence over ritual (Matthew 12:3-4).

Doeg the Edomite witnessed everything. By Saul's order, he kills eighty-five priests, then "Saul struck down with the edge of the sword Nob, the priestly city" (1 Samuel 22:18-19). Only Abiathar escapes and joins David.

ziph.bio: A desert region southeast of Hebron, where David hid; the Ziphites betrayed him twice to Saul.
ziph.histoire:
"Then the Ziphites came up to Saul at Gibeah, saying, 'Is David not hiding among us?'" (1 Samuel 23:19). It was in this wilderness that Jonathan came to strengthen David "in God" (1 Samuel 23:16).

During a second betrayal, David entered Saul's camp at night and took his spear and water jug, without laying a hand on the Lord's anointed (1 Samuel 26:1-12). Psalm 54 bears the title of this moment when the Ziphites delivered him up.

maon.bio: A city and wilderness of Judah, south of Hebron: David narrowly escaped Saul there; hometown of Nabal.
maon.histoire:
In the wilderness of Maon, Saul almost surrounded David, "when a messenger came to Saul, saying, 'Hurry and come, for the Philistines have invaded the land.'" The place is called Sela-Hammahlekoth (1 Samuel 23:26-28), meaning the rock of separation.

"Now there was a man in Maon whose business was in Carmel, and he was a very rich man": Nabal, husband of Abigail (1 Samuel 25:2-3). His harshness toward David could have cost him dearly, but for the wisdom of his wife.

carmel-juda.bio: A town in Judah near Maon, not to be confused with Mount Carmel: Saul set up a monument there, and Nabal sheared his sheep there.
carmel-juda.histoire:
After his victory over the Amalekites, Saul "set up a monument for himself" at Carmel, before being rejected by God for his disobedience (1 Samuel 15:12, 23).

It was also at Carmel that Nabal sheared his three thousand sheep and refused everything to David (1 Samuel 25:2-11). Abigail, his wife, saved the situation; widowed, she became the wife of David — hence her name "Abigail of Carmel" (1 Samuel 27:3).

guibea.bio: City of Benjamin north of Jerusalem, notorious for the crime in Judges 19; later "Gibeah of Saul," his capital.
guibea.histoire:
A Levite and his concubine spend the night there: "No one would take them into his house" (Judges 19:15). The abominable crime that follows triggers a war in which Benjamin nearly faces extinction (Judges 20:13). Hosea still sees in it the symbol of deep corruption (Hosea 9:9).

Yet it is from Gibeah that the first king comes: "Saul also went home to Gibeah. And valiant men went with him, whose hearts God had touched" (1 Samuel 10:26). From there, he goes to deliver Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11:4-11).

keila.bio: A city in the Shephelah of Judah, delivered from the Philistines by David, who consulted the Lord at every step.
keila.histoire:
"Behold, the Philistines are attacking Keilah." David consults the Lord, then consults Him again when his men are afraid: "Arise, go down to Keilah, for I will deliver the Philistines into your hand"; "So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah" (1 Samuel 23:1-5).

But when Saul draws near, David asks: "Will the men of Keilah deliver me? […] And the Lord said: They will deliver you." He leaves at once (1 Samuel 23:12-13). Serve without expecting recognition, and remain guided by God.

soco.bio: A city of Judah overlooking the Valley of Elah, where the Philistines camped when Goliath challenged Israel.
soco.histoire:
"The Philistines [...] gathered at Soco, which belongs to Judah; they camped between Soco and Azekah." Saul and Israel camp opposite them, "in the Valley of Elah" (1 Samuel 17:1-2).

It was in this valley that the young shepherd David came against the giant with his sling "in the name of the Lord of hosts" (1 Samuel 17:45). The place still exists today: the Valley of Elah, southwest of Jerusalem.

morija.bio: The land and mountain where Abraham was called to offer Isaac; the same mountain where Solomon built the temple of Jerusalem.
morija.histoire:
"Take your son, your only son, whom you love, Isaac; go to the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering" (Genesis 22:2). God stops Abraham's hand and provides a ram; Abraham calls the place Jehovah-Jireh: "On the mountain of the Lord it shall be provided" (Genesis 22:14).

Centuries later, "Solomon began to build the house of the Lord in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah" (2 Chronicles 3:1). Where God had spared the son of Abraham, He would have sacrifices offered—until He did not spare His own Son (Romans 8:32).

sorek.bio: Valley between the hills of Judah and the Philistine plain, where Delilah lived.
sorek.histoire:
"After this he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek whose name was Delilah" (Judges 16:4). The Philistine rulers each promise her eleven hundred shekels of silver to discover the secret of Samson's strength.

Three times Samson flirts with danger; the fourth time he gives away his secret. His hair cut off, "the Lord had departed from him" (Judges 16:20). The Valley of Sorek reminds us that repeated compromises eventually cost you your vision.

peniel.bio: "Face of God": the ford of the Jabbok where Jacob wrestled with God all night and received the name Israel.
peniel.histoire:
After the night struggle, "Jacob called the name of the place Peniel: 'For I have seen God face to face, and my life has been preserved.' And as he passed over Peniel the sun rose upon him. And he limped on his hip" (Genesis 32:30-31). Blessed, but marked forever.

Later, Gideon destroyed the tower of the inhabitants who had refused bread to his exhausted men (Judges 8:8-9, 17), and Jeroboam fortified it (1 Kings 12:25).

jabbok.bio: An eastern tributary of the Jordan River in Gilead: Jacob crossed its ford the night of his struggle with God.
jabbok.histoire:
Jacob fears meeting Esau. "That same night he rose and took his two wives, his two female servants, and his eleven children, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok." Left alone, he wrestles until dawn and does not let go: "I will not let you go unless you bless me" (Genesis 32:22-26).

The Jabbok also served as a border, particularly with the Ammonites (Deuteronomy 3:16).

mamre.bio: A grove of oak trees near Hebron where Abraham dwelt and received a visit from the Lord; the cave of Machpelah faces it.
mamre.histoire:
"Abram moved his tent, and went and dwelt by the oaks of Mamre, which are near Hebron. And he built an altar there to the Lord" (Genesis 13:18). It was there that "the Lord appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre," in the form of three visitors, to announce the birth of Isaac (Genesis 18:1-10).

Abraham purchases his only property in Canaan there: the cave of Machpelah, "opposite Mamre," where he buries Sarah (Genesis 23:19), and where he himself will be buried, as will Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob (Genesis 49:30-31).

guerar.bio: City in the southwest of Canaan, kingdom of Abimelech: Abraham and then Isaac made their wives pass for their sister there.
guerar.histoire:
Abraham stays in Gerar and says of Sarah: "She is my sister." God warns Abimelech in a dream (Genesis 20:1-7).

During a famine, "Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gerar." God told him: "Dwell in this land, and I will be with you"; Isaac repeats his father's mistake, but God blesses him nonetheless: "he reaped in that year a hundredfold" (Genesis 26:1-12). His disputed wells end at Rehoboth: "the Lord has made room for us" (Genesis 26:22).

tachpanes.bio: A border city of Egypt in the eastern delta, where the survivors of Judah forcibly brought Jeremiah.
tachpanes.histoire:
Despite God's word, Johanan led the remnant of Judah to Egypt: "they came to Tahpanhes" (Jeremiah 43:7). There, God commanded Jeremiah: "Take large stones in your hand and hide them [...] at the entrance of Pharaoh's house in Tahpanhes" — Nebuchadnezzar would set his throne there (Jeremiah 43:9-10).

This was the last known stage of Jeremiah's ministry, as he continued to warn the Jews in Egypt (Jeremiah 44:1).

ribla.bio: City in Syria, in the land of Hamath, headquarters of Pharaoh Neco and later of Nebuchadnezzar; Zedekiah had his sons killed there.
ribla.histoire:
Pharaoh Neco chains King Jehoahaz there (2 Kings 23:33). Twenty years later, Zedekiah, captured while fleeing Jerusalem, is brought "before the king of Babylon at Riblah." "The sons of Zedekiah were slain before his eyes, and the eyes of Zedekiah were put out" (2 Kings 25:6-7).

The last image the last king of Judah ever saw was the fruit of his refusal to listen to Jeremiah (Jeremiah 38:17-18).

carkemisch.bio: City on the Euphrates where Nebuchadnezzar crushed the Egyptian army of Neco in 605 BC, a battle that made Babylon the master of the region.
carkemisch.histoire:
It was while marching toward Carchemish that Neco killed Josiah at Megiddo (2 Chronicles 35:20-24).

Jeremiah dates his oracle: "Against the army of Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, which was by the River Euphrates at Carchemish, and which was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim" (Jeremiah 46:2). The balance of the world tips, just as the prophets had announced.

ono.bio: A plain near Lydda, where Sanballat and Geshem sought to lure Nehemiah to harm him.
ono.histoire:
As the wall nears completion, Sanballat and Geshem send word to Nehemiah: "Come, let us meet together in the villages of the valley of Ono." Nehemiah understands: "They were planning to do me harm" (Nehemiah 6:2).

His response became a model of staying focused on God's calling: "I am doing a great work and cannot come down; why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?" (Nehemiah 6:3). They insist four times; he answers the same way four times (Nehemiah 6:4).

bethphage.bio: Village on the Mount of Olives, near Bethany: Jesus sent his disciples here to fetch the donkey for his royal entry into Jerusalem.
bethphage.histoire:
"When they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, at the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two disciples" to find a donkey and her colt (Matthew 21:1-2).

This fulfills Zechariah: "Behold, your King is coming to you, lowly, and sitting on a donkey" (Matthew 21:5; Zechariah 9:9). From Bethphage begins the Palm Sunday procession, the start of Passion Week.

chorazin.bio: A village in Galilee north of Capernaum, witness to many miracles of Jesus, but which did not repent.
chorazin.histoire:
No miracle is recorded there, yet Jesus says there were many: "Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago" (Matthew 11:21).

The more light you have received, the more responsible you are (Luke 12:48). The ruins of its black basalt synagogue can still be visited.

decapole.bio: "Ten cities" of Greek culture, mostly east of the Jordan River: a demon-possessed man delivered there became the first evangelist.
decapole.histoire:
Crowds from the Decapolis follow Jesus from the beginning (Matthew 4:25). After his deliverance, the man from Gadara wants to follow Jesus; Jesus tells him: "Go home to your own people, and tell them all that the Lord has done for you"; "So he went away and began to tell in the Decapolis all that Jesus had done for him" (Mark 5:19-20).

Later, Jesus returns "by way of the Decapolis" and heals a deaf and mute man there (Mark 7:31-35): the ground had been prepared by a single testimony.
