gadareniens.bio: The eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee, in pagan territory, where Jesus delivered a man possessed by a legion of demons.
gadareniens.histoire:
"When he came to the other side, to the country of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men coming out of the tombs met him" (Matthew 8:28). Mark and Luke focus on one of them, called Legion (Mark 5:9); Luke speaks of the "country of the Gerasenes, which is opposite Galilee" (Luke 8:26).

The demons enter a herd of pigs that rushes into the sea. The inhabitants, frightened, beg Jesus to leave; the healed man, instead, is sent out as a witness (Mark 5:17-20).

tiberiade.bio: City founded by Herod Antipas on the western shore of the lake in honor of the emperor Tiberius; the lake also took its name from this city.
tiberiade.histoire:
John calls the lake "the Sea of Galilee, of Tiberias" (John 6:1). After the multiplication of the loaves, "other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread" (John 6:23).

It is "on the shores of the Sea of Tiberias" that the risen Jesus appears to the disciples after a night of unsuccessful fishing, and restores Peter (John 21:1, 15-17).

arimathee.bio: A city in Judea, hometown of Joseph, a member of the council who buried Jesus in his own new tomb.
arimathee.histoire:
Joseph was "from Arimathea, a city of the Jews, and he was waiting for the kingdom of God"; a counselor, "a good and righteous man," he "had not consented to their decision" of the Sanhedrin (Luke 23:50-51).

On the evening of the crucifixion, this "rich man from Arimathea" asks for the body of Jesus and places it "in a new tomb which had been hewn out of the rock" (Matthew 27:57-60), fulfilling Isaiah: "with the rich at His death" (Isaiah 53:9). Its exact location remains uncertain.

enon.bio: A place "near Salim," rich in water, where John the Baptist was baptizing while Jesus was beginning His ministry.
enon.histoire:
"John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because there was much water there; and people were coming and being baptized" (John 3:23).

When his disciples become concerned to see the crowds going toward Jesus, John responds with one of the most beautiful words of humility: "He must increase, but I must decrease" (John 3:30).

bethesda.bio: A pool with five porticoes near the Sheep Gate in Jerusalem, where Jesus healed a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years.
bethesda.histoire:
"Now there is at Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, which is called in Hebrew, Bethesda, having five porches" (John 5:2). Sick people waited there for the moving of the water.

Jesus asks a man lying there for thirty-eight years: "Do you want to be made well?" The man replies: "I have no one to put me into the pool." "Rise, take up your bed and walk," Jesus tells him (John 5:6-8). Excavations have uncovered two basins and their colonnades near the Church of Saint Anne.

gabbatha.bio: "The Pavement": the place of Pilate's judgment seat in Jerusalem, where Jesus was presented to the people and delivered to be crucified.
gabbatha.histoire:
"Pilate, hearing these words, brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Pavement, and in Hebrew, Gabbatha" (John 19:13). He said to the Jews, "Behold your King." They cry out, "Crucify Him!" (John 19:14-15).

The judge sits on his throne, yet he is the one being judged: the true King stands before him, crowned with thorns.

hakeldama.bio: "Field of Blood": a plot of land south of Jerusalem purchased with the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas.
hakeldama.histoire:
The field was acquired "with the wages of iniquity," and the story of Judas's death became so well known "that this field has been called in their own language Hakeldama, that is, Field of Blood" (Acts 1:18-19).

Matthew clarifies that the chief priests, unwilling to put this "price of blood" into the temple treasury, bought "the potter's field, to be a burial place for strangers" (Matthew 27:6-8), fulfilling a prophetic word (Matthew 27:9-10).

lydde.bio: A city in the coastal plain near Joppa, where Peter healed Aeneas, who had been paralyzed for eight years.
lydde.histoire:
"As Peter traveled about the country, he went to visit the Lord's people who lived in Lydda." There he found Aeneas, bedridden for eight years: "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; get up and roll up your mat. Immediately Aeneas got up" (Acts 9:32-34).

Result: "All those who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord" (Acts 9:35). From there, Peter is called to Joppa to Tabitha (Acts 9:38).

saron.bio: Fertile coastal plain between Joppa and Carmel, famous for its flowers and pastures.
saron.histoire:
The beloved in the Song of Solomon says: "I am a rose of Sharon, a lily of the valleys" (Song of Solomon 2:1). Isaiah announces the desert blooming again: "It shall be given the glory of Lebanon, the excellence of Carmel and Sharon" (Isaiah 35:2).

After Aeneas is healed, "all who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord" (Acts 9:35): the flowering plain becomes a harvest field.

ptolemais.bio: A port on the Phoenician coast (present-day Acre), where Paul greeted the brothers as he traveled up to Jerusalem.
ptolemais.histoire:
"Finishing our voyage, we sailed from Tyre to Ptolemais, where we greeted the brothers, and spent a day with them" (Acts 21:7).

A church already existed there, likely born from the scattering after Stephen's death (Acts 11:19). Wherever Paul goes, he finds brothers: God's family is already there.

antipatris.bio: A city built by Herod the Great between Jerusalem and Caesarea, where Paul's escort stopped for the night.
antipatris.histoire:
Threatened by a conspiracy of more than forty men, Paul is smuggled out at night: "Then the soldiers, as they were commanded, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris" (Acts 23:31).

The next day, the horsemen continue alone to Caesarea (Acts 23:32-33). God protects His servant through the very soldiers of the empire, as He had promised him (Acts 23:11).

antioche-pisidie.bio: A Roman colony in Asia Minor, not to be confused with Antioch of Syria: Paul delivered his first major sermon there and turned toward the Gentiles.
antioche-pisidie.histoire:
"From Perga they continued on and came to Antioch of Pisidia"; in the synagogue, Paul traced the history of Israel up to the risen Jesus (Acts 13:14-41). The following Sabbath, almost the entire city came to hear him.

Faced with opposition, Paul and Barnabas declared: "we are turning to the Gentiles," for the Lord said: "I have set you to be a light for the nations" (Acts 13:46-47). Driven out, they shook the dust from their feet (Acts 13:50-51); Paul would remember the persecutions he endured there (2 Timothy 3:11).

icone.bio: City of Lycaonia (modern-day Konya) where Paul and Barnabas made many disciples before being threatened with stoning.
icone.histoire:
"In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas went together into the synagogue of the Jews, and they spoke in such a way that a great multitude of both Jews and Greeks believed." The Lord bears witness to "the word of his grace" through miracles (Acts 14:1-3).

The city becomes divided; threatened with stoning, they flee to Lystra and Derbe (Acts 14:4-6). Later, the brethren at Iconium will give a good testimony about the young Timothy (Acts 16:2).

derbe.bio: A city in Lycaonia, the easternmost stop on Paul's first missionary journey, which he visited the day after his stoning.
derbe.histoire:
At Lystra, Paul is stoned and left for dead; "But while the disciples stood around him, he rose up and went into the city. And the next day he departed with Barnabas to Derbe" (Acts 14:19-20). There they make "a considerable number of disciples" (Acts 14:21).

Paul passes through again on his second missionary journey (Acts 16:1). Gaius of Derbe becomes one of the companions who accompany him to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4).

perge.bio: A city in Pamphylia on the southern coast of Asia Minor, where John Mark left Paul and Barnabas.
perge.histoire:
"Now when Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos, they came to Perge in Pamphylia. And John, departing from them, returned to Jerusalem" (Acts 13:13). This departure would later cause the separation of Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37-39).

On their return, they proclaim the word before going down to Attalia (Acts 14:25). Years later, Paul would say of Mark: "he is useful to me for ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11).

attalie.bio: A port city of Pamphylia (present-day Antalya) from which Paul and Barnabas embarked for Antioch at the end of their first missionary journey.
attalie.histoire:
After proclaiming the word at Perga, they "went down to Attalia. From there they sailed to Antioch, from which they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had completed" (Acts 14:25-26).

Upon their return, they reported "all that God had done with them, and how he had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles" (Acts 14:27).

seleucie.bio: Seaport of Antioch in Syria from which the first missionary journey departed.
seleucie.histoire:
After fasting and the laying on of hands, "Barnabas and Saul, sent out by the Holy Spirit, went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to the island of Cyprus" (Acts 13:4).

This is where the mission to the nations begins, concretely—the great adventure that will carry the Gospel all the way to Rome.

salamine.bio: Principal port on the east coast of Cyprus, the first stop of the first missionary journey.
salamine.histoire:
"When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. They had John as their assistant" (Acts 13:5).

Cyprus was the homeland of Barnabas (Acts 4:36): the mission begins with him there, then crosses the entire island to Paphos.

paphos.bio: Roman capital of Cyprus, on the western side of the island, where the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed in the Gospel.
paphos.histoire:
"When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they found a certain magician, a false prophet who was a Jew, named Bar-Jesus," who turned the proconsul Sergius Paulus away from the faith. Saul, "also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit," strikes him with blindness (Acts 13:6-11).

"Then the proconsul, seeing what had happened, believed, being astonished at the teaching of the Lord" (Acts 13:12). From that moment on, the narrative calls the apostle "Paul."

neapolis.bio: Port of Macedonia (present-day Kavala): the first footstep of the Gospel on European soil.
neapolis.histoire:
After the vision of the Macedonian man, Paul and his companions set sail from Troas: "we made a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day came to Neapolis" (Acts 16:11).

From there, they go to Philippi, where Lydia will be the first convert of Europe (Acts 16:12-15).

amphipolis-apollonie.bio: Cities of Macedonia on the Egnatian Way, crossed by Paul and Silas between Philippi and Thessalonica.
amphipolis-apollonie.histoire:
Released from the prison in Philippi, "Paul and Silas passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, and came to Thessalonica, where the Jews had a synagogue" (Acts 17:1).

They were following the Egnatian Way, the great Roman road that crossed Macedonia: the empire's roads served the spread of the Gospel.

cenchrees.bio: The eastern port of Corinth, where Paul had his head shaved for a vow; Phoebe served the Church there.
cenchrees.histoire:
Before leaving Greece, Paul embarks "with Priscilla and Aquila, after having his head shaved at Cenchrea, because he had made a vow" (Acts 18:18).

There was a church there: Paul recommends to the Romans "Phoebe, our sister, who is a deacon of the church at Cenchrea […] for she has been a helper of many and of me myself" (Romans 16:1-2). She likely carried the letter to the Romans.

milet.bio: A port city in Asia south of Ephesus, where Paul gave a moving farewell to the elders of Ephesus.
milet.histoire:
Eager to reach Jerusalem, Paul does not stop at Ephesus; "from Miletus Paul sent to Ephesus and called for the elders of the church" (Acts 20:17). He leaves them with a pastoral testament: serve with humility, care for the flock, remember that "it is more blessed to give than to receive" (Acts 20:35).

"And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. Then they all wept freely" (Acts 20:36-37). Later, Paul will leave Trophimus sick there (2 Timothy 4:20).

assos.bio: A port in Mysia where Paul, who had traveled on foot from Troas, joined his companions who had gone ahead by boat.
assos.histoire:
"So we went ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, there intending to take Paul on board; for so he had arranged, intending himself to go on foot" (Acts 20:13). Paul had just spent the night teaching at Troas, where Eutychus fell down and was restored to life.

They then continued toward Mytilene, Chios, Samos, and Miletus (Acts 20:14-15).

cos-rhodes-patara.bio: Islands and port of the Aegean Sea and Lycia, stopover points for Paul after Miletus on his way to Jerusalem.
cos-rhodes-patara.histoire:
"So when we had taken leave of them, we set sail and came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara." There they find a ship for Phoenicia (Acts 21:1-2).

Luke, present on the journey (the "we"), notes each stop with the precision of an eyewitness.

myra.bio: A port in Lycia where the prisoner Paul changed ships to an Alexandrian vessel bound for Italy.
myra.histoire:
"And when we had launched from there, we sailed under the shelter of Cyprus, because the winds were contrary. And when we had sailed over the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra, a city of Lycia. And there the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing to Italy, and he put us on it" (Acts 27:5-6).

It was likely a grain cargo ship: Myra was a stop on the major grain route between Egypt and Rome.

beaux-ports.bio: An anchorage on the south coast of Crete, near Lasaea, where Paul advised against wintering.
beaux-ports.histoire:
The ship sails along Crete with difficulty and arrives "at a place called Fair Havens, near the city of Lasaea" (Acts 27:8). The season is advanced; Paul warns: "I perceive that this voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and ship, but also our lives" (Acts 27:10).

"The centurion was more persuaded by the helmsman and the owner of the ship than by the things spoken by Paul" (Acts 27:11). They set sail again, and the storm breaks out.

clauda.bio: A small island south of Crete, in the shelter of which the crew prepared the ship for the storm.
clauda.histoire:
Swept away by the Euraquilo, "We passed under a small island called Clauda, and with difficulty we secured the skiff" (Acts 27:16); the ship was undergirded and the sails lowered "for fear we should run aground on the Syrtis" (Acts 27:16-17).

It is in the heart of this storm that the angel appeared to Paul: "Paul, do not be afraid" (Acts 27:24).

crete.bio: A large island in the Mediterranean Sea, which Paul's ship sailed past; Titus was left there to organize the churches.
crete.histoire:
Cretans were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:11). Paul's ship passed by the island before the storm: "you should have listened to me and not set sail from Crete," Paul would say (Acts 27:21).

He writes to Titus: "I left you in Crete so that you would set in order what remains to be done, and that [...] you would appoint elders in every city" (Titus 1:5), quoting a Cretan poet who was hardly flattering about his own people (Titus 1:12).

syracuse.bio: A major port city in Sicily where Paul stopped for three days on his way to Rome.
syracuse.histoire:
After three months in Malta, Paul boards a ship from Alexandria; "And landing at Syracuse, we stayed there three days" (Acts 28:11-12).

One more stop on the way to Rome, where God had said Paul must testify (Acts 23:11).

reggio.bio: A port at the tip of Italy, facing Sicily, Paul's last stop before Puteoli.
reggio.histoire:
"From there we sailed around and arrived at Rhegium. And after one day a south wind sprang up; and on the second day we came to Puteoli" (Acts 28:13).

After the storm, a favorable wind: God brings His servant all the way through.

pouzzoles.bio: A major port city in Campania, near Naples, where Paul landed in Italy and found believers.
pouzzoles.histoire:
"We came to Puteoli, where we found brethren, and were invited to stay with them seven days. And so we went toward Rome" (Acts 28:13-14).

Even before the apostle's arrival, the Gospel had already reached Italy.

forum-appius.bio: Stages along the Appian Way south of Rome, where Roman brothers came to meet Paul.
forum-appius.histoire:
"The brothers there had heard that we were coming, and they traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. At the sight of these men Paul thanked God and was encouraged" (Acts 28:15).

Three years earlier, Paul had written to these same believers expressing his desire to see them (Romans 1:11). The imprisoned apostle is comforted by the welcome of brothers he had not yet met.

illyrie.bio: Province on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, the western limit of Paul's evangelization when he wrote to the Romans.
illyrie.histoire:
Paul summarizes his ministry: "from Jerusalem and the surrounding regions all the way to Illyricum, I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ" (Romans 15:19).

His ambition: to preach Christ where He had not been named (Romans 15:20), and to go to Spain by way of Rome (Romans 15:24).

dalmatie.bio: A region of Illyricum on the Adriatic Sea, where Titus had gone during Paul's final imprisonment.
dalmatie.histoire:
In his final letter, Paul lists those who are absent: "Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me" (2 Timothy 4:10-11).

Even in prison, Paul continues to send his coworkers to the four corners of the empire.

nicopolis.bio: A city in Epirus on the western coast of Greece, where Paul wanted to spend the winter and asked Titus to join him.
nicopolis.histoire:
"When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make haste to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there" (Titus 3:12).

This mention suggests that Paul was released after his first Roman imprisonment and continued his ministry before being arrested again.

achaie.bio: A Roman province in southern Greece with Corinth as its capital: Paul, Apollos, and the household of Stephanas served there.
achaie.histoire:
Gallio was its proconsul when Paul was accused in Corinth (Acts 18:12). Apollos then passes through and becomes "very helpful to those who had believed" (Acts 18:27). The household of Stephanas is "the firstfruits" of it (1 Corinthians 16:15).

The churches of Achaia participate generously in the collection for Jerusalem: "Achaia has been ready since last year" (2 Corinthians 9:2), and the faith of the Thessalonians is known to all there (1 Thessalonians 1:7-8).

galatie.bio: Region and Roman province in central Asia Minor, recipient of the letter to the Galatians.
galatie.histoire:
Paul traveled through it on his journeys (Acts 16:6; 18:23) and addressed his letter "to the churches of Galatia" (Galatians 1:2). He fought there for the freedom of the Gospel: "O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you?" (Galatians 3:1).

Peter also wrote to believers "scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia" (1 Peter 1:1).

cappadoce.bio: Region in central-eastern Asia Minor: Jews from Cappadocia heard the Gospel on the day of Pentecost.
cappadoce.histoire:
Among the crowds at Pentecost are those "who dwell in Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia"; all hear the apostles speak "in our own tongues the wonderful works of God" (Acts 2:9-11).

A generation later, there are churches in Cappadocia: Peter writes to them (1 Peter 1:1). The pilgrims from Pentecost brought the good news back home.

pont.bio: A region in northern Asia Minor, on the Black Sea, the homeland of Aquila.
pont.histoire:
Jews from Pontus were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). Aquila, Paul's companion, was "a native of Pontus" (Acts 18:2).

Peter addresses his first letter to believers "scattered throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia" (1 Peter 1:1).

bithynie.bio: Region in northwestern Asia Minor where the Spirit prevented Paul from entering, directing him toward Macedonia instead.
bithynie.histoire:
"When they had come to Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit did not permit them" (Acts 16:7). The closed door prepares the way for the open door: the vision of the Macedonian man at Troas (Acts 16:9).

Yet the Gospel will reach that place: Peter writes to the believers in Bithynia (1 Peter 1:1).

mysie.bio: Region in northwestern Asia Minor, passed through by Paul on his way to Troas after the Spirit prevented him twice.
mysie.histoire:
Prevented by the Spirit in Asia and then in Bithynia, Paul and his companions "passed through Mysia and came down to Troas" (Acts 16:6-8).

There Paul sees a vision of a Macedonian man: "Come over to Macedonia and help us!" (Acts 16:9). Being led by the Spirit means accepting His "no" as well.

phrygie.bio: A region in central-western Asia Minor, crossed several times by Paul to strengthen the disciples.
phrygie.histoire:
Phrygians were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:10). Paul traveled through "Phrygia and the region of Galatia" during his second journey (Acts 16:6).

On his third journey, he traveled through Galatia and Phrygia again, "strengthening all the disciples" (Acts 18:23). Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis were located in this region.

lycaonie.bio: Region in central Asia Minor, with Lystra and Derbe, where the crowds mistook Paul and Barnabas for gods.
lycaonie.histoire:
Fleeing from Iconium, Paul and Barnabas "took refuge in the cities of Lycaonia, to Lystra and Derbe" (Acts 14:6). After healing a crippled man, the crowd cried out "in the Lycaonian language: The gods have come down to us in human form"; Barnabas was called Jupiter, Paul Mercury (Acts 14:11-12).

The apostles tore their clothes: "We too are men of like passions as you" (Acts 14:15).

pisidie.bio: A mountainous region in southern Asia Minor, between Pamphylia and Lycaonia, traveled through during the first missionary journey.
pisidie.histoire:
Paul and Barnabas went up from Perga to "Antioch of Pisidia" (Acts 13:14), then on their return, "passing through Pisidia, they came to Pamphylia" (Acts 14:24).

A difficult road, perhaps the one where Paul was "in perils on the rivers, in perils from robbers" (2 Corinthians 11:26).

smyrne.bio: A major port city in Asia (present-day Izmir), a poor and persecuted church with no reproach from the Lord.
smyrne.histoire:
Jesus presents Himself as "the First and the Last, who was dead, and came to life": "I know your tribulation and your poverty (but you are rich)" (Revelation 2:8-9).

"Do not fear any of the things you are about to suffer [...] Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life" (Revelation 2:10). In the second century, its bishop Polycarp would die there as a martyr.

pergame.bio: Religious capital of the province of Asia, "where Satan's throne is"; a faithful church but tolerating false doctrines.
pergame.histoire:
"I know where you dwell, where Satan's throne is. You hold fast my name, and you did not deny my faith even in the days of Antipas my faithful witness" (Revelation 2:13). The city housed a great altar of Zeus and a temple of the imperial cult.

But some follow "the doctrine of Balaam" (Revelation 2:14). To the one who overcomes, Christ promises "hidden manna" and a white stone bearing "a new name" (Revelation 2:17).

thyatire.bio: City of merchant guilds, hometown of Lydia; Church full of love and service, but tolerating "the woman Jezebel".
thyatire.histoire:
Lydia, "a seller of purple from the city of Thyatira," became the first convert in Europe at Philippi (Acts 16:14).

To the Church at Thyatira, Christ says: "I know your works, your love, your faith, your service, your patience"; "But I have this against you, that you allow the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess, to teach and seduce My servants" (Revelation 2:19-20). To the faithful: "hold fast what you have until I come" (Revelation 2:25).

sardes.bio: Ancient capital of Lydia, wealthy and reputed to be impregnable: A church that had the reputation of being alive, but was dead.
sardes.histoire:
"I know your deeds; you have a reputation of being alive, but you are dead. Wake up! Strengthen what remains and is about to die" (Revelation 3:1-2). The citadel of Sardis, deemed impregnable, had been taken twice by surprise due to a lack of vigilance.

Yet, "You have a few people in Sardis who have not soiled their clothes. They will walk with me, dressed in white" (Revelation 3:4).

philadelphie.bio: A city in Asia at the gateway to Phrygia: a weak but faithful church, before which Christ opened "an open door."
philadelphie.histoire:
Jesus presents Himself as "the One who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts": "Because you have little strength, yet you have kept My word and have not denied My name, I have set before you an open door, which no one can close" (Revelation 3:7-8).

In a city often shaken by earthquakes, the promise resonates: "He who overcomes, I will make him a pillar in the temple of My God, and he shall go out no more" (Revelation 3:12).

laodicee.bio: Wealthy banking city in the Lycus Valley, famous for its fabrics and eye salve: the Church that was "lukewarm."
laodicee.histoire:
Paul asked that his letter to the Colossians be read also "in the church of the Laodiceans" (Colossians 4:16). Epaphras prayed for them (Colossians 4:13).

Christ told them: "I know your works, that you are neither cold nor hot... because you are lukewarm... I will vomit you out of My mouth"; "you say, 'I am rich... and have need of nothing'" (Revelation 3:15-17). He advised them to buy from Him gold, white garments, and eye salve—everything the city boasted of. Then the invitation: "Behold, I stand at the door and knock" (Revelation 3:18-20).

hierapolis.bio: A thermal spring city in the Lycus Valley, neighboring Laodicea and Colossae, where beloved Christians lived under the care of Epaphras.
hierapolis.histoire:
Paul testifies that Epaphras "has a great concern for you, and for those in Laodicea, and for those in Hierapolis" (Colossians 4:13).

Its hot springs, which arrived lukewarm at neighboring Laodicea, perhaps shed light on the image of the "lukewarm" Church in Revelation (Revelation 3:16).

liban.bio: Mountain range north of Israel, famous for its cedars, which were used to build Solomon's temple.
liban.histoire: The righteous will flourish like the palm tree, They will grow like a cedar of Lebanon

syrie.bio: An Aramean kingdom whose capital was Damascus, a neighbor and often enemy of Israel; in New Testament times, a Roman province that included Antioch.
syrie.histoire:
David subdues the Syrians (2 Samuel 8:6). Later, their kings Ben-Hadad and Hazael harass Israel. From Syria comes Naaman, "commander of the king of Syria's army," a leper healed at the Jordan (2 Kings 5:1, 14). King Rezin allies with Israel against Judah (Isaiah 7:1).

In Jesus' time, "Quirinius was governor of Syria" (Luke 2:2), and Jesus' fame spreads "throughout all Syria" (Matthew 4:24). Paul is converted there, near Damascus, and begins his ministry at Antioch (Acts 9; 11:25–26; Galatians 1:21).

hamath.bio: Royal city in Syria on the Orontes River; "the entrance of Hamath" marked the ideal northern border of Israel.
hamath.histoire:
The spies explore the land "by way of Hamath" (Numbers 13:21); Solomon celebrates the feast with Israel "from the vicinity of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt" (1 Kings 8:65). Jeroboam II restored this border (2 Kings 14:25).

After the fall of Samaria, the Assyrian brings people "from Hamath and Sepharvaim" to repopulate the land (2 Kings 17:24) — the origin of the Samaritans. Amos announces a nation that will oppress Israel "from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of the Desert" (Amos 6:14).

seir.bio: A mountainous region of Edom, southeast of the Dead Sea, where Esau settled.
seir.histoire:
"Esau settled in the mountain region of Seir. Esau is Edom" (Genesis 36:8). It was toward Seir that Jacob sent messengers before reuniting with his brother (Genesis 32:3).

God commanded Israel not to attack the sons of Esau: "Do not harass them […] I have given the mountain of Seir as a possession to Esau" (Deuteronomy 2:5). Ezekiel prophesied against "the mountain of Seir" for its hatred toward Israel (Ezekiel 35).

hesbon.bio: Capital of Sihon, king of the Amorites, east of the Jordan River; its conquest opened Transjordan to Israel.
hesbon.histoire:
Israel asks to pass peacefully through Sihon's territory; "But Sihon king of Heshbon would not let us pass through his land" (Deuteronomy 2:30). He is defeated, and Israel settles in his cities (Numbers 21:21-25).

The city is assigned to Reuben and then to the Levites (Joshua 13:17; 21:39). Its pools are mentioned in the Song of Songs: "Your eyes are like the pools of Heshbon" (Song of Songs 7:5).

paran.bio: A vast desert in northern Sinai, where Ishmael lived and where Israel wandered; from there the twelve spies departed.
paran.histoire:
Ishmael, cast out with Hagar, "dwelt in the Wilderness of Paran" (Genesis 21:21). Israel camps there after Hazeroth (Numbers 12:16), and Moses sends the spies from there to explore Canaan (Numbers 13:3).

David withdraws there after Samuel's death (1 Samuel 25:1). The prophet Habakkuk sees God coming as at Sinai: "God comes from Teman, The Holy One from Mount Paran" (Habakkuk 3:3).

succoth.bio: "Booths" (or "Tabernacles"): a city in the Jordan Valley where Jacob settled after reuniting with Esau; its leaders refused bread to Gideon.
succoth.histoire:
"Jacob journeyed to Succoth. He built himself a house, and made booths for his livestock. Therefore the name of the place is called Succoth" (Genesis 33:17).

Gideon, pursuing the kings of Midian, asks the people of Succoth for bread for his exhausted men; the leaders of Succoth mock him: "Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your possession?" (Judges 8:5-6). He will punish them upon his return (Judges 8:16). Solomon has bronze objects for the temple cast there (1 Kings 7:46). Do not confuse with Succoth in Egypt, the first station of the Exodus (Exodus 12:37).

thirtsa.bio: The first capital of the northern kingdom, from Jeroboam until Omri, who left it to found Samaria.
thirtsa.histoire:
Jeroboam's wife, returning from the prophet Ahijah, "arrived at Tirzah; and as she was stepping over the threshold of the house, the child died" (1 Kings 14:17). Baasha, Elah, and Zimri reign there.

"Zimri reigned seven days in Tirzah"; besieged by Omri, he "withdrew into the citadel of the royal house, and burned the royal house over him" (1 Kings 16:15-18). Omri then transfers the capital to Samaria (1 Kings 16:23-24). Its beauty was proverbial: "You are lovely, my darling, like Tirzah" (Song of Songs 6:4).

rabba.bio: Capital of the Ammonites (present-day Amman), besieged by Joab; it was during this siege that Uriah was sent to his death.
rabba.histoire:
"David sent Joab with his servants and all Israel to destroy the sons of Ammon and to besiege Rabbah. But David remained in Jerusalem" (2 Samuel 11:1). It was then that he saw Bathsheba; and it was at the walls of Rabbah that Uriah was placed "in the forefront of the fiercest battle" (2 Samuel 11:15-17).

Joab takes "the city of waters" and calls David for the final victory; the crown of the king of Ammon is placed on his head (2 Samuel 12:26-30). The prophets will later announce its judgment (Jeremiah 49:2; Amos 1:14).

tekoa.bio: A village in the hills of Judah, south of Bethlehem, on the edge of the wilderness: homeland of the prophet Amos and of the wise woman sent by Joab.
tekoa.histoire:
Joab has a "wise woman" sought there to speak to David on behalf of Absalom (2 Samuel 14:2). Jehoshaphat leads his people there before the victory where the singers march in front (2 Chronicles 20:20-21).

Above all, it is the village of Amos: "The words of Amos, one of the shepherds of Tekoa" (Amos 1:1). A farmer from the countryside of Judah sent to cry out for justice in the heart of the northern kingdom.

guezer.bio: A strategic Canaanite city between the coast and Jerusalem, given as a dowry by Pharaoh to his daughter, Solomon's wife.
guezer.histoire:
The Canaanites of Gezer lived for a long time among the Ephraimites (Joshua 16:10). David defeated the Philistines "as far as Gezer" (2 Samuel 5:25).

"Pharaoh king of Egypt had come up and taken Gezer and burned it […] Then he gave it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife." Solomon rebuilt it (1 Kings 9:16-17). Excavations there have uncovered a monumental gate from that era, similar to those at Hazor and Megiddo.

beth-horon.bio: Two villages (upper and lower) commanding the ascent from the coastal plain to Jerusalem; the site of Joshua's victory in a hailstorm.
beth-horon.histoire:
Israel pursues the five Amorite kings "on the road that goes up to Beth-Horon"; "as they fled before Israel... the Lord threw large hailstones down on them from heaven" — more were killed by the hailstones than by the sword (Joshua 10:10-11). On that day the sun stood still (Joshua 10:12-13).

Solomon fortified "Lower Beth-Horon" (1 Kings 9:17): the road remained a decisive military passage for centuries.

hinnom.bio: Valley south of Jerusalem where children were sacrificed to Molech; its name, Gehenna, became the image of final judgment.
hinnom.histoire:
Idolatrous kings made their children pass through the fire there. Jeremiah denounces: "They have built the high places of Topheth in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom, to burn their sons and daughters in the fire: a thing I did not command" (Jeremiah 7:31). Josiah defiles Topheth to end this practice (2 Kings 23:10).

The Hebrew name "Valley of Hinnom" becomes in Greek "Gehenna." Jesus uses it to speak of judgment: "whoever says to him, 'You fool!' shall be in danger of hell fire" (Matthew 5:22). A place of abomination became the name of the place of perdition.

tsorea.bio: A town in the Shephelah, the homeland of Manoah and his son Samson; the Spirit of the Lord began to stir Samson between Zorah and Eshtaol.
tsorea.histoire:
"There was a certain man from Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah. And his wife was barren" (Judges 13:2). The angel of the Lord announces the birth of Samson.

"Then the Spirit of the Lord began to stir him at Mahaneh-Dan, between Zorah and Eshtaol" (Judges 13:25). It is there also that he will be buried, in the tomb of his father (Judges 16:31).

ajalon.bio: Valley west of Gibeon, where the moon stopped at Joshua's command.
ajalon.histoire:
On the day of the battle against the five kings, Joshua speaks to the Lord: "Sun, stand still over Gibeon, And moon, in the Valley of Aijalon!" And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped in its course" (Joshua 10:12-13).

"There has never been a day like it before or since, when the Lord listened to the voice of a man" (Joshua 10:14). Later, Jonathan will pursue the Philistines there (1 Samuel 14:31).

jabes-galaad.bio: City of Gilead delivered by Saul; grateful for his rescue, its inhabitants risked their lives to give him a proper burial.
jabes-galaad.histoire:
Besieged by Nahash the Ammonite, who threatens to gouge out the right eye of its inhabitants, Jabesh calls for help; Saul gathers Israel and delivers the city — his first victory (1 Samuel 11:1-11).

Forty years later, when the Philistines expose Saul's body at Beth-shan, "all the valiant men arose and went all night, and took the corpse of Saul from the wall of Beth-shan"; they bury it under the tamarisk tree and fast for seven days (1 Samuel 31:11-13). David will bless them for this faithfulness (2 Samuel 2:5).

aphek.bio: City in the coastal plain from which the Philistines set out to fight Israel; the ark was captured there.
aphek.histoire:
"Now Israel went out to battle against the Philistines [...] They encamped by Ebenezer, and the Philistines encamped at Aphek" (1 Samuel 4:1). Israel brings the ark as a good luck charm; it is captured, and Hophni and Phinehas die (1 Samuel 4:3-11).

Later, the Philistines gather there before the battle of Gilboa, and send David away from their army (1 Samuel 29:1-11). God will not be used as a talisman.

sittim.bio: Israel's last camp in the plains of Moab before crossing the Jordan: the place of the fall of Baal-Peor and the departure of the spies.
sittim.histoire:
"Israel dwelt in Shittim; and the people began to commit harlotry with the daughters of Moab"; "Israel joined himself to Baal-Peor" — a trap advised by Balaam (Numbers 25:1-3; 31:16).

Yet it was from there that "Joshua the son of Nun sent two men as spies secretly from Shittim" to Jericho, to Rahab's house (Joshua 2:1). Micah will invite you to remember the path "from Shittim to Gilgal," that of God's faithfulness (Micah 6:5).

etsjon-gueber.bio: A port at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, from which Solomon's ships departed for Ophir.
etsjon-gueber.histoire:
A stop on the Exodus (Numbers 33:35). "King Solomon built ships at Ezion-Geber, near Eloth, on the shores of the Red Sea"; with the sailors of Hiram, they brought back from Ophir "four hundred and twenty talents" of gold (1 Kings 9:26-28).

Jehoshaphat wanted to revive this glory, "but he did not go, because the ships were wrecked at Ezion-Geber" (1 Kings 22:49)—a judgment for his alliance with Ahaziah, according to Chronicles (2 Chronicles 20:37).

desert-sin.bio: Desert between Elim and Sinai where God gave Israel quail and manna.
desert-sin.histoire:
"The whole congregation of the children of Israel departed from Elim, and they came to the Desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai"; the people complain, longing for the pots of Egypt (Exodus 16:1-3).

In the evening come the quail; in the morning, "something fine, like frost on the ground." "What is it?" — "It is the bread which the Lord gives you for food" (Exodus 16:13-15). Jesus will present Himself as the true bread that comes down from heaven (John 6:31-35).

macpela.bio: A cave near Hebron purchased by Abraham from Ephron the Hittite: the burial place of the patriarchs and their wives.
macpela.histoire:
Abraham buried Sarah there, "in the cave of the field of Machpelah, before Mamre, which is Hebron"; "The field and the cave that is in it were deeded to Abraham as a possession for a burial place" (Genesis 23:19–20).

Dying Jacob asks to be laid to rest there: "There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife; there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried Leah" (Genesis 49:31). The only land the patriarchs possessed in Canaan was a tomb: a declaration of faith in God's promise.

micmasch.bio: Village of Benjamin opposite Geba, separated by a ravine; Jonathan and his armor-bearer attacked the Philistine garrison there alone.
micmasch.histoire:
"A garrison of the Philistines stationed themselves at the pass of Michmash" (1 Samuel 13:23). Between two rocky crags, Jonathan said to his armor-bearer: "Nothing can hinder the Lord from saving by many or by few" (1 Samuel 14:4-6).

They climbed up "using their hands and feet"; divine panic seized the Philistine camp, and Israel won the victory (1 Samuel 14:13-15, 23). The faith of one man can move an entire people.

beth-schean.bio: A fortified city at the crossroads of the Jezreel Valley and the Jordan Valley; the Philistines displayed Saul's body there.
beth-schean.histoire:
Manasseh could not drive out the Canaanites there (Judges 1:27). After Gilboa, the Philistines "put his armor in the temple of the Ashtoreths, and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shean" (1 Samuel 31:10).

The men of Jabesh came by night to recover the bodies (1 Samuel 31:12). In Jesus' time, the city, now called Scythopolis, was the principal city of the Decapolis.

sunem.bio: Village in the plain of Jezreel: camp of the Philistines before Gilboa, birthplace of the Shunammite woman who welcomed Elisha, and of Abishag.
sunem.histoire:
The Philistines "came and encamped in Shunem; and Saul gathered all Israel together, and they encamped at Gilboa" (1 Samuel 28:4).

"One day Elisha went to Shunem. Now there was a prominent woman there" who said to her husband, "Please, let us make a small upper room on the wall […] that he may turn in there whenever he comes to us" (2 Kings 4:8-10). Elisha announces to her that she will have a son, whom he will later raise from the dead (2 Kings 4:16, 32-37). Abishag, who cared for David, was also from there (1 Kings 1:3).

ophir.bio: A distant land, famous for its gold, from which the fleets of Solomon and Hiram brought back riches; its location remains unknown.
ophir.histoire:
Solomon's ships "went to Ophir and brought back gold, four hundred and twenty talents" (1 Kings 9:28); they also brought back algum wood and precious stones (1 Kings 10:11).

The "gold of Ophir" becomes synonymous with the purest gold (Psalms 45:10; Job 28:16). But Job reminds us that wisdom is worth more than all the gold of Ophir (Job 28:12-16). Arabia, East Africa, or India have been proposed, but nothing is certain.

lodebar.bio: A town in Gilead where Mephibosheth, the disabled son of Jonathan, lived in hiding before David called him to his table.
lodebar.histoire:
David asks: "Is there not still someone of the house of Saul, that I may show him the kindness of God?" Ziba answers that a son of Jonathan, "lame in his feet," lives "in the house of Makir the son of Ammiel, in Lo Debar" (2 Samuel 9:3-4).

David sends for him and has him eat at his table "as one of the king's sons" (2 Samuel 9:5, 11). From Lo Debar—whose name evokes a place without pasture—to the king's table: an image of grace.

kebar.bio: A canal near Babylon where the deported people of Judah lived; Ezekiel had his visions of God's glory there.
kebar.histoire:
"As I was among the captives by the River Kebar, the heavens were opened and I saw visions of God"; "the word of the Lord came to Ezekiel […] in the land of the Chaldeans, by the River Kebar" (Ezekiel 1:1-3).

Far from the temple, in exile, God reveals Himself in His glory upon a chariot of cherubim and wheels. His presence is not confined to Jerusalem: He comes to His people where they are.

ramses.bio: Warehouse city in the Nile delta built by the Hebrew slaves; the starting point of the Exodus.
ramses.histoire:
Joseph settled his family "in the best part of the land, in the region of Rameses" (Genesis 47:11). Later, the enslaved Israelites built "the cities of Pithom and Rameses, to serve as storehouses for Pharaoh" (Exodus 1:11).

On the night of Passover, "The children of Israel departed from Rameses for Succoth, about six hundred thousand men on foot, besides children" (Exodus 12:37). The bricks of slavery remained behind them.

mer-morte.bio: A salt lake at the lowest point on earth, called in the Bible the "Salt Sea" or "Sea of the Arabah"; Ezekiel announces its healing.
mer-morte.histoire:
The kings of the plain gathered "in the Valley of Siddim, which is the Salt Sea" (Genesis 14:3). When crossing the Jordan, the waters "which flowed down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off" (Joshua 3:16).

Ezekiel sees a river flowing out from the temple and descending toward it: its waters become fresh, and fishermen stand on its shores from En-Gedi to En-Eglaim (Ezekiel 47:8-10). Where the life of God comes, even the dead sea comes alive.

euphrate.histoire: It is the fourth river flowing out of Eden (Genesis 2:14). God promises to Abram:

nil.bio: River of Egypt, source of its wealth, often called "the river"; Moses was saved in it, and the first plague turned its water into blood.
nil.histoire:
In Exodus, it is simply "the river": Pharaoh has Hebrew boys thrown into it, and on its banks the daughter of Pharaoh finds and rescues Moses (Exodus 1:22; 2:3-6). The first plague turns its waters into blood (Exodus 7:20).

The prophets name it to announce God's judgment on Egypt, which believed itself strong because of its river (Jeremiah 46:7-8; Ezekiel 29:3).

magdala.bio: A fishing village on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee, the birthplace of Mary Magdalene; likely the Magadan of the Gospels.
magdala.histoire:
Mary was born there: "Mary, called Magdalene, out of whom went seven demons" (Luke 8:2). She would be the first witness of the Risen Christ (John 20:16-18).

After the feeding of the four thousand, Jesus came "into the region of Magadan" (Matthew 15:39)—Mark mentions Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10); many locate these near Magdala. Excavations there uncovered a first-century synagogue.

asie.bio: Roman province in western Asia Minor, with Ephesus as its capital: Paul preached there for two years, and the seven churches of Revelation were located there.
asie.histoire:
Jews from Asia were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:9). The Holy Spirit first prevented Paul from proclaiming the word there (Acts 16:6); later, his teaching in Ephesus lasted two years, "so that all who lived in Asia, both Jews and Greeks, heard the word of the Lord" (Acts 19:10).

John addresses the Revelation "to the seven churches that are in Asia" (Revelation 1:4). But Paul would also suffer abandonment there (2 Timothy 1:15).

italie.bio: Peninsula at the heart of the Roman Empire, destination of Paul's final journey.
italie.histoire:
Aquila and Priscilla arrived there, having been driven out of Rome (Acts 18:2). "And when it was decided that we should sail to Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to one named Julius, a centurion" (Acts 27:1): the voyage, despite the shipwreck, ended in Rome.

The letter to the Hebrews closes with these words: "Those from Italy greet you" (Hebrews 13:24)—a sign that the Gospel had taken root there.

grece.bio: Country of the Greeks (Macedonia and Achaia), where Paul established churches in Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, and Corinth.
grece.histoire:
After the uproar in Ephesus, Paul traveled through Macedonia, "Then he went into Greece, where he spent three months" (Acts 20:2-3); a plot forced him to leave again through Macedonia. It was likely then that he wrote his epistle to the Romans, from Corinth.

The Gospel there encountered Greek philosophy (Acts 17:18-34); Paul would say: "Greeks seek wisdom: but we preach Christ crucified" (1 Corinthians 1:22-23).

espagne.bio: The western edge of the known world, which Paul hoped to evangelize by passing through Rome.
espagne.histoire:
Paul preached from Jerusalem all the way to Illyricum; he aimed even further: "I hope to see you in passing when I go to Spain"; "I will go to Spain and pass by you" (Romans 15:24, 28).

The New Testament does not say whether he went there; some ancient writers affirm it. His missionary ambition remains a model: to proclaim Christ where His name has not yet been named (Romans 15:20).

arabie.bio: A desert region south and east of Israel; Paul withdrew there after his conversion, and Paul locates Mount Sinai there.
arabie.histoire:
The kings of Arabia bring gold to Solomon (1 Kings 10:15). Arabs are present at Pentecost (Acts 2:11).

After his conversion, Paul did not go immediately to Jerusalem: "I went away into Arabia. Then I returned again to Damascus" (Galatians 1:17). In his allegory, he writes: "Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia" (Galatians 4:25).

paddan-aram.bio: Region of Upper Mesopotamia around Haran, the birthplace of Abraham's family; Isaac and Jacob took their wives there.
paddan-aram.histoire:
Rebekah is "the daughter of Bethuel the Aramean, of Paddan-Aram" (Genesis 25:20). Isaac sends Jacob: "Arise, go to Paddan-Aram, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's father, and take a wife from there" (Genesis 28:2).

Jacob returns twenty years later with his family and his livestock "which he had acquired in Paddan-Aram" (Genesis 31:18), and camps "in peace" before Shechem (Genesis 33:18).

gueschur.bio: A small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee, the homeland of Absalom's mother, where he took refuge for three years.
gueschur.histoire:
Maacah, Absalom's mother, was "the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur" (2 Samuel 3:3). After the murder of Amnon, "Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihur, king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son every day" (2 Samuel 13:37).

"Absalom remained three years in Geshur" (2 Samuel 13:38), until Joab had him brought back (2 Samuel 14:23).

guihon.bio: Jerusalem's main water source, at the foot of the City of David: Solomon was anointed king there, and Hezekiah diverted its waters through a tunnel.
guihon.histoire:
To thwart Adonijah, David ordered: "Have Solomon my son ride on my mule, and bring him down to Gihon. There, Priest Zadok and Prophet Nathan will anoint him king over Israel" (1 Kings 1:33-34).

Before the Assyrian invasion, Hezekiah "blocked the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and channeled them down to the west side of the City of David" (2 Chronicles 32:30): Hezekiah's tunnel, still visible today, leads to the Pool of Siloam. Do not confuse with the Gihon River of Eden (Genesis 2:13).

lachai-roi.bio: A well in the southern desert where the Angel of the Lord found Hagar fleeing; she named God there
lachai-roi.histoire: Hagar flees the harshness of Sarai. The Angel of the Lord finds her by a spring and announces the birth of Ishmael.

hatseroth.bio: Desert station after Kibroth-Hattaavah, where Miriam was struck with leprosy for speaking against Moses.
hatseroth.histoire:
"And the people journeyed from Kibroth-Hattaavah to Hazeroth, and they stayed at Hazeroth" (Numbers 11:35). There, "Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses"; God took the defense of His servant, and "Miriam became leprous, as white as snow" (Numbers 12:1, 10).

Moses intercedes for her; she is confined seven days outside the camp, "and the people did not journey on until Miriam was brought back in" (Numbers 12:13-15).

kibroth-hattaava.bio: "Graves of Craving": a wilderness place where the people, gorged on quail, were struck down for their lust.
kibroth-hattaava.histoire:
Tired of manna, the people weep, demanding meat. God sends quail in abundance; "While the meat was still between their teeth, before it was chewed, the anger of the Lord was aroused against the people" (Numbers 11:33).

"The name of that place was called Kibroth Hattaavah, because there they buried the people who had yielded to craving" (Numbers 11:34). The psalmist sums it up: "He gave them what they asked for, but sent a wasting disease upon them" (Psalm 106:15).

perse.bio: Empire that succeeded Babylon: its kings Cyrus, Darius, Ahasuerus, and Artaxerxes allowed the return and rebuilding of Jerusalem.
perse.histoire:
"In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the Lord by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus" (Ezra 1:1-2); his decree allowed the return and rebuilding of the temple.

The book of Esther takes place at the Persian court in Susa (Esther 1:2-3), and Daniel lived there under Darius (Daniel 6). Nehemiah, the king's cupbearer, obtained permission from him to rebuild the walls (Nehemiah 2:1-8). God holds the hearts of kings.
